findings.title: Walk-forward analysis does not actually fit per-window parameters, and several of its reported figures are hardcoded placeholders
findings.evidence: Confirmed by reading run_walk_forward_analysis: self._get_best_parameters(self._optimization_history) was called ONCE before the loop and the resulting fixed parameter set was evaluated on every window's train AND test period -- a fixed strategy re-run on rolling windows, not walk-forward analysis. Investigating this surfaced a more fundamental, previously untracked defect (filed and fixed separately as BT-02, commit 29e319d): BacktestRuntime.run_backtest never used start_date/end_date to select data at all, so every window's backtest ran on byte-identical 'most recent bars' regardless of its own dates, which would have made even a correct per-window fit numerically meaningless. Fixed run_walk_forward_analysis (depends on BT-02) by adding _optimize_on_window: a copy of the caller's config with parameters[start_date/end_date] overridden to the window's own train period, dispatched through the same search method (_grid_search/_random_search/_bayesian_optimization/_genetic_algorithm) the caller chose, with the window's own trials kept OUT of self._optimization_history so one window cannot leak into another's fit or into the whole-period benchmark (the OPT-03-shaped cross-contamination, reintroduced inside one engine instance if not guarded against). Also fixed the three hardcoded report figures the finding names: _run_buy_hold_benchmark (was the literal total_return_pct=50.0/sharpe_ratio=1.0/max_drawdown=20.0 for every call) now fetches the strategy's own symbol/timeframe over the same window via BT-02's since_ms/until_ms and computes all three from the closes actually fetched, reporting computed=False/None rather than a fabricated number when the fetch fails; _calculate_beta (was the literal 1.0) now computes cov(strategy_returns, benchmark_returns)/var(benchmark_returns) from both backtests' own return series, returning None rather than 0.0/1.0 when there are too few paired observations or the benchmark has zero variance; complexity score (was the literal 0.8) now scales with the strategy's own tunable-parameter count (1.0 at zero parameters, 0.0 at a documented 10-parameter cap), matching the 'higher is better' convention every other component of the weighted score already uses. New tests/test_opt02_walk_forward_fits_per_window_and_report_figures_are_real.py (10 tests) against a deterministic, parameter- and window-dependent fake backtest_runtime: different windows provably choose different winning parameters (not merely 'ran without crashing'); the fitted parameters carry unchanged from train to test; two windows' calls carry two different date ranges (the BT-02 dependency, checked directly); buy & hold computes a real return/Sharpe/drawdown from a controlled price series and reports not-computed on empty data; beta computes exactly (2.0 for a strategy whose returns are exactly 2x the benchmark's) and is None on zero variance or too few observations; alpha/beta are both None together when the benchmark could not be measured; complexity varies from 1.0 to 0.0 with parameter count. One real bug the test suite itself caught before commit: the first _calculate_beta draft mixed np.cov's sample covariance (ddof=1) with np.var's population variance (ddof=0), scaling every beta by N/(N-1) for no reason -- caught because the exactly-2.0 test came back 2.4, fixed by aligning both to ddof=1. Full regression: test_save_performs_no_backtest.py + test_opt01_optimize_config_field_name.py + test_strategy_analysis_endpoint_accuracy.py + test_opt03_optimization_engine_is_not_a_shared_singleton.py + test_bt02_backtest_honors_requested_date_range.py (100 passed, 1 pre-existing unrelated import-pin failure confirmed via git-stash comparison to predate this change entirely); test_validation_sweep.py (373 passed, 2 skipped).
findings.remaining_action: None identified at the code level for the two defects this finding names. The fix credits two commits: 29e319d (BT-02, the data-range prerequisite) and be82e3d (this finding's own per-window fitting and report-figure fixes). The validation_method field on OptimizationConfig (TIME_SERIES_CV/BLOCKED_CV/ROLLING_VALIDATION/WALK_FORWARD) is still read only for a log line in run_walk_forward_analysis and does not select a different windowing or fitting strategy -- that is a separate, smaller gap this pass did not scope in, since the finding's own title and remaining_action named only the per-window fitting and the hardcoded figures.

findings.title: Optimization engine is a process-wide singleton that leaks one tenant's best parameters into another tenant's walk-forward/sensitivity results
findings.evidence: Confirmed by reading backend_app/backend/optimization_engine.py::get_optimization_engine and backend_app/backend/backtest_runtime.py::get_backtest_runtime: both are plain module-level singletons (global _x; if _x is None: _x = X(); return _x). Grepped every call site in the repo (exactly two): backend_app/routers/strategy_operations.py's POST /strategies/{id}/optimize and backend_app/routers/strategies.py's POST /walk-forward both called them directly, so every tenant's call shared the SAME OptimizationEngine instance and therefore the SAME _optimization_history list -- every one of run_walk_forward_analysis/run_sensitivity_analysis/run_monte_carlo_simulation/run_benchmark_comparison reads its 'best parameters' back via self._get_best_parameters(self._optimization_history), so a tenant whose call overlapped or ran back-to-back with another tenant's in the same process could have had that tenant's optimization results folded into their own. The shared backtest_runtime singleton compounded it: constructed once with the class defaults ($10,000 capital, 0.1% fees, 0.05% slippage), so both endpoints' submitted capital/fee/slippage/risk fields were accepted and then silently ignored -- confirmed this is the EXACT SAME bug class backend_app/routers/strategy_operations.py::_backtest_runtime_for's own docstring already names and fixes for the plain (non-optimization) backtest endpoint (that fix's own comment explicitly calls out get_backtest_runtime() by name as the thing it is NOT calling, for this exact reason) -- the optimize/walk-forward endpoints had simply not received the same fix. Fixed both call sites the same way: new backend_app/routers/strategy_operations.py::_optimization_engine_for(body) constructs a fresh OptimizationEngine() and a fresh BacktestRuntime(...) (from the request's own initial_capital/commission/slippage/risk_per_trade/max_drawdown/daily_loss_limit fields) per request; backend_app/routers/strategies.py's /walk-forward closure does the equivalent inline, reusing the values already read into its OptimizationConfig (so no duplicate payload.get() calls). get_optimization_engine()/get_backtest_runtime() themselves are UNCHANGED -- kept, not deleted, since tests/test_save_performs_no_backtest.py's Requirement-22.1 tripwire still needs to patch get_backtest_runtime by name in both router modules to prove a strategy SAVE never starts a backtest. Removed a redundant local re-import of OptimizationEngine/BacktestRuntime inside /walk-forward's closure that would otherwise have shadowed the module-level names and silently defeated test patching at the new injection points. New tests/test_opt03_optimization_engine_is_not_a_shared_singleton.py (6 tests, direct construction, no mocking -- mirrors tests/test_task_6_1_backtest_execute.py's existing proof pattern for the sibling bug): two calls return two different engine instances with independent _optimization_history (the concrete cross-tenant leak, reproduced then shown closed); the runtime carries the SUBMITTED capital/fee/slippage/risk values, not the class defaults; two different configurations produce two differently-configured runtimes; the engine returned is wired to THIS call's own runtime; the singleton accessors themselves are unchanged and still work (negative control). Updated tests/test_strategy_analysis_endpoint_accuracy.py's two walk-forward tests, which mocked get_optimization_engine/get_backtest_runtime by name, to patch the new injection points (OptimizationEngine/BacktestRuntime class constructors) instead -- both still pass. Full regression (opt03 + endpoint_accuracy + backtest_execute + validation_sweep + route_contract + router_registration_completeness, 441 tests) clean except the 2 unrelated pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session; tests/test_save_performs_no_backtest.py's pre-existing 10 failed/10 errored (an unrelated environment gap, confirmed identical on the pre-change baseline via git stash) are untouched by this fix.
findings.remaining_action: This closes the isolation half (OPT-03's own title and remediation note) for both call sites that exist. NOT attempted: OPT-02's separate, deeper finding that walk-forward analysis does not actually fit per-window parameters and reports several hardcoded placeholder figures -- a correctness question about the ALGORITHM, independent of this finding's isolation question, and out of this fix's scope.

findings.title: The dedicated websocket service (ws_server.py) is completely broken; a terraform apply of the existing ALB fix would take down all realtime
findings.evidence: INVESTIGATED THIS SESSION, deliberately NOT fixed. Confirmed the 'completely broken' half precisely: backend/event_publisher.py::EventPublisher (publish_order_filled/publish_position_updated/publish_pnl_update/etc, writing to Redis channels 'orders', 'positions', 'pnl', 'portfolio', 'signals', 'market_data', 'alerts', 'circuit_breaker') is never instantiated or called anywhere outside its own defining module (grepped the whole backend_app/ tree for EventPublisher()/get_event_publisher/publish_order_filled/publish_position_updated/publish_pnl_update -- zero hits outside event_publisher.py itself). backend/ws_server.py subscribes to exactly those channels and broadcasts whatever it receives to connected clients -- so it is wired correctly to a Redis bus that nothing in the real order/position/pnl code path ever publishes to. The REAL in-process realtime mechanism, confirmed by grep, is api_ws/ws_manager.py::ConnectionManager, used directly by paper_channel.py, paper_session_service.py, core/realtime_sync.py and routers/library.py -- an entirely separate, in-process path from the dedicated ws_server.py microservice. backend/dag_event_loop.py's own comment (task 14.2/14.3, Requirement 23.7) confirms this independently and from the OTHER direction: it documents that this method used to publish a signal-status frame via EventPublisher.publish_signal_trace, that ws_server.py's _redis_listener 'fans straight back out' under the Signal_Trace flat-broadcast channel, that this is an UNAUTHORISED-BROADCAST pattern Requirement 23.7 forbids (the channel 'names no owner and no deployment, so its subscribers are never authorised against the resource the frame describes'), and that task 14.2 REPLACED this emission with a per-deployment, authorised channel instead. Terraform confirms the deployment side is real, not just app-level drift: terraform/alb.tf defines aws_lb_target_group.websocket (port 8002, matching ws_server.py's own WS_SERVER_PORT) and aws_lb_listener_rule.websocket_rule (path /ws/*, priority 90); terraform/ecs.tf defines a full aws_ecs_task_definition.websocket + aws_ecs_service.websocket pointed at that target group. No .github/workflows reference exists to build or push the vyomquant-websocket image, consistent with this being built but never actually deployed through the current CI pipeline. THE REASON NEITHER OPTION WAS TAKEN: tests/test_task_14_3_legacy_broadcast_retired.py -- the test suite task 14.3 itself wrote when it performed the Requirement 23.7 replacement described above -- contains test_the_dedicated_ws_server_still_subscribes_to_it, which asserts the legacy channel remains in ws_server.CHANNELS, with the comment 'ws_server.py's fanout is the "any other consumer" the task protects.' This is a DELIBERATE, DOCUMENTED decision from that earlier task: it explicitly chose to leave ws_server.py and EventPublisher in place, unconnected to the new per-deployment channels, rather than delete them, on the stated reasoning that something outside that task's own scope ('any other consumer this spec does not cover') might still need the legacy flat-broadcast channel to exist. tests/test_websocket_auth_fail_closed.py separately exercises ws_server.py's OWN FastAPI app directly (4 tests: /ws/public/{channel} and /ws/{tenant_id} both fail-closed on no/invalid/mismatched token) -- so the SERVER's own authentication is itself already correct and tested, which rules out 'the server's auth is the broken part'. Deleting ws_server.py now would directly contradict task 14.3's own explicit decision without visibility into what that 'any other consumer' might be, and deleting it would break 6 existing, passing tests across two files that specifically pin its continued existence. Repairing it (wiring EventPublisher into the real order/position/pnl code paths) would mean duplicating what ConnectionManager already does in-process, for unclear benefit, and is exactly the kind of cross-cutting change to the live order-execution code path this session has consistently declined to improvise without a clearer mandate. RESOLVED this session (commits c02b2bf, ba01c2c). This entry's own remaining_action named the exact open question: 'confirm with whoever owns this area whether any other consumer of the legacy flat-broadcast channel still exists in production'. Delegated a dedicated investigation (full code search, the frontend's own websocket client, this repo's own architecture docs, git history) rather than guessing, with the product owner's explicit authorization to decide based on the findings. Verdict: zero evidence of any consumer, internal or external, that code search can surface -- zero production callers of EventPublisher's own publish_* methods anywhere in the backend; the frontend (algo22-terminal)'s websocket client exclusively targets api_ws/ws_routes.py's endpoints, never ws_server.py's; docs/history/END_TO_END_DATAFLOW_MAP.md and ROOT_CAUSE_VERIFICATION.md already record ws_server.py as unreachable through the real deployment's public URL; the one test that named 'any other consumer' as its reason to exist (test_task_14_3_legacy_broadcast_retired.py) was pointing at ws_server.py's own fanout circularly, not at anything external. Deleted ws_server.py, event_publisher.py's Dockerfile (Dockerfile.websocket), and the six tests that exercised ws_server.py's own endpoints directly across two test files, updating both to explain why. event_publisher.py's own module file is deliberately KEPT (no production caller either, but a regression suite still uses it as a mock/tripwire target, and it carries no deployed infrastructure of its own -- unlike ws_server.py, which had its own ECS task/ALB target group). Verified: full app import succeeds end to end; regression across every directly and indirectly affected test file (618 passed, 2 skipped, 0 failed).
findings.remaining_action: DONE. The code-level half was already complete: ws_server.py, its Dockerfile and the six tests that pinned its existence as 'any other consumer' were deleted, confirmed dead by a dedicated investigation. The remaining risk this entry's title named -- a terraform apply of these resources taking down real traffic -- is now resolved with real evidence, not a guess: `elbv2 DescribeTargetGroups` and `DescribeListeners` on the real `vyomquant-alb` (ap-southeast-1, live scoped CI credential) show only `vyomquant-api-tg` and `vyomquant-web-tg` exist, and the ALB has exactly one listener (HTTP:80) with a single default action forwarding everything to `vyomquant-api-tg` -- no websocket target group, no `/ws/*` listener rule, has ever been applied to this account. Nothing could have had live traffic because the resources were never created. Also checked (via CloudFront's real distribution config, EEOXECPHQ8SR0) that `/ws/*` traffic is actually routed by CloudFront's own cache behavior to the ALB origin, which (with no dedicated listener rule) falls through to the default action and is served by the API service's in-process ConnectionManager -- confirming this effort's own prior finding about the real realtime mechanism from the other direction. Removed terraform/alb.tf's `aws_lb_target_group.websocket`/`aws_lb_listener_rule.websocket_rule`, terraform/ecs.tf's `aws_ecs_task_definition.websocket`/`aws_ecs_service.websocket`, and terraform/outputs.tf's `websocket_endpoint` output (commit e1e6e0c) -- confirmed via grep that nothing else in terraform or the test suite referenced them. `terraform validate` passes; no `terraform apply` was needed or run, since these resources never existed in AWS to begin with (there is nothing for a plan to destroy). INF-01's own ALB health-check fix (also now applied and verified against real production, see INF-01's entry) is unaffected -- it only ever touched the API target group, which this entry's cleanup did not change.

findings.title: Per-deployment execution-config limits (notional cap, position cap, slippage tolerance) are validated and stored but no execution path reads them
findings.evidence: SECOND PASS (this session): real enforcement for two of the five fields, replacing the prior pass's blanket deploy-time refusal for those two. max_order_notional and max_open_positions are now genuinely consulted by master_executor.evaluate_deployment_execution_limits, called from BotRunner._inner_loop immediately before the risk-manager check on every tick -- the real order-construction path for both paper and live deployments. max_order_notional REFUSES (does not clamp) an order whose notional exceeds the deployment's own cap, the same disposition ExecutionGuard._validate_order_size already applies for its own process-wide ceiling. max_open_positions refuses opening a new position once the deployment already holds this many; measured against the architecture (one BotRunner is one (user, symbol, strategy) and deployment_binding.resolve_binding_market's own MARKET_AMBIGUOUS gate forbids more than one market per version, so a deployment can hold at most ONE net position) this cap genuinely binds only at max_open_positions=0 -- stated plainly in the function's own docstring and in this entry rather than oversold. slippage_tolerance_bps, order_timeout_seconds and retry_policy remain refused (UNENFORCED_EXECUTION_CONFIG_FIELDS): this platform's order path (ExecutionEngine.execute_with_idempotency / exchange_executor.place_order, market orders only per deployment_runtime.EXECUTABLE_ORDER_TYPES) has no slippage-tolerance check, no per-order timeout and no retry policy for a value to apply to, so wiring them would have been cosmetic. normalise_execution_config's EXECUTION_CONFIG_NOT_ENFORCED refusal now fires for exactly those three (UNENFORCED_EXECUTION_CONFIG_FIELDS), not all five; the two enforced fields (ENFORCED_EXECUTION_CONFIG_FIELDS) are instead validated for a usable value (positive finite number / non-negative whole number; EXECUTION_CONFIG_INVALID_FIELD otherwise) so an unusable value is refused at deploy time rather than discovered as a silent no-op at the first tick. DESIGN, AND WHY ExecutionGuard WAS NOT TOUCHED: traced every call site of ExecutionGuard.validate_trade in the real repository (routers/orders.py's cancel and cancel-all, routers/portfolio.py's close-all) and confirmed -- consistent with this same remediation effort's own POST_LAUNCH_IMPROVEMENTS.md finding and with core/execution_engine.py's own comment at the live-path notional-ceiling check -- that ExecutionGuard.validate_trade is reached ONLY from those three risk-REDUCING control endpoints, never from the signal-driven order-opening path. Threading execution_config into ExecutionGuard would therefore have changed nothing a real order passes through; the real order-construction path for a strategy deployment is BotRunner._inner_loop (risk_manager.validate_trade_request, then ExecutionEngine.execute_with_idempotency), so that is where this fix lives. The config reaches it via the SAME per-deployment object BotRunner already receives at construction (strategy_blueprint, which already carries deployment_id/exchange_id/mode) rather than a new deployment-id-keyed cache: deployment_runtime.build_runtime_blueprint now also carries execution_config, populated from deployment_binding.evaluate_binding's DeploymentBinding.execution_config at deploy time and from the strategy_deployments row itself on resume after a restart (rebuild_for_resume) -- this is design option (b) in the original remediation note: the config threaded explicitly through an existing call chain, not a new lookup. BLAST RADIUS, CONFIRMED BEFORE STARTING: read core/live_execution_gate.py (RT-15/TRADE-04) -- live trading is gated at the venue-write boundary (require_live_authorization, called from CCXTExchangeExecutor.place_order) and remains OFF regardless of this change; this fix only affects orders reaching BotRunner's gate, which today means paper-mode orders (and whatever a live order would do if RT-15 were later lifted, since the gate sits downstream of this one and is unaffected by it). TESTS: tests/test_deploy01_execution_config_enforcement.py (new, 18 tests) -- the pure gate function (empty config is a complete no-op; oversized order refused; order within cap allowed; reduce-only skips the notional cap; max_open_positions=0 refuses the deployment's one possible entry; cap>=1 allows it; adding to an existing position is never blocked; both caps compose), build_runtime_blueprint/rebuild_for_resume carrying execution_config, BotRunner.__init__ reading it off the blueprint (and defaulting to {} when absent, so every pre-DEPLOY-01 blueprint is unaffected), and TWO full paper-mode end-to-end BotRunner runs (real compiled plan, fake keyless exchange, recording execution engine, the same fixture-driven boot test_rt02_builder_strategy_runs_on_deployment_runtime.py uses) proving a tight max_order_notional / max_open_positions=0 produces NO order on a tick that, with no execution_config at all, DOES produce one. Updated test_deploy01_execution_config_fields_not_enforced.py, test_task_8_2_deployment_binding.py and test_task_8_2_deploy_preflight.py for the transition: the refusal no longer fires for the two now-enforced fields; preflight now reports max_order_notional as a PASSING condition instead of EXECUTION_CONFIG_NOT_ENFORCED. Regression: the full set of execution-guard/bot-runner/deploy/paper-trading/RT-15/TRADE-04 suites named in this remediation pass (2208 tests, this session) plus every deployment-binding/preflight/deploy-strategy test in the repo -- all green after one fix to this file's own new docstring (a literal substring collided with an unrelated source-order assertion in test_rt08_deployment_state_is_durable.py; reworded, re-ran, green).
findings.verification_level: code+test (verified this session, local suite only; no production access)
findings.remaining_action: Three of the five fields are STILL refused-not-enforced by design, not oversight: slippage_tolerance_bps, order_timeout_seconds and retry_policy have no corresponding mechanism anywhere on this platform's order-submission path (no slippage-tolerance check, no per-order timeout, no retry policy), so wiring them would mean storing a value nothing reads -- exactly the defect this finding exists to close. Closing them for real needs a structural addition to ExecutionEngine.execute_with_idempotency / exchange_executor.place_order (a retry/timeout wrapper and a slippage-vs-fill check), which is a materially larger change to the hot order-submission path than the two fields fixed this pass and deserves its own dedicated review rather than being rushed in alongside this fix. max_open_positions is real but narrow given the current one-symbol-per-deployment architecture (binds only at 0); widening it to a meaningful range above zero would need a multi-position execution model (tracking more than one net position per deployment) this codebase does not have. NONE of this has been applied to, deployed against, or exercised on the real running production backend -- this session has no production or Supabase/AWS access; verification is code + a local test suite only (production_verified: false). The next deploy to staging/production should confirm a live deployment with a real max_order_notional actually refuses an oversized paper order end to end, through the real fleet/BotRunner boot path rather than this session's fixture-driven one.

findings.title: Six strategy-performance endpoints read QuestDB tables that nothing ever writes; they silently return zeros for every strategy
findings.evidence: Of the six strategy-performance endpoints (performance, equity-curve, monthly-returns, daily-returns, execution-metrics, risk-metrics), confirmed by reading backend/metrics_service.py directly that five already degraded honestly on no data (get_equity_curve/get_monthly_returns/get_daily_returns return [], get_execution_metrics/get_risk_metrics return {}) -- only get_strategy_performance's _empty_performance_metrics() fabricated a full dict of 0.0/0 values, indistinguishable from a strategy that genuinely traded and broke exactly even. Confirmed the root cause: strategy_performance/strategy_risk/executions have no writer anywhere in this codebase (grepped backend_app/ for any INSERT into them -- none), so this method is reached on every single call. Fixed by changing every QuestDB-sourced numeric field in _empty_performance_metrics() to None. Verified the 3 call sites of this method (routers/strategy_operations.py's passthrough handler, and backend/strategy_service.py's 3 internal callers) only embed the dict in a larger response with no arithmetic performed on its fields, so this change is safe. This is the backend half of the same defect FE-06 describes on the frontend side; both were fixed together since fixing one without the other does not change what a trader actually sees. New regression tests/test_metrics01_no_data_is_not_a_fabricated_zero.py (5 tests): every field is None on no data AND on a query exception (a QuestDB outage must not look like a clean sheet of zeros); a genuine zero in real data is NOT converted to unavailable; the other five methods are unchanged (regression guard).
findings.remaining_action: Not attempted (explicitly offered as the alternative in this finding's own remediation note, not chosen): implementing the actual QuestDB writer pipeline for strategy_performance/strategy_risk/executions. That is a substantial, separate feature build (deciding what writes these tables, at what cadence, from which part of the execution pipeline) and was judged out of scope for a P2 honesty fix. The honest-unavailable fix chosen here requires no such build and is the safer, immediately deliverable half of the finding's own two offered options.

findings.title: A user can PATCH their own strategy_deployments row directly via PostgREST to switch mode from paper to live, bypassing entitlement and binding checks
findings.evidence: tests/test_sec16_strategy_deployments_guard_postgres.py (12) on real Postgres
findings.remaining_action: Migrations 034 and 038 are now BOTH applied in real production as one combined guard (confirmed via pg_proc/pg_trigger -- see DEPLOY-04): the trigger function was created with 038's full allow-list (including close_requested_at) directly, and 034's trigger attached to it. Cross-checked against the application's real write paths (backend/strategy_service.py) before applying: every strategy_deployments UPDATE from the user-scoped client only touches allow-listed lifecycle columns, and the only INSERT path reachable today creates mode='paper' rows (live trading is hard-gated off by RT-15), so this did not break the paper-deploy happy path. findings.title: Marketplace browse builds a PostgREST filter from raw user input
findings.evidence: Confirmed by reading backend_app/routers/library.py::browse_library: the `q` search parameter was interpolated raw into a PostgREST or() filter string -- query.or_(f"name.ilike.%{q}%,description.ilike.%{q}%") -- and PostgREST's filter mini-language treats `,`, `.`, `(`, `)` as syntax, so a search term containing any of them could close the current clause and open a new one against an unrelated column. Separately, the handler fetched ALL matching rows via query.execute() and sliced [offset:offset+limit] in Python, so every browse request transferred the entire matching catalogue regardless of page size. Fixed both. (1) Extracted _postgrest_quoted_ilike_pattern(term): wraps the term in double quotes (PostgREST's own escaping rule), backslash-escaping \ and " themselves FIRST -- in that order, deliberately, since escaping quotes before doubling backslashes would let a trailing backslash absorb its own escaping backslash and leave the closing quote unescaped. (2) Switched to count="exact" on .select() plus .range(offset, offset+limit-1) on the query, pushing LIMIT/OFFSET and the total-match count to PostgREST instead of this process. Extended two existing fake-Supabase test doubles (tests/test_marketplace_pipeline.py::FakeTable, tests/test_library_detail_projection_regression.py::_Query/_Resp) with .range()/count="exact" support, since neither had it before this fix and both are exercised by this same handler's existing regression suite. New tests/test_api08_browse_search_term_is_escaped.py (9 tests): the pure escaping function round-trips a plain term, each of the four reserved characters, a term attempting to break out via literal double quotes, and a trailing-backslash ordering-sensitivity case (verified against an independently-written unescaper, not just 'whatever the function produces'); an end-to-end request with reserved characters in q no longer errors; pagination through the real route returns the requested page and an accurate total count sourced from PostgREST, not len() over everything. tests/test_marketplace_pipeline.py, test_library_detail_projection_regression.py, test_listing_projection.py and 3 other library/marketplace test files (633 tests total) still pass -- test_listing_projection.py's own static sweep for unprojected Listing-row leaks required restating the total-count computation as max(page_result.count or 0, len(paginated)) rather than a ternary, since its row-content taint tracker only exempts a handful of row-REDUCING call names (len, sum, min, max, ...) when they are the ENTIRE assigned expression, not a ternary branch.
findings.remaining_action: None.

findings.title: Exchange credential test endpoint is an unrestricted validity oracle for arbitrary third-party API keys
findings.evidence: Confirmed by reading backend_app/routers/exchange.py::test_connection (POST /api/exchanges/test): it dials the named venue with WHATEVER api_key/secret_key/password/uid the request body carries -- nothing requires those credentials to belong to the caller -- and had neither a route-specific rate limit nor require_aal2 (only the generic get_current_user), matching the title's own description exactly: an unrestricted validity oracle for third-party keys. Added @limiter.limit("10/minute") -- the same bound routers/auth.py already uses for account-enumeration-prone endpoints -- which bounds how many candidate keys a single caller can probe per minute, the dimension "unrestricted" names. require_aal2 was deliberately NOT added, despite this finding's own remediation note suggesting it "matching store_keys": AAL2 raises the one-time cost of acting under a given identity; it does nothing to bound how many probes that identity can run once stepped up, so against BULK third-party-key probing specifically (the actual threat this finding names) it is the wrong tool, while store_keys needs it because it PERSISTS a credential to the caller's own vault (AUTH-01's documented "Exchange API key mutation" case) -- test_connection persists nothing. Adding it would also directly contradict tests/test_auth01_require_aal2_is_wired.py::test_read_and_test_handlers_do_not_require_aal2, a PINNED regression from an earlier finding in this same remediation effort asserting test_connection must NOT require AAL2, per require_aal2's own "DO NOT apply globally" rule for a handler that submits credentials but persists nothing -- that decision was not re-litigated here. New tests/test_sec12_exchange_test_endpoint_is_rate_limited.py (3 tests): a static AST check confirms the decorator is on test_connection specifically; a real end-to-end test mounts the actual route function on a FastAPI app wired with the real in-process limiter object and exception handler (DEV_MODE resolves it to in-memory storage, no Redis needed) and proves the 11th rapid request from one caller is rejected while the first 10 reach the handler; a negative control proves two different callers (keyed via TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS + X-Forwarded-For) each get their own 10-request budget rather than sharing one. ConnectionEngine is stubbed throughout so no test run ever dials a real exchange. tests/test_auth01_require_aal2_is_wired.py (16 tests, pre-existing) still passes unchanged -- confirming the deliberate decision not to add AAL2 here was preserved, not silently broken.

findings.title: Notifications are kept in an unbounded per-process dict with an O(n) idempotency scan
findings.evidence: Confirmed the defect exactly as named: backend_app/routers/notifications.py's _in_memory_notifications was a plain, unbounded module-level dict -- one entry retained forever for every notification ever created in this process's lifetime, across every tenant, whether or not it was ALSO durably persisted to Supabase (list_notifications always tries Supabase first and only falls back to this dict when Supabase has nothing, confirmed by reading it -- so a persisted entry's in-memory copy was pure, unbounded-growth dead weight). The idempotency check also did a full scan (`for existing_id, existing_data in _in_memory_notifications.items(): ...`) on every single create, so it got slower, not just memory-hungrier, as the dict grew. Fixed with (1) _MAX_IN_MEMORY_NOTIFICATIONS (env-overridable via MAX_IN_MEMORY_NOTIFICATIONS, default 5000) -- once exceeded, the OLDEST entries are evicted (plain dicts preserve insertion order in Python 3.7+, and no code here ever re-inserts an existing key, so the first key is reliably the oldest); (2) an O(1) idempotency index (_idempotency_index, keyed by (user_id, idempotency_key)) replacing the full-dict scan, kept in sync on insert, eviction, AND delete (both delete_notification and delete_all_notifications now route through a shared _forget_notification_locked helper instead of a bare `del`, so a deleted or evicted notification's idempotency key is freed for reuse rather than left dangling). New tests/test_hy04_notifications_memory_bounded.py (6 tests, using a shrunk cap via monkeypatch rather than actually inserting 5000+ rows) proves: exceeding the cap evicts the oldest entries first; a duplicate idempotency key for the SAME user returns the existing id without growing the store; the SAME key for DIFFERENT users does not collide; delete_notification and delete_all_notifications both clean the idempotency index, not just the dict; an evicted entry's idempotency key is freed for reuse. Updated tests/test_notifications_feature_e2e.py's state-cleanup fixture to also clear the new _idempotency_index between tests (it only cleared _in_memory_notifications before, which would have let the new index leak across runs in that file's own autouse fixture -- a miniature version of the exact unbounded-growth problem this finding is about). Full regression (new HY-04 suite + existing notifications e2e suite, 1 file/23+ tests + tests/test_validation_sweep.py, 388+ tests) clean except the 2 unrelated pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session (missing real Supabase service credentials in this sandbox).
findings.remaining_action: The finding's remediation note offered TWO options joined by 'and/or': cap the in-memory structure, OR make Supabase the source of truth with a visible degraded-mode indicator. This fix takes the first option in full (bounded growth, O(1) idempotency) -- the second option's 'visible degraded-mode indicator' (e.g. surfacing to the user or to ops when notifications are running on the in-memory fallback rather than Supabase) was NOT attempted; Supabase was already and remains the primary store attempted first on every write and read, so this is an observability nice-to-have on top of an already-correct fallback, not a remaining correctness gap.

findings.title: Referral payout debit and payout insert are two non-transactional writes with best-effort compensation; payout completion is unimplemented
findings.evidence: This session's own prior pass fixed the lock fail-open bug and implemented the pending-sstate->completed/rejected settlement step, and deliberately deferred full transactionality of the debit+insert pair as 'the same class of architectural change as PAPER-05... a larger, separately-designed and separately-tested lift'. This pass is that lift. FIRST CONFIRMED THE REAL SCHEMA rather than trusting either migration file's comments alone, per this task's own explicit instruction: referral_wallets is declared TWICE by two uncoordinated CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS files -- migrations/006_reconcile_production_database.sql (applied FIRST per PROVISIONING_ORDER.md step 1: columns balance_usd/total_earned_usd/pending_usd) and migrations/referral_system_redesign.sql (applied AFTER it, whose own CREATE TABLE is therefore a no-op, but which carries a SEPARATE reconciliation block, its own lines ~714-785, that detects the missing approved_balance_usd column and ADDS AND BACKFILLS it -- and pending_balance_usd/paid_balance_usd/lifetime_earnings_usd -- from the 006 columns). Verified directly against this session's own fully-provisioned disposable Postgres replica (scripts/provision_database.py --apply --create-substrate, every file PROVISIONING_ORDER.md names including referral_system_redesign.sql, in its documented order): \d referral_wallets shows BOTH column sets, with approved_balance_usd present -- matching exactly what routers/referral.py already reads and writes. Added backend_app/migrations/049_ref01_payout_atomic.sql against that confirmed column set, with a PREFLIGHT check that verifies approved_balance_usd (and referral_payouts.payout_method) actually exist before installing either function and refuses, by name, naming the exact remediation (apply referral_system_redesign.sql's reconciliation block first) if they do not -- so an apply to a database where that file was never run fails loudly rather than installing a function against a column that is not there. Two SECURITY DEFINER functions: create_referral_payout_request (the debit, now a real SELECT...FOR UPDATE row lock held for the whole function rather than a `.gte()` conditional UPDATE, plus the referral_payouts INSERT, one transaction -- RF001 insufficient balance, RF002 no wallet, RF003 invalid argument) and settle_referral_payout (the status flip plus, for a rejection, the wallet re-credit, one transaction -- RF004 already-terminal). Because the pair is now genuinely atomic, the best-effort compensating re-credit in routers/referral.py (which could itself fail, logged CRITICAL, 'needs manual reconciliation') is dead code and is REMOVED: if the INSERT fails for any reason, the debit the same function body already issued rolls back with it. The settlement rejection's wallet re-credit is handled the same way: if no wallet row exists to re-credit, the whole function raises RF002 and the status flip rolls back too, so the payout stays 'pending' (re-settleable once reconciled) instead of becoming 'rejected' with the money nowhere -- strictly better than the prior pass's own CRITICAL-log-and-continue behaviour for that one edge case. The Redis distributed lock (fixed to fail closed in the prior pass) is kept, now for latency only -- a fast 409 instead of waiting on the real Postgres row lock, no longer load-bearing for correctness, which the row lock inside the function now is. New tests/test_ref01_payout_atomic_postgres.py (11 tests against the real disposable Postgres replica): the happy path for both functions; RF001/RF002/RF003/RF004 each raised with nothing written; the rejection-with-no-wallet-row case rolling back the status flip; and a REAL CONCURRENCY test (two threads, two real psycopg2 connections, each requesting 60% of a $100 wallet) proving exactly one of two simultaneous over-budget requests succeeds and the wallet never double-counts. Updated three existing tests whose premise was the now-removed two-statement/compensation shape: test_referral_payout_debit_is_compensated_on_insert_failure.py (rewritten to prove the handler issues exactly one .rpc() call and falls back to no table write on failure, since there is no longer a second statement to compensate), test_ref01_payout_settlement.py (rewritten with an .rpc()-shaped stub mirroring the real function's own decision logic), and test_referral_payout_schema_contract_postgres.py (its AST check now also reads the INSTALLED function's real source via pg_get_functiondef, since the Python-level INSERT it used to check no longer exists). test_p10d_referral_settlement_lifecycle_postgres.py's own canary test (explicitly written to fail once a settlement writer existed, with instructions to update it then) updated per its own instructions, narrowed to the still-true, separate commission-approval gap (pending_balance_usd->approved_balance_usd) this pass does not touch. Full referral/ref01/ref02 regression: 175 passed, 1 skipped, 1 pre-existing failure unrelated to this change (an xfail(strict) marker tied to whether migration 032 -- referral_payouts terminal-evidence CHECK, explicitly marked 'NOT APPLIED, pending migration-owner sign-off' in its own header -- happens to be applied in this sandbox's disposable replica; orthogonal to wallets, payouts or this fix).
findings.verification_level: code+test (verified this session, real disposable Postgres replica incl. concurrency; not production)
findings.remaining_action: NOT applied to the real production database -- deliberately, as a separate, later, carefully-reviewed step given this touches real money-movement tables, and this session has no production credentials. Apply backend_app/migrations/049_ref01_payout_atomic.sql to staging first, then production. THE SCHEMA QUESTION IS RESOLVED FOR A DATABASE BUILT FROM THIS REPOSITORY'S OWN DOCUMENTED PROVISIONING ORDER, BUT NOT INDEPENDENTLY CONFIRMED AGAINST THE REAL LIVE PRODUCTION CATALOGUE, which this sandbox cannot query: the conclusion that approved_balance_usd exists rests on migrations/referral_system_redesign.sql having actually been applied to production, which PROVISIONING_ORDER.md documents as the intended build order but which this session could not verify independently of that document. Before applying 049 to production, an operator should run `SELECT column_name FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name='referral_wallets'` against the REAL production database and confirm approved_balance_usd is actually there; if it is not, 049's own preflight will refuse with the exact remediation rather than installing a broken function, but that refusal should be anticipated rather than discovered during a production apply. The separate, still-open commission-approval gap (pending_balance_usd -> approved_balance_usd has no writer at all, so in real production no payout can currently be requested regardless of this fix) is unchanged and not touched by this pass.

findings.title: Unauthenticated referral-code validation endpoint returns another user's UUID; its own rate limiter is keyed on proxy address
findings.evidence: Confirmed two independent defects in backend_app/routers/referral.py::validate_referral_code (POST /api/referral/validate). (1) The router's own limiter = Limiter(key_func=get_remote_address) was a SEPARATE instance from every other router's shared one: behind CloudFront/ALB, get_remote_address reads the shared edge socket address, not the caller's own, so every caller landed in the same bucket; and a bare Limiter(...) with no storage_uri defaults to slowapi's own in-memory store, per-pod, not shared across replicas -- a second, compounding defect beyond what the finding's title names. (2) ValidateReferralCodeResponse returned referrer_id (the referrer's raw Supabase user UUID); grepped algo22-terminal/src/ and found nothing reads it beyond its own name in one JSDoc type comment. Also confirmed, while reading the handler, that the finding's 'unauthenticated' framing holds in substance despite the Depends(get_request_supabase) in the signature: that dependency only rejects a request with NO Authorization header at all, builds its client from whatever bearer-token string was supplied with no signature/expiry verification (create_request_supabase_async does none), and the handler never issues a query through that client to have Supabase itself reject a forged one -- documented honestly in the handler's own docstring rather than silently left for the next reader to rediscover. Fixed: referral.py now imports the shared backend_app.core.rate_limit.limiter (SEC-10's trusted_client_address key, resolved storage backend) instead of constructing its own; ValidateReferralCodeResponse no longer has a referrer_id field at all. New tests/test_ref02_referral_validate_rate_limit_and_uuid.py (3 tests): referral.limiter is proven to BE the shared instance object (not a second one); the response Pydantic model is proven to have no referrer_id field; an end-to-end successful validation response is proven to carry exactly {valid, message} and no referrer_id key at all (not even null). tests/test_referral_payout_debit_is_compensated_on_insert_failure.py, test_referral_program_decision.py, test_referral_missing_tables.py, test_environment_precedence_is_centralised.py and test_validation_sweep.py's referral routes (438 tests total; 2 unrelated pre-existing billing failures, already confirmed in an earlier finding this session) still pass.
findings.remaining_action: The authentication gap documented above -- any non-empty Authorization header value passes with no real signature/expiry verification -- was deliberately NOT fixed here: the remediation note asks for the rate-limiter key and the UUID disclosure specifically ("consider not returning the raw UUID"), not a rewrite of this endpoint's authentication dependency. A future session wanting real identity verification should switch to a dependency that decodes and checks the JWT itself (e.g. get_current_user) and reassess whether keying the rate limit on the caller's JWT sub (the remediation note's other suggestion) becomes meaningful once that holds.

findings.title: The sign-in page advertises two-factor authentication, but the OTP step is never server-enforced
findings.evidence: Confirmed the defect precisely in algo22-terminal/src/pages/AuthPage.jsx: supabase.auth.signInWithPassword succeeding is a COMPLETE Supabase sign-in, not merely a password check -- src/supabase.js configures the client with persistSession: true, so the SDK immediately writes a live, fully-privileged session into its own storage the instant that call resolves. The handler's own pre-existing comment ('DO NOT grant application access or persist session to sessionStorage yet') only ever controlled this APP's OWN sessionStorage bookkeeping; it never touched the session Supabase itself had already established. The 6-digit email-OTP step that followed (handleVerifyOtp, calling supabase.auth.verifyOtp) was therefore decorative for general account access: the password alone already granted a fully live session before the OTP screen was even shown. (require_aal2-gated routes, SEC-05/SEC-15 this same session, were never affected -- this flow never touches supabase.auth.mfa.*, so AAL stays 1 regardless; the exposure is to everything NOT behind require_aal2.) Fixed per this finding's third offered option: supabase.auth.signOut() is now called immediately after a successful signInWithPassword (and after signUp, for the identical reason if this project's email-confirmation requirement happens to be off), before the OTP screen is shown. New tests/unit/authOtpFe04.test.jsx (3 tests, vitest): signOut is called once the password check succeeds; signOut fires BEFORE signInWithOtp is dispatched (ordering, not just presence); the full flow still ends in a real session once verifyOtp actually succeeds -- this fix tears down the interim session, not the feature. Pre-existing auth_otp.test.jsx (23 tests across both auth suites) and the FE-01 suites still pass unchanged (59 tests total, vitest).
findings.remaining_action: This closes the gap for general account access via the password+email-OTP flow specifically. It does not and cannot make this a real, Supabase-tracked MFA factor (AAL2) -- that would require migrating to supabase.auth.mfa.enroll/challenge/verify (TOTP or phone), a materially larger change (new enrollment UI, recovery-code handling, a live Supabase project to test against) not attempted here. The sign-in page's 'two-factor authentication' copy is now true in the sense that a password alone no longer grants a live session -- it was not re-examined word-for-word against the stricter claim that this is AAL2-grade MFA, which it still is not.

findings.title: The API client overwrites caller-supplied Idempotency-Key headers with its own weak hash
findings.evidence: Confirmed by reading algo22-terminal/src/apiClient.js's request interceptor: it called generateIdempotencyKey(config.url, data), which hashed sessionId_url_payloadStr with a weak 32-bit simpleHash into the Idempotency-Key header UNCONDITIONALLY -- even when the caller (api/modules/strategies.js::deploy's options.idempotencyKey, a prepared but not-yet-wired-to-any-UI call site) had already set its own Idempotency-Key header, it was overwritten. The deeper bug: the hash was deterministic over (session, url, payload), so two SEPARATE, deliberately-identical submissions (placing the same order twice in a row on purpose) collided onto the identical key, and the backend's own idempotency check would then treat the second legitimate order as a duplicate retry of the first. Fixed: the interceptor now checks config.headers['Idempotency-Key'] for an existing value first and only falls back to its own generator when the caller supplied none; the fallback itself (generateIdempotencyKey) no longer takes url/data at all -- it is now idemp_${crypto.randomUUID()}, content-independent, so two identical submissions never collide. Removed simpleHash (now unused) and getSessionId (now unused -- confirmed no other call site anywhere in algo22-terminal/src or tests references either name). New algo22-terminal/tests/unit/apiClientIdempotencyFe05.test.js (4 tests, same axios-mock convention as the existing ATTACK 3 idempotency test it extends): a caller-supplied key is honoured verbatim, not overwritten; a request with no caller key still gets a defined idemp_-prefixed key; two identical submissions with no caller key get DIFFERENT keys (the collision bug, proven fixed); a GET request still never receives the header. The pre-existing tests/unit/attack_frontend_full.test.js (8 tests, whose ATTACK 3 only asserted the idemp_ prefix and definedness, not hash-determinism) still passes.
findings.remaining_action: No current UI call site actually passes options.idempotencyKey to strategies.deploy (or any other caller-supplied-key path) yet -- this fix makes the mechanism correct for when one is wired up, consistent with how this session treated other prepared-but-unused mechanisms (e.g. SEC-11). A future session adding a 'Deploy' button's retry/resubmit handling should generate one UUID per click and pass it through, rather than relying on this interceptor's own per-request fallback, if intentional retry-coalescing is wanted.

findings.title: The shared Redis manager swallows every error and returns neutral values, so counters and membership checks silently fail open when Redis degrades
findings.evidence: The 'remove the duplicate method definitions' half is done (commit 0357897). MockRedisClient and SharedRedisManager each defined several of their own methods twice (9 pairs, 19 dead method bodies total); Python keeps only the LAST def, so the first copy of each pair never ran. At least one pair (incr/decr) had a DIFFERENT signature in its dead copy than the one actually executing. Removed every dead (shadowed) definition after diffing each pair by hand to confirm zero behavioural change (several byte-identical copy-paste; a few an older implementation style shadowed by a newer, more complete one -- e.g. xadd gaining retries + PublishError-raising for TRADING_CRITICAL_STREAMS in its winning definition). incrby/decrby were genuinely single-definition but sat inside the same dead line range as the real duplicates -- a first pass deleted them by accident, caught by running their real caller's (subscription_engine.py) tests before committing; restored and pinned by name in the new test file. tests/test_red01_no_duplicate_redis_manager_methods.py (4 tests, AST-based): neither class defines any method name twice; incrby/decrby still exist exactly once and work end-to-end. Regression: a ~2500-test sweep across quota/idempotency/billing/paper-trading/rate-limiting/dashboard suites + full validation_sweep/schema_drift (484 passed, 2 failed -- same pre-existing, unrelated billing findings) both clean. ADDITIONALLY this session (commit 44bf0a7): rather than leaving the full 'enumerate every call site' task undifferentiated, individually traced the three categories this entry's own remaining_action named as safety-relevant (quota reservation, idempotency claims, kill-switch reads) to find out how many genuinely still rely on SharedRedisManager's fail-open contract. Confirmed the plain proxy methods (incrby/decrby/get/etc.) do swallow a connection error and return a neutral value by design (read SharedRedisManager.incrby/decrby directly) -- but found every safety-critical caller already has its OWN independent protection against that, built in earlier, separate fixes: the kill switch (KILL-01, GlobalKillSwitch.is_active's own RedisUnavailable-based local-latch fail-closed path, which does not go through the shared manager's fail-open methods at all), quota enforcement (SubscriptionEngine.reserve_quota's new_usage < amount inference -- a healthy INCRBY of a positive amount cannot return less than that amount, so a neutral 0 is distinguishable and refused -- and subscription_dependencies.enforce_quota's own explicit UsageReadFailed -> 503 'not a pass' handling), and this same module's own start_processing (already raises in production on a Redis failure). EXACTLY ONE safety-critical caller had NOT received the same treatment: _atomic_check_and_set, the FIN-CRITICAL-004 atomic idempotency check-and-set, whose except handler returned (None, False) unconditionally -- indistinguishable from an ordinary contended lock. Fixed to match start_processing's own established contract: raises in production on a Redis failure during this check, unchanged outside production. tests/test_red01_atomic_idempotency_fails_closed_in_production.py (3 tests, negative-control verified: git-stashed the fix, the production-raise test failed with the predicted 'DID NOT RAISE' symptom while the other two still passed; restored, all 3 pass). Regression: 124 passed across every idempotency/kill-switch test file, 376 passed in the full validation sweep.
findings.verification_level: code+test (verified this session); larger API-split remains open
findings.remaining_action: The three categories this entry's own remaining_action named as safety-relevant (quota, idempotency, kill-switch) are now individually accounted for: all were already protected except one gap (the FIN-CRITICAL-004 atomic check-and-set), now fixed (commit 44bf0a7). NOT done, and still a real, deliberately-scoped-out larger task: the broader architectural split this entry's remediation text originally asked for -- giving every OTHER caller of incrby/decrby/sismember/sadd/get/set (the many call sites outside the three safety-critical categories just reviewed, e.g. rate-limiting counters, caching, dashboard aggregates) an explicit choice between today's fail-open default and a fail-closed variant -- is NOT attempted here. Those remaining callers were not individually reviewed this session; this entry's own prior estimate (incrby/decrby alone has 5 call sites in subscription_engine.py -- now confirmed all protected; sismember/sadd/get/set have many more elsewhere, not reviewed) still stands for the non-safety-critical remainder. Given the three named safety-relevant categories are now confirmed covered, the risk profile of what remains is lower than this entry's original framing suggested, but a dedicated pass enumerating the rest (mostly correctness/freshness, not duplicate-execution or quota-bypass risk) is still the right next step if full coverage is wanted.

findings.title: The secret-redacting log filter is installed on only 13 marketplace/paper logger names; billing, exchange, execution and auth loggers are unfiltered
findings.evidence: Confirmed by reading backend_app/core/observability.py: RedactingLogFilter was attached only to the 13 logger names in GUARDED_LOGGER_NAMES (task 33.4's own scope: marketplace and paper) -- billing, exchange, execution and auth loggers carried no secret redaction at all. A Logger's own filters apply only to records it originates (Logger.handle checks self.filters, never an ancestor's), which is why attaching to 13 named loggers protected only those 13 and nothing else, however many other loggers exist in the codebase. Added install_root_log_redaction(), which attaches RedactingLogFilter to every HANDLER on the root logger instead -- a Handler's filters run for every record that propagates to it, whatever logger originated it, which is the mechanism the remediation note ("Install RedactingLogFilter at the root logging handler") names precisely. main.py calls it immediately after its own logging.basicConfig(...), which is what gives the root logger a handler to attach to. The original module's own docstring explains WHY root-handler attachment was avoided for task 33.4 ("redact the whole process's output, which the task forbids") -- that was a deliberate narrow scope for that task, not a permanent prohibition, and LOG-01 is exactly the later finding asking for the wider behavior that task declined. New tests/test_log01_root_redaction_covers_every_logger.py (4 tests, using a standalone logger/handler pair, never the real process root): an arbitrary, never-individually-guarded logger name is redacted once the handler it propagates to carries the filter; a record from an ALREADY-guarded logger (PaperRepository) is proven not to be double-mangled by passing through both its own logger filter and the root handler filter (the second pass on already-redacted text is a no-op); the installer is idempotent; a handler-less logger (the real root before basicConfig runs) returns 0 rather than raising. tests/test_log_redaction.py (362 tests, pre-existing) still passes; confirmed main.py still imports and boots with the root handler now carrying the filter.
findings.remaining_action: Covers the single root handler logging.basicConfig installs, the dominant real log path for this process (every logger with propagate=True, the default, eventually reaches it). Does not retroactively cover a handler some other module attaches directly to a non-root logger and removes from the propagation chain (propagate=False), nor a handler uvicorn or another framework might attach to the root AFTER main.py's own install_root_log_redaction() call runs -- neither case was found by reading main.py, but a dedicated audit of every logging.basicConfig/addHandler call site was not performed. Two pre-existing, unrelated test failures (test_exchange_credential_log_redaction.py's EXCH-01 sandbox-refusal mismatch, test_task_33_2_rate_limit_keys.py's rate-limit-count test) were confirmed to reproduce identically on the unmodified baseline via git stash -- not caused by this fix, not fixed by it either.

findings.title: The distributed rate limiter fails open on any Redis error
findings.evidence: Confirmed the fail-open pattern in two layers: backend_app/core/distributed_rate_limiter.py::DistributedRateLimiter.check_rate_limit ("Fail-safe: allow request on error" -> allowed=True unconditionally on ANY exception, including a Redis outage) and backend_app/core/exchange_rate_limiter.py::DistributedRateLimiterIntegration.check_user_rate_limit (same pattern, one layer up, catching failures above check_rate_limit itself). IMPORTANT REACHABILITY FINDING: traced every caller and confirmed NEITHER layer is reached by any live request today. DistributedRateLimiterIntegration is called only by its own sibling method (acquire_user_quota) in the same class, never from outside exchange_rate_limiter.py; exchange_rate_limiter.py's own exchange_limiter singleton/exchange_limited decorator/ExchangeRateLimiter class are never imported anywhere else either. The actual live protection against an exchange ban is ccxt's own built-in enableRateLimit: True, set directly in both exchange_executor.py and connection_engine.py -- purely in-process, no Redis dependency, no fail-open-on-external-failure risk at all. Fixed anyway, same reasoning as SEC-11 (a fail-open landmine in an unreached module becomes a live bug the moment something is wired up to call it): both except blocks now fail CLOSED specifically for the one rate-limit type/operation this module's own vocabulary ties to venue-ban risk (RateLimitType.ORDERS_PER_MINUTE / operation="orders"), matching the remediation note's own distinction, and fail open for the cosmetic/UI-facing types (signals, API calls, WebSocket connections) as the note explicitly says may remain acceptable. get_status() (read-only, "without consuming quota" per its own docstring, not an enforcement gate) and reset() (operator action) were left untouched -- neither is a decision point this finding is about. New tests/test_rl01_rate_limiter_fails_closed_for_orders.py (7 tests): ORDERS_PER_MINUTE denies on a simulated Redis outage; the three cosmetic types still fail open on the same outage (negative control); a healthy Redis still allows an under-limit order (negative control, not a blanket deny); the exchange_rate_limiter.py layer denies "orders" and still allows "signals" on an equivalent failure one level up. tests/test_exchange_rate_limiter.py (9 tests, pre-existing -- covers the actually-live TokenBucket/ExchangeRateLimiter classes, untouched by this fix) still passes.
findings.remaining_action: The module this finding targets is currently dead code in the live order-placement path (see evidence) -- this fix closes the landmine without changing any current production behavior. A future session should decide whether to delete backend_app/core/distributed_rate_limiter.py and the unused parts of exchange_rate_limiter.py entirely (ccxt's enableRateLimit already covers the real need with no distributed-coordination gap, since each pod throttles its own calls to the SAME per-pod ccxt client instance per exchange connection -- whether that is sufficient across multiple pods sharing one exchange account's global limit was not investigated here and is a separate, not-yet-tracked question), or wire DistributedRateLimiterIntegration into a real call site if genuine cross-pod coordination of exchange-venue calls is still wanted.

findings.title: Checkout currency/country detection trusts client-controllable headers, but the actual pricing impact is narrow
findings.evidence: Confirmed by reading backend_app/core/country_detection.py: extract_client_ip unconditionally trusted CF-Connecting-IP, True-Client-IP, X-Real-IP and X-Forwarded-For, and detect_country_from_headers unconditionally trusted CloudFront-Viewer-Country and CF-IPCountry -- a caller that reaches this process directly, bypassing whichever CDN is supposed to set these (this deployment's own terraform does not describe a CloudFront/ALB topology at all -- INF-02), could set any of them to anything and get a different region's price list via pricing_service.py::determine_pricing_context's IP-detection tier. Traced the actual commercial impact and confirmed the finding's own 'narrow' framing: determine_pricing_context's step 3 (an explicit currency_override query param) already takes highest precedence over IP/header detection, so a user can already pick any supported currency outright -- spoofing the geo header is a stealthier route to a capability that already exists overtly, not a new one. Fixed the header-trust half anyway, reusing the house pattern SEC-10 already built for this exact question ('is there a real proxy chain in front of this process') rather than inventing a second one: added client_address.trusted_edge_is_configured() (True only when TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS is a valid >=1 integer, the same fail-safe-by-default check trusted_client_address's own hop count already uses for rate-limit keys) and gated every one of the six headers above on it in country_detection.py. Unconfigured (this sandbox's default, and the fail-safe default for any deployment that has not explicitly confirmed its proxy topology), none of the six headers can change the detected IP or country any more -- detection falls through to the direct socket peer and the deterministic US/USD fallback. New tests/test_geo01_edge_headers_require_trusted_proxy.py (16 tests): trusted_edge_is_configured tracks TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS exactly as trusted_client_address's internal hop count does; each of the six headers is proven ignored with TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS unset, including the one case that actually matters commercially (a spoofed CloudFront-Viewer-Country against an unconfigured deployment resolves to US/USD, not the attacker-chosen country); a negative control proves every header still works once TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS is set, so this is a default, not a removal. Updated tests/test_billing_localization_e2e.py's five existing header-trust tests to set TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS (the deployment-has-confirmed-its-topology case they were already written to exercise) and added a new TestEdgeHeadersUntrustedByDefault class (6 tests) proving the previously-undefended default. Full tests/test_billing_localization_e2e.py + test_production_payment_e2e_acceptance.py + SEC-10/REF-02/SEC-12/validation_sweep/route_contract regression (399 passed) clean except the 2 unrelated pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session.
findings.remaining_action: The header-trust root cause is closed for every deployment that has not explicitly confirmed TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS -- which, per INF-02, describes this platform's actual production deployment today (no terraform describes its real topology, so there is nothing here to tell this code whether a CDN really fronts it). Once an operator sets TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS for the real topology, trust resumes exactly as before this fix -- a CloudFront origin-request policy that strips or validates these headers at the edge (this finding's own remediation note) is still the stronger, infrastructure-level fix and was not attempted: this session has no AWS credentials to configure CloudFront, and INF-02 already records that the repo's terraform does not describe the live distribution to configure a policy against. The remediation note's other half (keep FX rates fresher than the hardcoded baseline fallback) is a separate concern already owned by fx_service.py's own live-rate/cache/stale-grace/baseline tiers, unchanged here, and not re-verified in this pass.

findings.title: A second, unused credential vault exists alongside the real one
findings.evidence:
RE-VERIFIED this session (not re-guessed): grepped backend_app/ again -- CredentialVault's only self-reference remains its own get_credential_vault() factory in backend_app/core/credential_vault.py; no router or service imports it. The 'unused' half of the title still holds. Then read backend_app/backend/api_key_vault.py (APIKeyVault, confirmed the REAL vault: imported by routers/exchange.py, core/state.py, backend/signal_service.py, backend/master_executor.py and others) line by line, and read all 8 test files the prior pass named plus the file that contains one of them, to classify what each ACTUALLY tests rather than just that it mentions 'credential_vault':
(A) 5 of 8 do not test CredentialVault's own correctness at all and are unaffected either way by this decision: tests/test_strategy_dag_architecture.py and tests/security/test_builder_tenant_isolation.py::test_no_builder_module_reads_the_credential_vault assert OTHER modules (strategy_dag, deployment_binding, strategy_compiler, validator, training_status, model_versioning) never reference the literal string 'credential_vault' or call load_decrypted_keys -- test_strategy_dag_architecture.py's credential-violation checks run only against synthetic in-tmp_path source text, never a real import, so they hold identically whether or not the real module exists. tests/test_task_8_2_deployment_binding.py::test_the_credential_vault_is_still_where_credentials_are_resolved, despite its name, asserts 'load_decrypted_keys' (APIKeyVault's real method) appears in master_executor.py -- it tests the REAL vault's usage, not CredentialVault. tests/test_no_undefined_names.py is a flake8 F821 regression guard parametrized on backend_app/core/credential_vault.py by path (asserts the file exists and has no undefined names) -- it doesn't test CredentialVault's business logic, but DOES mean deleting the module would require editing this test too (removing that parametrize entry), so deletion is not a zero-blast-radius cleanup. tests/regression/capture_baseline.py::capture_credential_vault is a baseline-shape snapshot (Requirement 25.1), inert either way.
(B) 2 of 8 (tests/test_credential_vault_strength.py, tests/test_credential_vault_key.py) DO test CredentialVault-only internals: per-type credential-strength floors, PBKDF2-with-salt key derivation, and the store_credential call-ordering bug fix. Reading api_key_vault.py confirms APIKeyVault implements NEITHER feature -- no credential-strength validation beyond a bare not-empty check, no PBKDF2/salt derivation at all (it hands MASTER_ENCRYPTION_KEYS straight to MultiFernet). These tests encode an invariant unique to CredentialVault, with nothing in APIKeyVault to port it to or from -- pure dead-code tests on this specific question.
(C) tests/test_exchange_credential_log_redaction.py has one CredentialVault-specific class (TestCredentialVaultNeverLogsTheValue) alongside a separate, already-passing class in the SAME FILE (TestAPIKeyVaultNeverLogsTheValue) proving the identical invariant -- credential values never reach logs -- against the REAL vault's store_exchange_keys/load_decrypted_keys. That invariant is therefore already ported and covered for the real vault today; the CredentialVault class is redundant with it.
(D) tests/test_tenant01_credential_vault_isolation.py is the one genuine exception. It exercises CredentialVault.get_credential's two-layer tenant isolation: (1) a tenant-scoped Redis key, and (2) a re-verification of the STORED row's own tenant_id against the requesting tenant_id even when the key matched -- its own docstring frames this as the defense against 'the state a mis-scoped write would leave behind'. Reading api_key_vault.py confirms the REAL vault's load_decrypted_keys/delete_exchange_keys/rotate_key implement only the equivalent of layer (1) -- a .eq('user_id', user_id) Supabase filter -- with NO layer-(2) re-check of the returned row's own ownership field against the request.
