findings.title: The admin-only portfolio-management API is largely non-functional (unawaited coroutines, nested-lock deadlock risk)
findings.evidence: The three asks in the original remaining_action (add missing awaits; fix the non-reentrant lock being re-entered; fix forced_reduction's close percentage) were the tip of a much deeper problem: this module (admin-only, mounted at /api/internal/portfolio-mgmt behind get_admin_user, confirmed separate from the real live-trading routers/portfolio.py) had ZERO prior behavioral test coverage anywhere in the repo, and crashed or hung at nearly every call site once actually exercised. Found and fixed, layer by layer, by actually calling the code rather than reading it: (1) validate_consistency() was called from both open_position and close_position but was never defined ANYWHERE on PortfolioManager -- AttributeError on every single open or close, before any other bug was even reached. Implemented it for real: checks each strategy's used_capital+available_capital==allocated_capital invariant and that open_positions/strategy_positions only reference live, correctly-filed positions. (2) Missing awaits on get_margin_metrics/_check_exposure_limits/register_strategy and several GET endpoints (exposure/margin/margin/health/margin/status/pnl/detailed-summary/prices/update) -- all returned unexecuted coroutine objects instead of data. (3) asyncio.Lock is not re-entrant: get_portfolio_summary held its own lock and then called three other lock-acquiring methods; open_position's conflict-cancellation step called the lock-acquiring close_position while already holding that lock; update_prices did the same into margin_monitor.check_margin_health -> _forced_position_reduction -> close_position. All three are guaranteed deadlocks the moment missing-await bug #2 is fixed first (which is presumably why nobody had hit this in whatever manual testing existed). Fixed by splitting get_margin_metrics/get_exposure_metrics/get_pnl_summary/_check_exposure_limits/close_position into `_locked` bodies the caller can invoke directly while already holding the lock, with public async wrappers that acquire it fresh; narrowed update_prices' own lock scope so the margin check and any resulting forced liquidation run after the price-update lock is released. (4) get_exposure_metrics built an ExposureMetrics() instance and then read/wrote MarginMetrics-shaped fields on it (margin_used, margin_level, margin_call_threshold...) that ExposureMetrics does not declare as fields at all -- AttributeError on every call where margin_used<=0, i.e. an EMPTY portfolio, the ordinary starting state. This was a copy-paste of the margin calculation onto the wrong dataclass; rewrote it to populate ExposureMetrics' own real fields (symbol/strategy exposure breakdown, gross/net/long/short exposure, leverage, concentration), which is also the shape every caller (get_portfolio_summary, create_snapshot) already assumed when reading .symbol_exposure/.gross_exposure off the result. (5) create_snapshot (called from inside open_position/close_position, i.e. on every trade) read self.pm.available_capital/self.pm.used_capital, neither of which exists on PortfolioManager at all (only per-strategy StrategyAllocation.available_capital/used_capital do) -- AttributeError on every single snapshot. Fixed to sum across self.pm.allocations.values(). Also fixed create_snapshot's exposure_metrics.total_exposure read (ExposureMetrics has no such field either) to use the real gross_exposure field. (6) MarginMonitor's forced-liquidation path called self.pm.close_position(position_id=..., close_price=..., reason=...) -- but close_position's parameter is named exit_price, not close_price -- TypeError on every forced liquidation. Fixed, and made check_margin_health/_forced_position_reduction/get_margin_status async so they can properly await the manager calls they depend on (they were plain sync methods calling async methods, which can never actually run the async body). (7) the liquidation log said 'reducing by 25%' while the code's own comment admits there is no partial-close method and it always closes the entire position -- an operator reading logs during a real margin event would see a false 'only trimmed 25%' when 100% was actually liquidated. The log and the result's 'action' field now both say 'full_close', matching what actually happens. New tests/test_pm01_portfolio_manager_is_functional.py (8 tests, every call that used to deadlock wrapped in asyncio.wait_for with a 5s timeout so a regression times out loudly instead of hanging the whole suite) exercises register_strategy, open_position (including the real conflict-cancellation path with two opposing positions), close_position, update_prices, a real forced-liquidation scenario (drives an actual margin_level under the 110% threshold and asserts the position is actually closed, not just logged about), and get_portfolio_summary/get_margin_status end to end. Full regression (new suite + every other portfolio-management test in the repo + validation_sweep, 450+ tests) clean except the 2 unrelated pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session.
findings.remaining_action: True partial position reduction (closing e.g. 25% of a position's size rather than always closing 100%) is NOT implemented -- PortfolioManager has no partial-close primitive (resizing a Position's quantity while keeping it open and correctly re-deriving its realized/unrealized PnL split) and adding one is a real feature, not a bug fix, with its own design and test surface. This pass fixed the DISHONESTY (claiming 25% while doing 100%) and the crashes/deadlocks around it, not the missing feature -- always closing fully on a liquidation-risk margin event is a conservative, safe behavior, not an unsafe one, so this is a legitimate deferral rather than a masked defect.

findings.title: Alembic's baseline migration DROPs core trading tables; running it against an existing, unstamped production database would destroy data
findings.evidence: Confirmed by reading backend_app/alembic/versions/4ef23035a692_baseline.py: it has no down_revision -- the first thing alembic upgrade head runs against an unstamped database -- and its upgrade() unconditionally DROP TABLE ... CASCADEs orders, positions, fills, transaction_records, transaction_checkpoints, transaction_rollbacks and idempotency_keys. On a fresh database this is a no-op; against an EXISTING, unstamped production database (this platform's own parallel raw-SQL migration system, backend_app/migrations/*.sql, already creates orders/positions/fills independently of Alembic, with real rows), running it would silently destroy every one of them. Added _refuse_if_any_target_table_has_rows(bind), called as the FIRST statement in upgrade() before any DROP: checks all seven target tables for even one row (EXISTS(SELECT 1 FROM ... LIMIT 1), not a full COUNT) and raises, having altered nothing, naming every populated table and pointing the operator at alembic stamp 4ef23035a692 as the actual next step, per the remediation note. A table that does not exist yet (the fresh-database case this revision was written for) is skipped, not flagged. New tests/test_db_alm01_baseline_refuses_on_populated_tables.py (5 tests, real SQLite engine, loaded by path same as scripts/-style files): a populated table trips the guard and leaves its row in place; an EMPTY existing table does not (negative control -- not "refuse if the table exists"); a nonexistent table does not (negative control -- the fresh-database case); multiple populated tables are all named, not just the first; and a source-inspection check proves the guard call is literally the first statement in upgrade(), ahead of every op.execute DROP -- not merely defined and never called. tests/test_bug049_sql_and_alembic_agree.py (15 tests, pre-existing, also inspects this versions/ directory) still passes.

findings.title: Two independent sequence allocators for paper session events can collide and drop a bar on feed disconnect
findings.evidence: Confirmed the collision mechanism exactly as named: paper_market_feed.FeedHandle._emit_feed_disconnected allocated its sequence from paper_repository.next_session_event_sequence (max(paper_events.sequence) + 1, read off the LOG), while every other Paper_Channel event (paper_events.record_event -> next_sequence -> paper_repository.allocate_session_event_sequence) allocates from an atomic compare-and-swap on the paper_sessions.event_sequence COUNTER. Traced the actual failure mode: the feed writer's INSERT (via insert_session_event) advances the LOG but never touches the COUNTER, so a subsequent ordinary event's counter-based allocation can read a stale, lower number and collide with the sequence the feed writer already used; uq_paper_event_seq then refuses that ordinary event's INSERT with PaperDuplicateSessionEvent, and neither paper_session_service._emit nor the bar-stepping loop that calls it catches or retries that exception -- so the bar is dropped, not merely delayed. Fixed by routing _emit_feed_disconnected through allocate_session_event_sequence instead, so there is only one source of truth for the next sequence number and the race cannot happen at all. next_session_event_sequence itself is kept (it has its own direct test coverage and tests/property/test_paper_channel_sequence.py reuses it as a synthetic log-based second writer to stress-test the counter allocator's retry logic in general) -- only its one production caller moved. Along the way, fixed a stale property test harness bug this change exposed: tests/test_paper_market_feed_selection.py's shared _session_row() fixture never carried an event_sequence key at all, and the fake client's eq-filter compares str(row.get(col)) against the literal given -- an ABSENT key reads back as 'None', which never equals '0', so allocate_session_event_sequence's own compare-and-swap would lose all three attempts against this fixture even though the real column defaults the row to exactly the value the swap expects. Seeded it at 0 (the column's real DEFAULT per migration 009), which is behaviourally transparent to every other reader (the allocator's own code already treats an absent/NULL value as 0) and only matters for this exact-string-equality fake match. Updated the two stale docstring claims in test_paper_channel_sequence.py that called next_session_event_sequence 'task 24.4's feed writer's allocator ... a real production path', which is no longer true after this fix. New tests/test_paper06_feed_disconnect_shares_the_allocator.py (3 tests): an AST check that the feed-disconnect writer's own source calls allocate_session_event_sequence and not next_session_event_sequence (catches a revert even without a live collision); a real disconnect advances the counter to exactly match the log's own highest sequence (they can no longer diverge); and the exact scenario this finding describes -- a disconnect immediately followed by an ordinary event -- allocates consecutive, non-colliding sequence numbers end to end, with both rows landing. Full regression: the new suite + every paper-trading test in the repo (tests/ -k paper, 1590 passed) + test_validation_sweep.py (373 passed), clean except 2 unrelated pre-existing EmptyCategoryError collection failures (confirmed pre-existing and unrelated earlier this session, e.g. test_dag_hash_sensitivity.py) and the 2 unrelated pre-existing billing failures already confirmed earlier this session.

findings.title: Owner-path RLS bypass (FORCE RLS unset), api_key_vault isolation is a Python argument not a DB policy, and billing-webhook writes trust a caller-supplied user_id behind HMAC+IP alone
findings.evidence: Not a new discovery -- this is MY OWN independent re-verification (this session, against current source, not by trusting the prior report) of the three architectural residuals staging/REMEDIATION_REPORT.md's TENANT-01 section (line 677 'TENANT-01 -- DOWNGRADED P1 -> P2, NOT CLOSED') names, per EXT-01's remaining_action. All three are CONFIRMED STILL PRESENT: (1) grepped backend_app/migrations/*.sql for 'FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY' -- zero tables have it set (one comment in 026_fee_records_row_level_security.sql explains why: enabling FORCE without first wiring a tenant-context setter would turn every owner-path (SQLAlchemy, table-owner) read into a silently empty result set, which is worse than the current state). (2) backend_app/backend/api_key_vault.py: every method (load_decrypted_keys/delete_exchange_keys/list_connected_exchanges/rotate_key) isolates by a plain Python user_id argument passed through .eq('user_id', user_id) on what the prior report characterizes as a service-role-reaching client -- isolation is enforced by the caller passing the right id, not by the database. (3) backend_app/routers/billing.py's Stripe webhook handler (checkout.session.completed and subsequent branches, lines ~2557-3292) reads user_id from session.client_reference_id / event metadata -- attacker-reachable content IF the webhook's HMAC signature is ever forged (requires the signing secret), protected only by signature verification + IP allowlist (which BILL-02, this same session, already hardened the diagnostics for, but did not and could not determine the correct TRUSTED_PROXY_HOPS value from this sandboxed environment). The prior report's own decision NOT to wire TenantMiddleware (reasoning: there is no tenant above the user in this product -- core/dependencies.py resolves tenant_id=user_id in practice; TenantMiddleware would set request.state.tenant but never call set_config('app.current_tenant_id', ...), so installing it closes nothing; and it has its own documented CVE-class startswith auth-skip bug) was reviewed and is independently judged sound, not re-litigated here. Its own real-Postgres negative matrix (tests/test_tenant01_cross_tenant_matrix_postgres.py, 11 passed, 13 tables, 0 leaks, with positive/weakened-policy/RLS-off controls) is accepted as real measured evidence, not re-run this session (would require a real Postgres instance this sandbox does not have). ADDITIONALLY this session: this sandbox's 'needs a disposable Postgres instance' blocker, repeated across TENANT-01/RECON-01/PRIV-01/AUD-01/MKT-03, is PARTIALLY LIFTED -- a real, disposable local PostgreSQL 16.2 was provisioned end-to-end this session via the repo's own staging/bootstrap_pg.py + scripts/provision_database.py (the full 61-file migration set + root_migrations + alembic + privilege-hardening all applied clean, zero failures), and tests/test_tenant01_cross_tenant_matrix_postgres.py's full 11-test real-Postgres negative/positive/detection matrix was run against it for the first time this session and passed in full (the PostgREST-style path -- SET LOCAL ROLE authenticated + SET LOCAL request.jwt.claim.sub -- correctly blocks every cross-tenant SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE attempted across all 29 target tables, with both the positive control and the deliberately-weakened-policy detection control confirming the harness itself is not vacuous). (Getting a pgserver-packaged PostgreSQL to run and dlopen its own plpgsql.so at all took real diagnostic work worth recording for whoever next needs this: pgserver's postgres binary resolves $libdir via its own compiled-in pkglibdir, which strace confirmed points at wherever pip installed the pgserver package -- installing it under this session's default scratchpad venv, whose parent directory is mode 700, got EACCES on every extension load; the fix was installing pgserver into a second, normally-permissioned venv under /opt, not touching the scratchpad's permissions, which the harness's own security classifier correctly refused when attempted directly. The server's postmaster is also in its launching process's group and dies when that process exits -- same reason staging/pg_keepalive_r1.py exists for pgdata_r1 -- so it is kept alive via an equivalent keepalive loop for the default pgdata, run with run_in_background.) THIS DIRECTLY ANSWERS THE OPEN QUESTION THIS ENTRY'S OWN REMAINING_ACTION ASKED A FUTURE SESSION TO RESOLVE: 'a tenant-context setter wired at the one or two owner-path call sites that matter most, then FORCE RLS, verified by re-running the existing real-Postgres negative matrix before and after.' Reading the real code found exactly which two call sites those are -- backend_app/core/database_pool.py's get_db/get_db_context is imported by 27 files, but grepping every actual call site found only 2 of them are genuine per-request, user-scoped HTTP paths with Depends(get_db) (routers/billing.py's get_payment_methods and delete_payment_method); the other 21 (dag_worker.py, task_recovery.py, execution_engine.py, reconciliation_scheduler.py, safety_audit.py, startup_recovery.py, main.py's watchdog/pnl sessions, dag_task_queue.py) are background/worker processes with no single tenant to scope by, and forcing RLS platform-wide would silently empty every one of their reads the moment a session ran with no request.jwt.claim.sub set -- confirming the original 'repo-wide, do not rush' caution was correct. Both real call sites touch exactly one model, PaymentMethodModel/public.payment_methods (confirmed: grepping for that model/table name across backend_app/backend/ and backend_app/core/ found zero other callers), and BOTH ALREADY correctly filter by .filter(PaymentMethodModel.user_id == user['id']) in application code today -- so this specific gap is a defense-in-depth hardening item, not a reproduced live exploit, consistent with this entry's own 'no reproduced exploit this session' framing. THE ACTUAL BLOCKER ON FLIPPING FORCE RLS, NEWLY DISCOVERED AND EMPIRICALLY CONFIRMED THIS SESSION: FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY only changes behaviour for the TABLE OWNER; it has zero effect on a role that is a Postgres superuser or carries BYPASSRLS, both of which unconditionally skip RLS regardless of FORCE (documented Postgres semantics, and empirically reproduced here: `SELECT current_user, rolsuper, rolbypassrls FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname = current_user` against this session's own freshly-provisioned replica, connected exactly the way backend_app/core/database_pool.py's DATABASE_URL/SUPABASE_DB_URL resolution does for a direct Postgres DSN, returned ('postgres', True, True) -- superuser AND bypassrls both true. On a Supabase project, the direct-connection DSN authenticates as the project's 'postgres' superuser by default, which is exactly this. Verified by seeding a real row and setting FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on public.payment_methods on the live replica: the connecting role's own pg_roles record alone settles the question (a superuser's queries are never subject to RLS, FORCE or not), reverted afterwards (NO FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY; test rows deleted) so the replica is left as it was provisioned. THIS MEANS THE REMAINING_ACTION'S OWN PRESCRIPTION -- 'wire a tenant-context setter, then FORCE RLS' -- WOULD NOT CLOSE THIS GAP ON ITS OWN if production's SQLAlchemy connection authenticates the same way this replica's does (which, for a standard Supabase direct DSN, it does by default): a tenant-context setter plus FORCE RLS is necessary but not sufficient while the connecting role bypasses RLS outright. Not attempted further this pass for exactly that reason: writing speculative role/credential-provisioning code with no real target to test the actual deployment step against risks exactly the kind of unverified claim this ledger's whole discipline exists to prevent. findings.title: Venue-side duplicate-order protection is missing for coinbase/kraken, and a timeout leaves an execution in an indeterminate state rather than FAILED
findings.evidence: Designed and implemented the defined terminal state the prior corpus's D3 report (section 7.3) flagged as the single highest-severity remaining DUP-01 item, declined there pending authorisation ('P0, not done, needs authorisation'). Scope, deliberately narrow and conservative: the new terminal state -- ExecutionStatus.FAILED with the 'confirmation_lost' marker folded into exchange_status, written by the new ExecutionRecordRepository.give_up_on_unresolved_submission -- is reached ONLY from the two branches of OrderWatchdog._adjudicate_ambiguous_execution that get genuinely NO signal from the venue ('no executor available' and 'venue lookup failed'). It is never reached from a branch that got a real answer (a definite not_found stays immediate and unaffected) or partial positive evidence (a status with no attributable order id, or an order still open at the venue -- both stay UNKNOWN unconditionally, however old the row is, because that is affirmative evidence of life, the opposite of 'no signal'). It additionally requires that the row has already been through one prior adjudication attempt (from_status == UNKNOWN, i.e. reached via the new OrderWatchdog.recheck_unresolved_submissions / ExecutionRecordRepository.classify_unresolved_submissions path, not its first look) AND that CONFIRMATION_LOST_AFTER_SECONDS (86400s / 24h -- this codebase's own existing 'give up' convention for a durable TTL, e.g. core/fill_deduplication_manager.py's fill-dedup registry, core/redis_cluster.py's idempotency keys, core/webhook_idempotency.py's processing TTL -- reused rather than invented) has elapsed since submitted_at. A row's FIRST adjudication attempt always stays UNKNOWN regardless of age, which closes an edge case found while implementing this: a long watchdog outage could otherwise let a never-yet-examined EXECUTING row look 'old enough' to give up on immediately, and give_up_on_unresolved_submission's WHERE clause (scoped to transition ONLY from UNKNOWN, by design, so it can never downgrade a row a concurrent worker just attached positive evidence to) would then silently match zero rows and leave it EXECUTING forever -- worse than the pre-fix defect this whole finding is about. has_unresolved_submission (RT-17's per-symbol freeze) was widened to match this new state exactly as it already matches UNKNOWN, so the new, more legible terminal label is never SAFER to retry against than UNKNOWN was -- that was the one safety property that had to be proven, not assumed. submission_may_have_reached_venue (DUP-02's client-side retry refusal) already covered the new state with NO code change at all -- it refuses retry for any non-COMPLETED status once submitted_at is set, which this state always has by construction -- pinned here by a regression test rather than re-derived from memory. recheck_unresolved_submissions is wired into OrderWatchdog._monitoring_loop's existing 30-second cycle, immediately after the pre-existing recover_unsubmitted_executions call, so a row that gave up once because the venue could not be asked at all IS looked at again on every later cycle rather than being permanently invisible to the recovery path the way a plain UNKNOWN write left it before this change -- that retry loop, not merely the final status label, is the mechanism that was actually missing. Checked and recorded per this session's own task instruction: live trading is hard-gated off (RT-15), and separately -- independently confirmed by reading core/execution_engine.py's own constructor docstring and _execute_trade_internal's branch selection -- a PAPER-mode ExecutionEngine is always constructed with exchange_executor=None (BotRunner's paper fast-path depends on exactly that null), so _execute_trade_internal takes the simulated branch unconditionally and NEVER calls mark_submitted or create_order. Paper executions therefore do not reach submitted_at, _adjudicate_ambiguous_execution, or any of this session's new code at all today -- this is a dormant control pending live trading re-enablement, not something exercised by current traffic of either kind. 21 new focused tests (tests/test_dup01_venue_confirmation_lost_terminal_state.py) cover: the first-attempt-always-stays-UNKNOWN edge case explicitly; the give-up transition from both no-signal branches once the threshold is crossed; that every real-answer branch (not_found / filled / still-open / status-without-id) never gives up however old the row is; that a raced give-up write does not get double-handled; has_unresolved_submission matching the new state (and NOT matching an ordinary determinate FAILED, which would have frozen every everyday rejected order); the PostgreSQL-only query/write methods' fail-safe behaviour on a non-PostgreSQL dialect; and the new recheck_unresolved_submissions method's wiring and its own failure handling. Full regression sweep of 330 tests across the execution-engine, watchdog, DUP-01/DUP-02, RT-16/RT-17, TRADE-01/TRADE-04/TRADE-07 and P10D exchange-reconciliation-fails-safely suites: 314 passed, 15 skipped (PostgreSQL-gated, no database provisioned in this environment), 1 xfailed (pre-existing, unrelated), 0 failed, 0 regressions. TRACEABILITY CORRECTION (this session): fix_commit was the untraceable placeholder '(this commit)', which made this entry's claim unverifiable against the repository -- acceptance criterion 12 asks that the branch and commit contain the exact changes validated. Resolved to ffcace90 by searching `git log --all --grep` for this finding's own id and confirming each hash is an ancestor of main with `git merge-base --is-ancestor`. No code, status, severity or evidence claim was changed by this correction. THE POSTGRESQL HALF IS NOW VERIFIED (Kiro, commits 337baeaf + b08139a8). This entry's own remaining_action said the raw SQL 'was verified to fail safely on SQLite ... but was NOT executed against a real PostgreSQL server'. It has now been. New tests/test_dup01_confirmation_lost_postgres.py (24 tests) runs in the provisioning job's PostgreSQL lane against postgres:17-alpine, and all 24 pass -- the lane's step went from 648 passed/2 failed to 650 passed, 11 skipped, 0 failed (run 39752856204). That gap mattered specifically because both guarantees live only in SQL and cannot be checked any other way: classify_unresolved_submissions uses make_interval(secs => :threshold), which is PostgreSQL-specific and returns [] on every other dialect BY DESIGN, so a SQLite test can prove it is fail-safe but never that it selects correctly; and give_up_on_unresolved_submission closes its concurrent-worker race 'by the WHERE clause itself, not by locking', which nothing in Python observes. WHAT IS NOW PROVEN, not reasoned about: the classifier selects old UNKNOWN rows with no venue order id and computes age_seconds from a real EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (now() - submitted_at)); it excludes fresh rows, rows holding a platform order_id however old, rows in any status but UNKNOWN (parametrised over FAILED/COMPLETED/EXECUTING/PENDING, so a row already given up on is terminal and not re-offered), and never-submitted rows (TRADE-07's population -- conflating them would let an order that never reached the venue be labelled confirmation-lost); an explicitly supplied short threshold selects what the default leaves alone, which is what proves make_interval uses the parameter; the tenant filter excludes another tenant's row; results are oldest-first and honour LIMIT. The give-up writes FAILED with the confirmation_lost marker, COMMITS (verified from an independent session, so another worker sees the terminal state rather than re-adjudicating), and is REFUSED without writing anything when the row meanwhile acquired a venue order id, when it is no longer UNKNOWN, or cross-tenant; an over-long detail is truncated rather than overflowing the column. THE RACE ITSELF was exercised with two real connections (NullPool) released together through a threading.Barrier against one row: exactly one give-up wins. And the property the docstring names as the one thing that must never happen -- the new label being SAFER to retry against than plain UNKNOWN -- is pinned both ways: RT-17's has_unresolved_submission still freezes the symbol after the give-up, with a negative control proving a plain FAILED row WITHOUT the marker does NOT freeze it (otherwise the first assertion would pass for the wrong reason). A FINDING FROM THE FIRST REAL RUN, recorded rather than quietly patched: 22 of 24 passed and 2 failed with ForeignKeyViolation on fk_execution_records_order_id -- execution_records.order_id references orders.id, so the two tests that set it to a literal string had to create a real orders row (fixed in b08139a8, no assertion weakened). That is a schema fact no SQLite run could have surfaced, and it STRENGTHENS the finding: order_id IS NOT NULL is not a free-text note, the database guarantees it points at a real platform order, so the classifier's exclusion and the give-up's refusal rest on a constraint rather than a convention.
findings.verification_level: code+test; the PostgreSQL-only SQL is now VERIFIED against a real PostgreSQL 17 server in CI. Venue-side certification remains externally blocked.
findings.remaining_action: STATUS MOVED FIXED_UNVERIFIED -> EXTERNAL_BLOCKED, deliberately, because what is left is no longer unverified work this environment could do -- it is work that cannot be done without access this environment does not have. The database half is VERIFIED (see evidence: 24 tests on real PostgreSQL 17 in CI). What remains: (1) VENUE-SIDE CERTIFICATION for binance/bybit/okx -- those three have real sandboxes (SANDBOX_MECHANISMS: URL_SWAP, URL_SWAP, HEADER x-simulated-trading) and the design could be certified against them once testnet credentials exist, which they do not here. (2) coinbase and kraken CAN NEVER BE CERTIFIED THIS WAY, by this finding's own premise -- both are declared UNSUPPORTED in SANDBOX_MECHANISMS ('no sandbox exists' on the installed ccxt), which is exactly why the give-up design is deliberately conservative (a 24h threshold, the first-attempt exemption, never overriding positive evidence, never assuming success OR failure from an inconclusive lookup) rather than compensating for the missing venue signal with a shorter wait. That half is permanently blocked, not pending. (3) The mechanism is still DORMANT in production for an orthogonal reason: live trading is hard-gated off (RT-15) and paper-mode executions never reach this path at all (exchange_executor is None for a paper-mode ExecutionEngine), so no real traffic exercises it yet -- which is a containment fact, not a verification one, and does not make the above verified in production.
