findings.title: ExchangeReconciliationService exists but is never started anywhere; no leader election or tenant enumeration is wired for it
findings.evidence: Surfaced by this session's synthesis of the repo's own prior corpus (named there as RECON-01, referenced in staging/REMEDIATION_REPORT.md Phase 10 and PHASE11A_LAUNCH_GATE_REGISTER.md), then independently confirmed against current source: grepped the whole repository for ExchangeReconciliationService( and found it constructed nowhere outside its own defining module (backend/exchange_reconciliation.py) -- no call site in main.py, any scheduler module, or anywhere else starts it. This is a DIFFERENT mechanism from RT-16's OrderWatchdog (already fixed/in-progress this session under RT-16: _get_executor_for_order now builds a real per-tenant executor) -- the two are separate reconciliation subsystems and this finding is not already covered by RT-16's fix. ADDITIONALLY this session: read backend_app/backend/exchange_reconciliation.py's ExchangeReconciliationService in full to check whether the leader-election primitive this session already built for INF-04's ReconciliationScheduler (core/reconciliation_scheduler.py -- a DIFFERENT class, confirmed by grep: three distinct 'reconciliation' modules exist in this codebase, exchange_reconciliation.py/distributed_execution/exchange_reconciliation_engine.py (confirmed unreachable dead code, flagged in this session's own HY-02 investigation)/core/reconciliation_scheduler.py) could simply be reused here to close the 'no leader election' half cheaply. Found a THIRD, more fundamental blocker the prior corpus's own two-item list did not name: ExchangeReconciliationService.__init__ takes exactly ONE exchange_client for the WHOLE service instance (self.exchange), and start_reconciliation_loop(tenant_id, ...) loops forever reconciling that ONE tenant_id's DB-side orders against that SAME single client -- there is no per-tenant executor resolution inside _fetch_exchange_orders the way RT-16's OrderWatchdog fix (this session, commit 3c333e0) already gave the order-watchdog path via order_control._executor_for. So even with leader election AND a tenant-enumeration source both wired, starting ONE instance of this service cannot correctly reconcile MULTIPLE tenants' real exchange accounts -- it would need either (a) one dedicated instance PER TENANT, each independently leader-elected (a tenant-scoped lock, not a single global one), or (b) a rewrite of _fetch_exchange_orders to resolve a per-tenant executor inside the loop, closer in shape to RT-16's own fix. Deliberately did NOT attempt either: both are genuine architecture decisions on the live reconciliation path for real exchange accounts, not a wiring fix, and guessing wrong here risks reconciling a tenant's orders against the WRONG account's exchange client -- a materially worse outcome than the service remaining unstarted. ADDITIONALLY this session (commit ea69b94): closed the third of this entry's three named blockers -- 'architected for exactly ONE tenant_id and ONE exchange_client per instance'. _fetch_exchange_orders now resolves a FRESH executor scoped to the (tenant_id, exchange_id) pair of EACH call, via the same order_control._executor_for helper RT-16's OrderWatchdog fix and RT-21's manual cancel already use, when an optional new `vault` constructor parameter is set -- instead of trusting a single, constructor-injected exchange_client to belong to whichever tenant_id a caller passes in. The old exchange_client path is kept unchanged for every existing caller/test. Also added ExchangeExecutor.fetch_open_orders(symbol=None), extracted from cancel_all_open_orders' own internal listing step, so a caller comparing orders does not have to go through a cancel-named method. tests/test_recon01_per_tenant_executor_resolution.py (6 tests): the actual correctness property this exists for -- two tenants through the SAME service instance get their own executors and never see each other's orders -- plus the refusal when a vault has no exchange_id to resolve against, backward compatibility for the old shared-client path, and the new executor method's healthy/error behaviour. Negative-control verified: git-stashed both source files, 5 of 6 failed with the predicted TypeError/AttributeError (the backward-compat test correctly still passed); restored, all 6 pass. Regression: 81 passed across every exchange-executor/reconciliation/cancel test file, 376 passed in the full validation sweep. BLOCKER 1 IS NOW CLOSED (Kiro, commit 2dde6f7d). Measured before changing anything, via a negative control reading HEAD's own text with `git show` and the working tree untouched: start_reconciliation_loop had NO leadership check of any kind, no _try_become_leader method, and no lock key -- so every gunicorn worker that started it would reconcile the same rows against the same venue account concurrently, each cancelling, re-querying and transitioning orders the others were already working on. REUSED, NOT COPIED, exactly as this entry asked ('the template to reuse, not yet applied here'): the mechanics now live once in the new backend_app/core/leader_lease.py (try_acquire_or_renew) and BOTH ReconciliationScheduler and ExchangeReconciliationService delegate to it. ReconciliationScheduler._try_become_leader keeps its name and signature, so INF-04's existing test file -- which calls that method directly by name eight times -- is the regression net for the refactor rather than something to rewrite; it passes unchanged (24 tests with the distributed-lock-faking guard). The same negative control confirms the scheduler went from owning its own nx=True implementation to delegating, so there is no second copy of the rule left to drift. DISTINCT KEYS, deliberately: vyomquant:leader:exchange_reconciliation is not the scheduler's key, because sharing one would make whichever process won suppress the OTHER subsystem's loop entirely -- a failure mode that presents as 'the loop is running', with a leader elected and nothing erroring, while half the work silently never happens. TTL 60s against the 5s default interval gives twelve cycles of headroom so a holder never loses a lease it is still using, while still letting a crashed leader's hold expire on its own rather than deadlocking the subsystem. The check runs EVERY cycle, not once at startup (a test reads the loop's own source to pin it inside the while body): a hoisted check would let a process that won once keep reconciling after its lease lapsed, including after a partition healed and another worker legitimately took over. NEW tests/test_recon01_exchange_reconciliation_leader_election.py, 16 tests, against a SHARED fake Redis store -- the shape N worker processes talking to one real Redis actually see, unlike MockRedisClient's per-process dict, which is the bug class test_redis_fallback_does_not_fake_a_distributed_lock.py already guards for the other locks here. Covers: exactly one of two instances wins, with a negative control proving the two have distinct instance ids so the second is not merely the first renewing; the incumbent keeps winning every cycle (a renewable lease, not a one-shot lock that would churn leadership every cycle); a challenger cannot take a live lease; a crashed leader's lease expires and a successor takes over; the acquiring SET uses NX+EX and the renewal deliberately does not use NX; failing closed on both an absent and a raising Redis client; the loop honouring the verdict -- a non-leader cycle reconciles NOTHING, with a positive control proving a leader cycle does, so the first assertion cannot pass for a trivial reason; one shared primitive with no second copy; two distinct keys; and the service still being absent from main.py. Regression slice across reconciliation/leader/redis/watchdog: 246 passed, 5 skipped, 0 failed. *** THE TENANT-ENUMERATION BLOCKER IS CLOSED (Kiro, 2026-10-23). *** This entry's remaining_action named it: 'NO TENANT-ENUMERATION SOURCE IS WIRED. Nothing calls reconcile_open_orders for any real tenant, so the service is still invoked nowhere in production.' `start_reconciliation_loop` took a single tenant_id and there was no answer to 'which tenant?'. THE DECISION THIS ENTRY DEFERRED, NOW TAKEN WITH A MEASUREMENT. It recorded the open choice as 'whether one leader instance reconciles every tenant in sequence (simple, but one slow venue delays everyone) or whether the lease is held per tenant/exchange pair (parallel, but N leases and N executors to manage)'. Measured against production before choosing: public.execution_records holds 198 rows -- 108 COMPLETED, 90 FAILED, and ZERO PENDING or EXECUTING -- across 40 distinct tenants, against 182 profiles. So enumerating TENANTS would resolve a per-tenant executor for 40+ tenants, each needing a vault decryption and a venue session, in order to reconcile nothing. `enumerate_reconcilable_pairs` therefore derives the work from the OPEN ORDERS, not from a tenant list: distinct (tenant_id, exchange_id) where status is PENDING or EXECUTING and a venue identifier exists. One indexed query, empty today, scaling with open exposure rather than with signups. It returns PAIRS rather than tenants because `reconcile_open_orders` resolves one executor per (tenant, exchange) and a tenant may hold orders at more than one venue. The venue-identifier predicate checks venue_order_id FIRST and order_id second, for the reason RT-16 established: TRADE-12 moved the exchange's id into venue_order_id and the live engine leaves order_id NULL, so a filter on order_id alone misses every row the engine created -- the same blind spot RT-16 found in OrderWatchdog's own population queries. Pinned by test_a_venue_order_id_alone_is_enough. ONE LEASE PER CYCLE, NOT PER PAIR, also decided rather than inherited: N is zero today and production runs a SINGLE ECS service with no worker services at all (INF-03), so there is nothing to parallelise across. N leases for N=0 is complexity bought on speculation, and the enumeration already returns pairs, so moving to a per-pair lease later is a contained change. The head-of-line concern the entry raised is real but becomes real only with several tenants holding orders at a slow venue at once. `start_reconciliation_loop_all_tenants` acquires leadership BEFORE the enumerating query, so a non-leader costs nothing per cycle rather than one query per process per interval, and failure is isolated PER TENANT -- one unreachable venue or one unloadable credential does not cost the other tenants their reconciliation in that cycle. tests/test_recon01_tenant_enumeration.py: 16 tests covering the empty production state, both open statuses, rows with no venue id (not enumerated), legacy-order_id-only rows (still enumerated), venue_order_id-only rows, distinctness, one tenant at two venues, two tenants, non-scaling with closed history, the loop reconciling every pair, a non-leader reconciling nothing, per-tenant failure isolation, and an empty cycle being a no-op. Regression: 215 passed / 24 skipped across the recon/leader/p10d selection, with both pre-existing posture tests untouched and still passing. ||| FINAL DISPOSITION (Kiro). BOTH BLOCKERS NAMED IN THIS ENTRY'S OWN TITLE ARE CLOSED, A THIRD DEFECT THAT WOULD HAVE FIRED ON THE FIRST CYCLE WAS FOUND AND FIXED, AND THE SERVICE IS STILL DELIBERATELY NOT STARTED -- for a reason different from the one previously recorded. HOW THIS WAS REACHED: the previous plan here was to host the loop in the web process with leader election plus a heartbeat, because the worker route looked blocked. Before writing that, the one claim in this entry that had never been tested was tested -- the p10d test's assertion that 'OrderWatchdog already runs a reconciliation loop over the same execution_records rows'. It is TRUE, and it is live: backend_app/main.py constructs OrderWatchdog and awaits .start() in the lifespan (service_status['order_watchdog']='ACTIVE'), its _reconciliation_loop polls the same PENDING/EXECUTING population every 5-10s, and RT-16 gave it a real per-tenant executor via _get_executor_for_order. So the capability RECON-01 exists to guarantee -- open orders are checked against the venue -- IS already provided in production, by another route, which was not the case when this entry was written. THE DEFECT THIS INVESTIGATION FOUND, and the reason starting the service would have been actively harmful rather than merely unhosted: reconcile_open_orders compared the two sides of the reconciliation BY TWO DIFFERENT KEYS. The exchange side is keyed by the venue's id (it has no other); every DB-side lookup used db_order.order_id alone -- at the CASE 2/3 match (exchange_orders_by_id.get(db_order.order_id)), inside _find_db_order_by_exchange_id (order.order_id == exchange_order_id), and at _handle_missing_exchange_order's authoritative-query guard (and db_order.order_id). TRADE-12 split those identifiers apart deliberately: order_id carries the FK to orders(id) and is THIS platform's id, venue_order_id is the exchange's, and the live engine writes the venue id to venue_order_id leaving order_id NULL. RT-16 had already found and fixed this exact blind spot in OrderWatchdog -- which is why OrderWatchdog.venue_identifier exists -- and this module did not import it. _fetch_db_active_orders applies no identifier filter, so engine rows ARE in the population. CONSEQUENCE, for one real resting order, on the same cycle: CASE 1 compared the venue's id against a NULL order_id, found no match, and declared the tenant's OWN genuine open order a ghost -- and _handle_ghost_order does not log, it db.add()s and db.commit()s a SECOND execution_records row (exec_ghost_<venue id>, status EXECUTING, strategy_id='reconciled', price=None) duplicating a row already present under its real execution_id; while CASE 2, looking the same order up by NULL, missed it and routed it to _handle_missing_exchange_order as absent from the venue. Fabricated duplicate position state for real money, not a missed check. THIS WAS ARMED BY CLOSING THIS ENTRY'S OWN ENUMERATION BLOCKER: enumerate_reconcilable_pairs WAS taught the TRADE-12 lesson and says so in its docstring, citing venue_identifier by name; the matching below it was not. So the enumeration fix widened the population to exactly the rows that mismatch. Nothing exercised the ghost path -- grepped: no test in the repo referenced _handle_ghost_order or INSERT_GHOST_ORDER before this change. FIXED: venue_identifier is now IMPORTED from order_watchdog and reused (not copied -- pinned by a test asserting the two are the same object and that no second definition exists in this module; no import cycle, order_watchdog does not import this module, and backend_app.main still imports clean). Applied at the CASE 2/3 match, inside _find_db_order_by_exchange_id (which also now refuses to pair on a null id, so two rows that both lack an identifier are not treated as the same order), at _handle_missing_exchange_order's guard and its fetch_order call, and across all 11 ReconciliationResult.exchange_order_id reporting fields -- a field named for the exchange's id that was reporting this platform's. Also removed a dead statement: `{o.execution_id: o for o in db_orders}`, a dict comprehension whose result was discarded. Also fixed get_reconciliation_service, which could not forward the `vault` parameter __init__ grew for per-tenant executor resolution -- so the single documented entry point could only ever build the unsafe single-shared-client shape this entry names as its own defect. REGRESSION + NEGATIVE CONTROL: tests/test_recon01_venue_identity_matching.py (12 tests). Negative control run by restoring HEAD's source with the new tests in place: 10 of 12 FAILED, including both headline properties -- the tenant's own order was declared a ghost, and an extra execution_records row was committed for it. The 2 that passed are honest: the order_id-only legacy row is backward compatible by construction, and the CASE 2 'not reported absent' property was already protected by p10d's own hardening, which logs RECONCILIATION WITHHELD and preserves state when no fetch_order is available (that log line was captured in the control run). Restored; all 12 pass. Wider regression: 87 passed across every recon/p10d/RT-16 file, then 344 passed / 10 skipped / 0 failed across the whole recon+watchdog+execution_record+order_control+rt16+rt21+exchange_executor selection. BLAST RADIUS IS ZERO BY MEASUREMENT: grepped for importers of this module across backend_app -- the only occurrence in production code is inside a COMMENT in exchange_websocket_listener.py describing the dead _fallback_poll body p10d already removed. The module has no live importer, so this hardening cannot change running behaviour; it makes the module safe for whenever it IS wired up. WHY IT IS STILL NOT STARTED -- restated from current measurement, because the two reasons previously recorded in the three posture tests had both expired and a reader who checked them would have found them false and reasonably deleted the tests: (1) _handle_ghost_order answers 'a venue order with no DB row' by MANUFACTURING an execution_records row with strategy_id='reconciled' and price=None -- an execution no strategy owns, created on a live-money path with no risk check. Whether the platform should invent position state for orders it cannot explain is an OWNER'S POLICY DECISION, not a wiring fix. (2) backend_app/core/models/execution_record.py:677 records the invariant directly -- 'OrderWatchdog is the only owner of adjudication, and introducing a second one would be worse than the defect' -- and OrderWatchdog is already started and already reconciles these rows. Starting this service adds the second owner that comment forbids. The three posture tests are therefore KEPT AND STILL PASSING, with their reasoning rewritten to the above rather than left citing closed blockers; a stale citation of tests/test_recon01_leader_election.py (a file that does not exist) is corrected to the real filename, and the module docstring claiming 'RECON-01's second blocker is still open -- nothing enumerates tenants' is corrected. OBSERVED AND NOT CHANGED, belonging to OrderWatchdog rather than here: the watchdog has NO leader election (grepped: no leader/lease/lock primitive, only a per-position SELECT ... FOR UPDATE with an explicit non-blocking fallback that proceeds unlocked), and startup.sh:102 runs gunicorn --workers ${WORKERS:-2}. So the 'N processes reconcile the same rows concurrently' condition this entry cites as disqualifying for the unstarted service is LIVE TODAY for the started one. That is an argument for fixing the running service, not for starting a second -- recorded here because it was measured here, and it is not RECON-01's to fix.
findings.verification_level: Source-measured and test-pinned, with a negative control against HEAD. NOT production-verified, and deliberately so: the service is not started, so there is nothing of it running in production to verify. The fix hardens a module with zero live importers. The claim that the equivalent capability IS live rests on reading backend_app/main.py's lifespan (OrderWatchdog constructed, .start() awaited) in current source, not on observing the deployed container.
findings.remaining_action: ONE OWNER DECISION, no engineering: should the platform create an execution_records row for a venue order it cannot attribute to any strategy (_handle_ghost_order's current behaviour -- strategy_id='reconciled', price=None, status EXECUTING, no risk check)? Answer 'no' and this entry is finished as-is: the two named blockers are closed, the identity defect is fixed, and OrderWatchdog already covers the lost-fill risk in production. Answer 'yes' and the ghost path needs an attribution and risk policy before the service is hosted anywhere. SEPARATELY, and tracked under INF-03 rather than here: if the service is ever to be hosted, the worker route needs an IAM change -- see INF-03's corrected entry. NOT A BLOCKER FOR LAUNCH on the evidence above, since the risk this entry names is already mitigated by a different, running component.

findings.title: Backtests, optimization trials and walk-forward windows ran on the most recent bars regardless of the requested start_date/end_date
findings.evidence: Discovered while investigating OPT-02 (walk-forward does not fit per-window parameters): confirmed the root cause is upstream of optimization_engine.py entirely. backend_app/backend/backtest_runtime.py::run_backtest logs start_date/end_date and stamps them onto the backtests row's metadata, then calls self.data_engine.fetch_historical_ohlcv(symbol=symbol, timeframe=timeframe, limit=10_000, max_retries=3) with NO date-range argument at all. backend_app/backend/data_seeking_engine.py::fetch_historical_ohlcv had no date-range parameter to pass -- with since=None it always answers 'the most recent N bars', per its own docstring. Grepped every start_date/end_date usage in backtest_runtime.py and confirmed neither is used to filter/select data anywhere. Consequence: a backtest requested over 2020 and one requested over 2023 fetched and ran on byte-identical data (whatever was most recent when called); every optimization trial, Monte Carlo run, sensitivity run and benchmark comparison inherited the same defect through the one shared run_backtest call; and a walk-forward window's train and test periods -- different date ranges by construction -- ran on that same identical data, which is what made genuine per-window parameter differentiation (OPT-02) structurally impossible regardless of how the optimization logic itself was fixed. Fixed by adding a second, optional since_ms/until_ms mode to fetch_historical_ohlcv (a new _fetch_ohlcv_bounded that pages FORWARD from since_ms, trimming rather than rounding past a page straddling until_ms) while leaving the existing no-argument 'most recent' mode completely untouched -- the existing DATA-01 regression suite (7 tests) still passes unmodified. Wired run_backtest to use it via a new _requested_window_ms(start_date, end_date) helper that converts the two ISO strings already received into (since_ms, until_ms), with an unreadable/blank date falling back to (None, None) -- the prior 'most recent' behaviour -- rather than a new failure mode. New tests/test_bt02_backtest_honors_requested_date_range.py (13 tests): the bounded fetch's exact-window, multi-page, mid-page-trim and open-vs-closed-window-warning behaviour; _requested_window_ms's ISO/naive-UTC/blank handling; and two end-to-end wiring tests proving run_backtest actually calls fetch_historical_ohlcv with the window implied by start_date/end_date, including that two DIFFERENT requested windows are passed two DIFFERENT bounds -- the exact guarantee OPT-02's per-window fit now depends on. Full regression: the untouched-path DATA-01 suite plus 10 other backtest/optimization test files (224 passed total).
findings.remaining_action: None at the code level for the data-fetch mechanism itself. This finding only makes per-window / per-date-range backtesting POSSIBLE; it does not itself change optimization_engine.py's walk-forward logic to actually use different windows for fitting -- that is OPT-02's own remaining scope, tracked separately. Also not addressed: fetch_historical_ohlcv's 10,000-bar cap could still truncate a very wide requested window silently (it already warns via the existing under-coverage path when the window is open-ended, but a closed window wider than the cap is trimmed to its first bars with no warning, by design, since a closed window's own date bound is what the caller asked for) -- not flagged separately since it matches the existing cap-and-warn contract this function already had for the no-range mode.

findings.title: _handle_ccxt_error misclassifies a network/timeout failure as a non-retryable InsufficientFundsError when its message mentions an unrelated operation name (e.g. fetch_balance)
findings.evidence: Surfaced by this session's EXT-01 corpus synthesis (staging/PHASE11B_*.md), left explicitly unverified and without its own ledger row at that time ('a future pass should read core's _handle_ccxt_error directly and decide whether to track it'). Independently re-verified against current source this session, not taken on faith: backend_app/backend/exchange_executor.py's CCXTExchangeExecutor._handle_ccxt_error classified errors by a fixed-order substring match that checked 'insufficient'/'balance' BEFORE 'network'/'timeout'/'connection' -- so a transient network error from an operation literally named fetch_balance (ccxt's own message text for a failed balance call, e.g. 'Request timeout fetching balance') matched the funds check first and was returned as InsufficientFundsError (retryable=False) instead of NetworkError (retryable=True). Confirmed the real blast radius before fixing anything: grepped the whole codebase for `.retryable` (read in exactly one place, a log line) and for `isinstance(..., InsufficientFundsError)`/`isinstance(..., NetworkError)` (zero hits anywhere) -- nothing branches on this misclassification's result, so it affects a log line's accuracy, not an actual retry decision or order safety, matching the corpus's own characterisation exactly. Fixed by classifying by ccxt's own exception type FIRST when the error is a recognised ccxt type (ccxt.async_support is already imported as `ccxt` in this file and already used for isinstance checks elsewhere) -- a type cannot be fooled by what operation name happens to appear in the message -- ordered most-specific-first (RateLimitExceeded before the broader NetworkError it nests under; InsufficientFunds/BadSymbol/InvalidOrder/AuthenticationError before the broader ExchangeError they nest under), wrapped in try/except TypeError so a test that patches `ccxt` out to a non-exception double falls through cleanly to the substring fallback. That fallback (for anything not a recognised ccxt type: a raw asyncio.TimeoutError, an aiohttp/OS error, or ccxt unavailable) is itself reordered -- network/timeout checked before insufficient/balance -- for the same reason. New tests/test_w6_ccxt_error_classification.py (9 tests): the exact W-6 scenario (a real ccxt.RequestTimeout/NetworkError mentioning 'balance'/'insufficient' is still classified NetworkError, retryable); a genuine InsufficientFunds/RateLimitExceeded/BadSymbol/AuthenticationError still classified correctly (no overcorrection); three non-ccxt fallback cases unchanged. Verified as real regression tests: git-stashed the fix and reran, 4 of 9 failed with exactly the predicted misclassification; restored and reran, all 9 pass. Full regression: tests/test_exchange_credential_log_redaction.py + test_dup02_ambiguous_submission_is_not_retried.py + tests/test_validation_sweep.py (410 passed, 2 skipped, 1 pre-existing unrelated failure confirmed via git stash to predate this change -- an EXCH-01 sandbox-verification log line, not this classifier).
findings.remaining_action: None identified. This closes the finding as the corpus originally scoped it (telemetry/alerting accuracy for a misclassified error type) -- it does not claim to have found or fixed every possible substring collision in the fallback path (still string-based for non-ccxt exceptions), only the specific balance/timeout collision the corpus named and the symmetric insufficient/network collision found while verifying it.

findings.title: The catalog-driven privilege-hardening check DB-03 built is never invoked by anything
findings.evidence: Found while running, for the first time in this remediation effort, the 37+ test files gated behind a real PostgreSQL DSN (this session provisioned a real, disposable local replica -- see TENANT-01's entry). scripts/post_migration_validation.py's fetch_privileged_tables_without_rls / evaluate_privilege_hardening (DB-03's own fix, status VERIFIED_FIXED, which correctly replaced a hardcoded table-name list with a catalog query) is exercised ONLY by its own test file -- grepped the whole repository (scripts/, backend_app/, every .github/workflows/*.yml) for any caller of validate_production_db or an import of the module: none, besides the test. Confirmed staging/run_all_probes.py (the probe suite .github/workflows/01-pr-check.yml's provisioning-and-isolation job actually runs) does not call it either. DB-03's own detection logic is correct and newly re-verified working this session (see the test fix below), but nothing in any CI job, deploy script, or migration step ever calls it against a real database -- it is written, tested, and inert. NOT as severe as it first looked: migrations/hardening/999_privilege_hardening.sql carries ITS OWN RAISE EXCEPTION backstop (SECTION 4, 'refuse to finish while a per-customer table is still exposed'), which DOES run automatically on every provision_database.py --apply and IS wired into that same CI job -- but it is deliberately narrower: it only flags a table that both grants anon a privilege AND carries an ownership column (user_id/tenant_id/profile_id/owner_id/author_id). Running DB-03's broader, uninvoked check against this session's own replica for the first time found exactly the gap between the two scopes: 5 real tables -- plans, plan_features, plan_limits, plan_prices, plan_migration_mapping (all from the single, never-revisited migrations/create_plan_tables.sql) -- grant anon/authenticated SELECT with RLS disabled, and 999's backstop correctly does not flag them because none carries an ownership column (confirmed by reading create_plan_tables.sql's own schema: id/key/name/plan_id/feature_key, no customer identity anywhere). This is global, non-tenant pricing/plan-catalog data -- SELECT-only, publicly cacheable, arguably correct to leave world-readable the way a pricing page needs to be -- not the per-customer leak DB-03's title or 999's backstop are both actually worried about. Separately confirmed this session's own real-Postgres finding that matters more generally: on this Supabase-shaped substrate, ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES grants anon/authenticated the FULL DML set (not just SELECT) on every bare CREATE TABLE automatically, verified directly against a fresh scratch table with no GRANT ever issued. Fixed the 2 stale tests in test_db03_privilege_hardening_detects_untracked_tables_postgres.py this same default-privilege behaviour broke (see commit c5a611d) -- that fix re-verified DB-03's own detector logic is sound; it does not wire the detector into anything. RESOLVED this session (commit 309d507): item (1) of this entry's own remaining_action, done. Added PUBLIC_CATALOG_TABLES (the 5 tables named above) + partition_privileged_tables() to apply it without special-casing table names inside evaluate_privilege_hardening() itself, then wired scripts/post_migration_validation.py into .github/workflows/01-pr-check.yml's provisioning-and-isolation job, after schema provisioning and before the existing PostgreSQL test lane. Verified first that the script's other five sections (table/column/RPC existence, metadata export) already pass cleanly against a real, fully-provisioned replica, so nothing unrelated to this fix risked a new CI failure. tests/test_db03_privilege_hardening_pure_logic.py (+4) + new tests/test_db04_privilege_hardening_script_is_wired_into_ci.py (3): negative-control verified, all 7 fail with the predicted symptom pre-fix, pass restored. Regression: full DB-03/DB-04 suite + validation_sweep.py (376 passed, 2 skipped, unchanged baseline) clean.
findings.verification_level: code+test (verified this session against real Postgres); CI wiring confirmed statically, not yet observed on a real GitHub Actions run
findings.remaining_action: Item (2) of this entry's own remaining_action is unchanged, and correctly so: whether plans/plan_features/plan_limits/plan_prices/plan_migration_mapping should have RLS enabled anyway (even with a permissive USING (true) policy) purely for documentation/consistency is a human product decision, not a security gap -- not attempted, not needed to close this finding. The CI wiring itself has not been observed passing on a real GitHub Actions run (this sandbox has none); it was verified by running the exact same script, with the exact same provisioning this job performs, against a real local replica, and by a static check that the workflow YAML actually invokes it in the right place -- the same verification-level gap this ledger already carries for every other workflow-file change made without a live Actions run to observe.

findings.title: The ALB's own public DNS name serves plaintext HTTP directly, bypassing CloudFront's TLS entirely, with the security group open to 0.0.0.0/0
findings.evidence: Surfaced this session by running checkov (a local, pip-installable Trivy-equivalent IaC scanner; CI-03's own remaining_action named Trivy CRITICAL findings that could not be reproduced for lack of a reachable binary -- checkov closes that gap) against terraform/, then independently verifying the flagged resources in source rather than trusting the scanner's framing alone. Confirmed directly: terraform/security_groups.tf's aws_security_group.alb allows ingress on port 80 (HTTP) from cidr_blocks=["0.0.0.0/0"] -- open to the entire internet, not just CloudFront. terraform/alb.tf's own code comment (lines ~89-101, written by a prior session) already documents the exact risk: "no HTTPS listener at all (count = 0)... the API and WebSocket rules attach to this plaintext listener... every request, including Authorization headers and broker credentials, is served in clear text over port 80" -- gated behind a terraform `validation` block requiring enable_custom_domain=true for a prod/production environment, specifically to prevent this. BUT the real, already-deployed production ALB (confirmed this session via live AWS evidence gathered for API-07/BILL-02) has exactly one listener, on port 80 (HTTP), with a single default rule forwarding everything to the API target group -- no HTTPS listener exists on the real infrastructure, meaning either the validation was added after the real ALB was created, or the real deployment was provisioned outside this terraform's own apply path (consistent with INF-02/CI-02's already-documented terraform-vs-reality drift). The real ALB's DNS name independently, publicly resolves and is directly reachable (confirmed via the API-07 investigation, which used it to reach /metrics bypassing CloudFront) -- so this is not a theoretical gap the validation already closed, it is the live, current state of production.
findings.remaining_action: APPLIED with the user's direct, explicit confirmation in this session (commit 81c3163), accepting the no-access-logs blind spot this entry's own evidence already flagged. Added the CloudFront-prefix-list ingress rule on port 80 FIRST (AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress, pl-31a34658), THEN revoked the old 0.0.0.0/0:80 rule (RevokeSecurityGroupIngress) -- add-before-remove, so there was never a window with zero valid ingress on the port carrying real traffic. VERIFIED END TO END immediately after: the real app domain through CloudFront (https://app.vyomquant.in/health) still returns 200; the ALB's own raw public hostname now times out (the bypass is closed); the API target stayed `healthy` throughout, checked both immediately and after a delay. Port 443's old 0.0.0.0/0 rule was also revoked, but WITHOUT a CloudFront-scoped replacement: AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress for it failed with RulesPerSecurityGroupLimitExceeded -- the CloudFront prefix list has 49 entries, each counting toward this account's default 60-rules-per-security-group quota, and port 80's own rule (plus the two pre-existing plain-CIDR rules) had nearly exhausted it. Since the real ALB has no HTTPS listener at all today (reconfirmed), port 443 having NO ingress rule is strictly safer than 0.0.0.0/0 and breaks nothing live -- net security improvement, just not symmetric with port 80's fix. Re-adding a scoped :443 rule once a real HTTPS listener exists will need either an EC2 security-group-rules-per-group quota increase or consolidating this group's other rule usage first -- flagged as the one residual, not something this pass could complete. RECONCILED with API-07 (also applied this session, commit 9747cda): this fix closes the raw-ALB-hostname bypass for every route; API-07's header-gated listener rule remains necessary on top of it for /metrics specifically, since CloudFront's own cache behavior still forwards that path through with no auth check otherwise -- both are applied, neither superseded the other. The deeper, longer-term fix (a real ACM certificate + working HTTPS listener, true end-to-end TLS) still needs a domain/certificate decision this session cannot make; this SG restriction is the faster mitigation matching AWS's own standard CloudFront-to-ALB reference pattern.

findings.title: Redis has no AUTH token anywhere in source; any task that can reach port 6379 connects with zero authentication
findings.evidence: Surfaced by the same checkov sweep that found SEC-17 (CKV_AWS_31: 'Ensure all data stored in the ElastiCache Replication Group is securely encrypted at transit and has auth token'). Confirmed in source: terraform/redis.tf's aws_elasticache_replication_group.redis and both replication groups in terraform/redis-only/main.tf set at_rest_encryption_enabled=true and transit_encryption_enabled=true, but none sets auth_token -- grepped all three resource definitions and the whole terraform/ tree for 'auth_token': zero matches. terraform/secrets.tf (the existing pattern for every other credential this platform stores -- database_url, supabase_key, jwt_secret, master_encryption_keys, credential_vault_salt) has no redis-auth-token secret either, so there is nothing to wire even if auth_token were added to the resource. backend_app/core/config.py reads a single REDIS_URL env var with no separate password field referenced anywhere in core/cache/redis_manager.py. The security group (terraform/security_groups.tf's aws_security_group.redis) does correctly restrict ingress on 6379 to aws_security_group.ecs_tasks only, not 0.0.0.0/0 -- this is NOT an internet-facing exposure like SEC-17; it requires an attacker to already have network reach from inside an ECS task (a compromised dependency, an SSRF, lateral movement from another container in the same cluster) before this gap is reachable at all. What makes it worth tracking at P2 rather than dismissing as defense-in-depth noise: this session's own earlier work (RED-01, KILL-01) spent real effort making SharedRedisManager's safety-critical callers -- the kill-switch latch, the FIN-CRITICAL-004 atomic idempotency check, quota/rate-limit enforcement -- fail closed specifically because Redis itself was assumed untrustworthy on FAILURE. An unauthenticated Redis extends that same untrusted-by-default posture to Redis being directly WRITABLE by anything on the right network segment, not just unavailable -- a compromised task could flip the kill-switch state, forge an idempotency lock to let a duplicate order through, or reset quota counters, not merely cause a timeout the existing fail-closed code already handles correctly.
findings.verification_level: code (source + secrets.tf cross-check) + real AWS confirmation (DescribeReplicationGroups); AUTH enablement itself BLOCKED on a genuine permission denial
findings.remaining_action: ATTEMPTED to execute the rollout this session with the user's direct, explicit confirmation -- BLOCKED at the first real step. `iam:SimulatePrincipalPolicy` confirms `elasticache:ModifyReplicationGroup` is an implicitDeny for this session's credential: no attached policy grants it (IAMFullAccess/AmazonEC2FullAccess/AmazonECS_FullAccess/SecretsManagerReadWrite are attached; nothing ElastiCache-related is). This is a genuine AWS-side denial, confirmed via the policy simulator, not attempted as a live test call against a replication group backing kill-switch/idempotency state -- deliberately did not run the real ROTATE call just to see whether it would also fail live, since a safety-critical resource is the wrong place to probe a permission boundary experimentally. Did what was possible without that permission: generated the real 64-char hex token and created both secrets (vyomquant/production/redis_url, vyomquant/production/redis_replica_url) via secretsmanager:CreateSecret (allowed), with the token embedded in the full rediss:// connection string exactly as designed -- each secret's own description states explicitly that it is NOT YET ACTIVE, since AuthTokenEnabled is still false on the real vyomquant-redis-production-cmd replication group. terraform/redis-only/main.tf was deliberately NOT updated to add auth_token -- doing so would document a state that isn't true yet, unlike CI-02/API-07/SEC-17 where terraform was updated to match an already-applied reality. STILL OPEN: the actual gap (Redis reachable from any ECS task with zero authentication) is unchanged -- only secret scaffolding exists now, ready for whenever a credential with elasticache:ModifyReplicationGroup is available. CONFIRMED directly against the real account: `elasticache DescribeReplicationGroups` (unfiltered this time) shows TWO replication groups, both AuthTokenEnabled=false -- vyomquant-redis-production (ClusterEnabled=true, this file's own comment calls it 'deprecated') and vyomquant-redis-production-cmd (ClusterEnabled=false, 'production'). CORRECTION: the real running task definition's own REDIS_URL/REDIS_REPLICA_URL (rediss://master.vyomquant-redis-production-cmd..., rediss://replica.vyomquant-redis-production-cmd...) prove the app actually connects to -cmd, not the plain one this entry originally named -- -cmd is the one any rollout must target; the plain one looks like an orphaned, still-billing, still-unauthenticated resource with no identified consumer (one-line follow-up, not part of this rollout). DESIGNED THIS SESSION (with explicit authority to move from 'confirm only' to 'design the rollout', still NOT applied): full write-up in scratchpad sec18_redis_auth_rollout_design.md. Key findings: (1) NO application code change is needed -- read core's redis_manager.py's get_redis_url() in full: REDIS_URL already takes precedence and its netloc (where embedded credentials live) survives untouched when the function reconstructs the URL per-DB, so embedding the token in REDIS_URL/REDIS_REPLICA_URL's own value is sufficient. (2) Two new secrets matching secrets.tf's existing per-credential-string pattern (redis_url, redis_replica_url -- full rediss:// URLs with the token embedded, same shape as database_url's own DSN). (3) CORRECTED the SET/ROTATE order from this entry's own prior (wrong) assumption via web research against AWS's documented ElastiCache AUTH semantics: ROTATE is the non-disruptive step that adds a token while STILL accepting unauthenticated connections (the right first step for a replication group with AuthTokenEnabled=false, this case exactly); SET is the disruptive step that removes unauthenticated-connection support, and must come LAST, only once every real client already has the token -- the reverse of what 'SET first... then require it' implied. Flagged this should still be re-confirmed against AWS's live documentation page directly before anyone runs it (this session only had web-search summaries, not the full page, and a conflicting third-party source exists). (4) A full ROTATE-verify-deploy-verify-SET rollout checklist with rollback guidance, keyed to this exact topology (dual-mode safety net before SET, no clean rollback after it -- which is itself the reason to soak-test thoroughly before that step, not a reason to rush it). (5) terraform/redis-only/main.tf's matching resource has no state in this account and no ignore_changes guard (unlike its deprecated sibling) -- recommending the real enablement happen via raw `aws elasticache modify-replication-group` calls, not `terraform apply`, with terraform updated to describe the result afterward, not to perform it. Still genuinely not a quick fix, still recommending a dedicated, unhurried pass to execute it -- this is preparedness so that future pass isn't improvised, not a signal it's now safe to rush.

findings.title: Alembic's BUG-033 and BUG-049 migrations (tenant_id/user_id -> uuid + FK) were never actually applied to production, despite the model code and DB-ALM-01's own remediation note assuming otherwise
findings.evidence: Discovered this session while verifying TENANT-01's migration 047 against the real production database: backend_app/core/models/billing.py declares payment_methods.user_id as a SQLAlchemy Uuid column, citing alembic revision d4e5f6a7b8c9 (BUG-049, 'normalise customer-identity columns to uuid and declare their foreign keys') as having already applied this. Querying the REAL production schema directly found user_id is still `character varying`, not uuid -- the ORM model's own assumption is false against the real database. Traced the full alembic revision graph (backend_app/alembic/versions/*.py) and queried the real production alembic_version table directly: it reads `d97ffff9c3bb` (execution_schema_rebuild), which is the EARLIEST point in the entire chain -- before the e88f9911b5a2/add_foreign_keys branch even forks, before merge_heads, before a1b2c3d4e5f6 (BUG-033, the tenant_id sibling d4e5f6a7b8c9's own docstring calls 'already fixed'), before b2c3d4e5f6a7 and c3d4e5f6a7b8, and long before d4e5f6a7b8c9 itself. Yet the real database plainly has referrals tables with real rows and RLS enabled on every table -- features those later revisions are themselves supposed to add -- proving production was never actually migrated forward via `alembic upgrade head` at all; it is built and maintained entirely through this platform's separate, parallel raw-SQL system (backend_app/migrations/001...047.sql), a structural fact DB-ALM-01 already named the DANGER of (running the alembic chain from scratch against this kind of already-provisioned database would DROP real tables) but did not itself check the real alembic_version value or the real column types, which this session did. Checked both migrations' full scope directly against the real schema: of BUG-049's 12 target columns, only exchange_keys.user_id is uuid (converted by some OTHER, untracked mechanism -- not by this alembic revision, and not by any grep match in backend_app/migrations/*.sql either); the other 11 (exchange_connections, notification_settings, referral_profiles, risk_settings, strategy_limits, billing_invoices, invoices, payment_methods, subscriptions, risk_settings_audit, security_logs) are all still their original text/varchar type. Of BUG-033's 10 target tenant_id columns, only execution_records and reconciliation_mismatches are uuid (same pattern -- converted some other way); the other 8 (dag_tasks, fills, idempotency_keys, orders, positions, transaction_checkpoints, transaction_records, transaction_rollbacks) remain varchar. Checked the actual payoff of the type conversion that DID happen on exchange_keys -- a `fk_bug049_*`-prefixed foreign key to profiles(id), which is the specific protection BUG-049's own docstring calls the worst-case risk ('encrypted exchange API credentials outliving the account that owned them'): zero `fk_bug049_%` constraints exist anywhere in the real schema, confirmed via pg_constraint. There are currently zero orphaned exchange_keys rows (checked directly), so there is no live incident today, but nothing in the real schema prevents one, and the FK add was never confirmed happening at all, for any of the 12 target columns. THIS SESSION, with the user's explicit go-ahead to proceed on this finding specifically: picked option (b) from this entry's own two options -- did NOT attempt alembic upgrade_head (the real alembic_version is stuck at the earliest point in the chain, d97ffff9c3bb, and running the intervening revisions against a database that diverged via the parallel raw-SQL system risks exactly the DROP-real-tables danger DB-ALM-01 already named) -- and instead applied the specific column conversions and FK additions directly, following the alembic files' own logic (preflight UUID-shape scan refusing on any bad row, postflight re-verification) but executed as plain SQL via the Supabase MCP server rather than through alembic itself. BEFORE touching anything, checked which of BUG-033's 8 tenant_id columns + 1 id column and BUG-049's 12 user_id columns actually have an RLS POLICY referencing them (queried pg_policies directly), because PostgreSQL refuses ALTER COLUMN TYPE on a column any policy's qual/with_check references, and a1b2c3d4e5f6's own _drop_policies/_restore_policies functions exist specifically to work around that -- DROP POLICY is, however, one of the DROP-family statements this session's Supabase MCP execute_sql tool times out on unconditionally (confirmed directly: DROP POLICY IF EXISTS on a policy name that does not even exist still hangs 60s, ruling out a lock/contention explanation), so that drop/alter/recreate cycle cannot be executed through this tool at all. Result of the policy check: 14 of the 18 non-already-uuid target columns (all 11 of BUG-049's targets -- exchange_connections, notification_settings, referral_profiles, risk_settings, strategy_limits, billing_invoices, invoices, payment_methods, subscriptions, risk_settings_audit, security_logs -- plus 3 of BUG-033's -- orders, positions, fills) have an owner-access RLS policy directly comparing auth.uid() to the target column, and are therefore BLOCKED by this tool limitation, exactly like MKT-04's DROP INDEX. The remaining 6 columns across 5 tables -- dag_tasks.tenant_id, dag_tasks.task_id, idempotency_keys.tenant_id, transaction_records.tenant_id, transaction_checkpoints.tenant_id, transaction_rollbacks.tenant_id -- have NO policy referencing them at all (confirmed: zero rows for these tables in pg_policies), so they needed no drop/recreate step and were safe to convert directly. Preflight re-verified directly against production for all 6 (not assumed from the ledger's own prior general statement): zero non-UUID-shaped values in any of them. Converted all 6 via ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE uuid USING ...::uuid. Then checked which of a1b2c3d4e5f6's 7 target foreign keys were newly addable: fk_dag_tasks_tenant_id (dag_tasks.tenant_id -> profiles.id) and fk_execution_records_task_id (execution_records.task_id uuid -> dag_tasks.task_id, now uuid) became addable from today's conversions; fk_execution_records_tenant_id (execution_records.tenant_id -> profiles.id) was ALREADY addable before today's work -- execution_records.tenant_id was already uuid (confirmed directly, matching this entry's own earlier note that execution_records was converted by 'some other, untracked mechanism') -- it simply had never been added. Checked all three for orphaned rows first (zero in every case) and added all three; re-queried pg_constraint afterward to confirm all three exist. fk_fills_tenant_id, fk_orders_tenant_id, fk_positions_tenant_id, fk_execution_records_order_id remain NOT addable: the first three need orders/positions/fills.tenant_id converted, which is in the 14-table policy-blocked set; the fourth needs orders.id/execution_records.order_id type-matching, out of this pass's scope (not a tenant_id/user_id column).
findings.verification_level: production (direct, real ALTER TABLE/ADD CONSTRAINT against the real Supabase project via the Supabase MCP server, each re-queried from information_schema/pg_catalog afterward -- not inferred)
findings.remaining_action: Real, concrete progress this session: 6 of BUG-033's 9 target columns are now uuid in production (dag_tasks.tenant_id, dag_tasks.task_id, idempotency_keys.tenant_id, transaction_records.tenant_id, transaction_checkpoints.tenant_id, transaction_rollbacks.tenant_id), and 3 of its 7 target foreign keys now exist (fk_dag_tasks_tenant_id, fk_execution_records_task_id, fk_execution_records_tenant_id) -- all re-verified directly against the real schema, not assumed. NONE of BUG-049's 11 remaining varchar/text user_id columns were touched -- every single one of them has an RLS policy referencing it, so all 11 are blocked by the same DROP-POLICY tool limitation as the 3 still-varchar BUG-033 columns (orders, positions, fills tenant_id) and MKT-04's DROP INDEX. WHAT IS NOW GENUINELY NEEDED, AND ONLY THIS: someone with a direct Postgres session (psql, or the Supabase dashboard's own SQL editor -- anything that is not this session's Supabase-MCP execute_sql tool, which cannot run DROP POLICY at all, timing out even on one that does not exist) needs to run, per remaining table, the same three-step cycle a1b2c3d4e5f6's own _drop_policies/_restore_policies functions already automate: capture each table's policies from pg_policies (qual/with_check/roles/cmd), DROP POLICY each one, run the ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE uuid USING ...::uuid (the preflight UUID-shape check this session already re-ran for the 6 safe columns should be re-run for these too, since production data can differ), then CREATE POLICY each one back verbatim from what was captured. Do this for: orders.tenant_id, positions.tenant_id, fills.tenant_id (unblocks fk_orders_tenant_id/fk_positions_tenant_id/fk_fills_tenant_id), and all 11 of exchange_connections/notification_settings/referral_profiles/risk_settings/strategy_limits/billing_invoices/invoices/payment_methods/subscriptions/risk_settings_audit/security_logs.user_id (BUG-049's targets, which also need the FK additions d4e5f6a7b8c9 itself declares -- read that file, not yet read this session, before doing this half). The actual Python alembic revisions (a1b2c3d4e5f6, d4e5f6a7b8c9) already contain this exact logic end-to-end and could simply be run directly against production with a real psql/direct connection (NOT via `alembic upgrade head`, which would also try to run every OTHER unapplied revision in between -- run `alembic upgrade a1b2c3d4e5f6` then `alembic upgrade d4e5f6a7b8c9` specifically, or extract and run just their upgrade() logic by hand) rather than needing to be re-derived as raw SQL again. Still true from this entry's prior text: alembic_version itself was never advanced (still d97ffff9c3bb) and a correct stamp target needs re-deriving against the real schema's current state, not just these two revisions' own position in the graph, since many other revisions between d97ffff9c3bb and head describe effects already present via the raw-SQL path.

findings.title: A missing import-name mapping in dependency_audit.py has silently gated out every downstream CI job on this branch -- Unit & Integration Tests, Database Tests, Execution Tests, Docker Build, Provisioning/Tenant Isolation have never actually run on GitHub Actions
findings.evidence: Discovered while checking TEST-01's own last open item ('the reliable next step remains opening a PR and reading the real 01-pr-check.yml unit-tests job result from GitHub Actions') against real GitHub Actions data, using the GitHub MCP tools available in this session for the first time. Checked the latest run of 01-pr-check.yml on this branch (run 39048975752, commit 641ba04) job by job: 'Code Quality & Static Audit' fails at its 'Automated Dependency Audit' step, and every downstream job -- 'Unit & Integration Tests', 'Database Tests (PostgreSQL)', 'Execution Tests (production posture)', 'Provisioning, Privilege Hardening & Tenant Isolation', 'Docker Build Validation' -- shows conclusion=skipped, because the workflow's own job-dependency graph gates all of them behind that one job succeeding. Pulled the real job log: scripts/dependency_audit.py reports 'Imported but not declared: 1 -- psycopg2 (mapped to: psycopg2)' and exits 1. Read the script: it scans backend_app/ for third-party imports (found in backend_app/core/bot_ownership.py, a pre-existing file unrelated to this remediation effort), maps the import name through PACKAGE_NAME_MAPPINGS to a PyPI package name, then checks that name against requirements-base.txt's own declared packages. requirements-base.txt already pins psycopg2-binary==2.9.9 -- the package genuinely IS declared -- but PACKAGE_NAME_MAPPINGS had no entry teaching the script that the import name psycopg2 corresponds to the PyPI package psycopg2-binary (unlike the dotenv/jwt/sklearn/yaml/cv2 entries already present for exactly this kind of import-name-vs-package-name mismatch), so the script looked for a package literally named 'psycopg2' and never found one. Checked every one of the last several runs on this branch: all show this same failure, meaning this specific set of downstream jobs has not actually executed via GitHub Actions on this branch at any point in this remediation effort -- every claim in this ledger of the form 'verified this session' for a Postgres-gated or full-suite test file was verified locally, against this session's own sandboxed Postgres replica, never against the real CI job this repository's own pipeline runs before a merge. Fixed with a single added mapping entry ('psycopg2': 'psycopg2-binary'), commit de9c3ed. Negative-control verified locally: git-stashed the one-line fix, reran scripts/dependency_audit.py directly, reproduced 'Imported but not declared: 1' / exit 1 exactly; restored, 'Imported but not declared: 0' / exit 0. VERIFIED FOR REAL this session: merged via PR #23 into main; the real push-triggered run (39051999222, commit 569e70e) shows 'Automated Dependency Audit' conclusion=success -- the first successful run of this step in this branch's entire history. The whole 'Code Quality & Static Audit' job passed, and for the first time ever on this branch, every downstream job actually started running (not skipped): Database Tests (PostgreSQL), Unit & Integration Tests, Docker Build Validation, Provisioning/Privilege Hardening & Tenant Isolation, Execution Tests (production posture) were all observed in_progress rather than conclusion=skipped. CLOSED THIS SESSION with the evidence this entry explicitly asked a future reader to go and get ("check back on run 39051999222 directly rather than assuming success"). Read the real GitHub Actions result for the newest 01-pr-check.yml run on main, run 39695784610, head dfd9ca24 (the merge of PR #51): ALL 8 jobs conclude success, including every one of the five this finding recorded as silently skipped -- Unit & Integration Tests (14,652 passed, 790 skipped, 343 deselected, 6 xfailed, 3 xpassed, 0 failed, 797.97s), Database Tests (PostgreSQL) (26 passed, 1 deselected), Execution Tests (production posture) (275 passed, 1 xfailed), Provisioning/Privilege Hardening & Tenant Isolation (RESULT: NO DRIFT; 233 passed, 7 skipped; then 22 passed, 13 deselected), and Docker Build Validation (success). Code Quality & Static Audit -- the job whose dependency-audit step was CI-06's actual defect -- passes, which is what lets the other five run at all. ADDITIONALLY, the nine failures CI-09's entry recorded as remaining in the full Unit & Integration lane are now ZERO: that run's summary line carries no 'failed' count and the log contains no FAILURES section and no short-test-summary block. findings.title: The real backend has not been deployed since 2026-10-05 -- every merge to main for this entire remediation effort has failed its deploy gate, so none of this effort's application-code fixes are live in production
findings.evidence:
Discovered while checking CI-03's own claim that '06 Frontend Deploy' now runs a version-match comparison against real production. Used the GitHub MCP tools to list every real '03 Deploy' (backend) and '06 Frontend Deploy' (frontend) workflow run on main. '03 Deploy' has run 248 times; the LAST ONE with conclusion=success is commit 074b772a, dated 2026-10-05T18:20:19Z ('Give the deploy gate permission to read the answer it refuses') -- before 'launch phase 1' (2026-10-11), before 'phase 2 launch', and before this remediation branch's own first commit (2026-10-14). EVERY merge to main since then -- PRs #10 through #22, every one of which the repo owner merged themselves via the normal GitHub UI, believing each merge would ship the work -- has produced a FAILING or SKIPPED '03 Deploy' run. The real ECS service (vyomquant-api-service-cjema2sl, confirmed via the AWS session's own SEC-01 reconnaissance this session) has been running whatever code commit 074b772a built for twelve days, through this entire multi-session remediation effort -- RT-01 through RT-25, every SEC-*, AUD-01, TENANT-01's own application-code half, every FE-*, all of it exists only in this repository, tested locally or against this session's own disposable Postgres replica, and has never reached the real running backend. '06 Frontend Deploy' shows the same pattern on its own gate. ROOT CAUSE, confirmed at the job level for multiple real runs (PR #17's and #22's merges checked directly): '03 Deploy''s 'Pre-Deployment Validation Gate' job fails at its FIRST step, 'Require the security scan to have passed for this commit' (scripts/require_security_scan.py, checking 05-security.yml's conclusion for the exact deploy SHA) -- which fails on CI-05's own pre-existing Trivy IaC CRITICAL finding (unrestricted egress on the alb/ecs_tasks/redis security groups), a finding unrelated to anything this remediation effort changed. That gate fails FAST (within ~1 second, since it only reads an already-completed run's conclusion) and short-circuits before the second step, 'Require the test workflow to have passed' (which would ALSO fail, on CI-06's psycopg2 mapping gap, if the security gate ever passed). '06 Frontend Deploy' has only the second gate (CI-06's), so it fails for that reason alone. Both CI-05 and CI-06 must be resolved before a real backend deploy can succeed; CI-06 alone is sufficient to unblock the frontend deploy. CRITICAL, SPECIFIC CONSEQUENCE FOR TENANT-01: migration 047 (the new payment_methods_app role, grants and RLS policies) WAS applied directly against the real production Supabase database this session and is genuinely live at the database layer -- but routers/billing.py's actual change (get_payment_methods/delete_payment_method depending on get_payment_methods_db instead of get_db) is application code, and per this finding has never been deployed. The REAL RUNNING BACKEND right now still calls these two routes through the OLD get_db dependency (the table-owner/superuser connection), so TENANT-01's actual protection is NOT active in production despite the database-side migration being live -- see TENANT-01's own entry, corrected accordingly. The same caveat applies, to varying degrees, to every other ledger entry whose 'production_verified' was based on code+test verification alone rather than a direct AWS/DB-API action: the code is real and tested, but 'is it live in the system real users and real money currently run against' is a NO for all of it until a real deploy succeeds.

Root cause corrected this session: 03-deploy.yml's 'Pre-Deployment Validation Gate' requires BOTH scripts/require_security_scan.py (05 Security passed for the exact deploy SHA) AND scripts/require_tests_passed.py (01 PR Check passed for the exact deploy SHA) -- confirmed directly from the real job log of the most recent deploy attempt (run 39396561836, commit 5d8665a, merge of PR #38): 'SECURITY GATE: ... PASSED' immediately followed by 'TEST GATE: ... REFUSING: 01 PR Check concluded failure'. 05 Security (which includes CI-05's Trivy IaC gate, now separately confirmed VERIFIED_FIXED above) has in fact been passing on main for some time -- this entry's own prior framing, that CI-05's egress findings were the active blocker, was already stale by the time this session re-checked it. The ACTUAL, current, sole blocker is 01 PR Check's own 'Unit & Integration Tests' job, which has never gone green on main throughout this remediation effort (see CI-09, now closed to 9 known failures) because of the drift-guard cluster this session also closed: 5 test_baseline_unchanged parametrizations (stale baselines for already-authorised AUTH-01/RL-02/SEC-12 fixes, re-recorded with provenance notes), test_schema_table_reference_drift.py (PRIV-01's new export/deletion code, not a regression), test_save_performs_no_backtest.py and test_p10d_exchange_reconciliation_fails_safely.py (both false positives in the tests themselves), and test_terraform_iam_ssm_scoping.py (also a test false positive, already merged via PR #39). CI-06 (de9c3ed) and CI-05 (0e6f37c) are both already on main, so neither is a prerequisite still outstanding.

CONFIRMED, this session: PR #42 merged to main as commit 11c8387. '01 PR Check' (run 39402885463) concluded SUCCESS on that commit -- the first time this has happened on main throughout this entire remediation effort. '03 Deploy' then ran (run 39403975551) and BOTH of its jobs succeeded: 'Pre-Deployment Validation Gate' (both require_security_scan.py and require_tests_passed.py passed for the exact deploy SHA) and 'ECS Fargate Deploy & Self-Healing Diagnostics' (ECR artifact verified, 'Execute Automated Deployment & Self-Healing Diagnostic Engine' step completed successfully). findings.title: 01-pr-check.yml's Database Tests (PostgreSQL) job never created the auth.users/auth.uid() substrate, so tests/test_atomic_order_cancellation_fix.py's autouse fixture failed on every run
findings.evidence: Root-caused against the real job log for run 39051999222 (PR #23's merge commit, job_id 117452877623, 'Database Tests (PostgreSQL)'): pytest summary `23 passed, 1 deselected, 16 warnings, 3 errors`, all 3 errors in tests/test_atomic_order_cancellation_fix.py (test_atomic_order_cancellation, test_concurrent_order_cancellation, test_order_cancellation_idempotency), each `sqlalchemy.exc.ProgrammingError: relation "auth.users" does not exist` on the autouse `_seeded_tenant` fixture's `INSERT INTO auth.users ...`. The job's own 'Provision schema' step only runs `alembic upgrade d97ffff9c3bb` against a bare postgres:17-alpine service container -- it never calls scripts/provision_database.py, so the Supabase-platform `auth` schema (which no alembic revision in this repo creates, correctly, since Supabase provides it) never exists here, unlike the separate 'Provisioning the full schema from repository source' job which runs `provision_database.py --create-substrate`. Confirmed the fixture's own docstring states the exact dependency: 'auth.users is seeded first ... because profiles.id references it.' Fixed by adding a new `--only-substrate` flag to provision_database.py (applies the existing SUBSTRATE_DDL -- auth.users, auth.uid(), auth.role(), auth.jwt(), the anon/authenticated/service_role roles -- and returns before steps 0/0b/1/3/4 and before invoking alembic at all) and a new CI step in the database-tests job that runs it immediately before the existing 'Provision schema' step. Verified locally with a throwaway pgserver instance before committing: `--only-substrate` creates auth.users/auth.uid()/auth.role()/auth.jwt(), the fixture's own `INSERT INTO auth.users` succeeds immediately afterward, and `public.profiles` / `public.schema_migrations` (the numbered-SQL-set and tracking tables) are confirmed NOT created -- i.e. the new flag only adds the substrate, nothing else, and does not risk interfering with this job's own alembic step that runs right after it.

findings.title: Now that CI-05..CI-08 finally let the full test suite execute, Unit & Integration Tests and Execution Tests (production posture) surface 45 pre-existing failures in execution-critical code -- never previously visible in any CI run on this branch
findings.evidence:
Run 39051999222 (PR #23's merge commit 569e70e), two jobs:

`Unit & Integration Tests` (job 117452877629): `40 failed, 14553 passed, 761 skipped, 343 deselected, 6 xfailed, 3 xpassed, 1026 warnings, 4 errors in 522.71s`. Named failures in the tail: test_trade04_live_order_gate_at_venue_boundary.py::test_risk_not_evaluated_blocks_the_exchange_write and ::test_risk_explicitly_rejected_blocks_the_exchange_write both assert 'submission_unknown' == 'failed' (got 'submission_unknown' instead) -- the venue-boundary gate is not labeling a risk-blocked order's status the way the test (and by implication some caller) expects. test_validation_sweep.py has 7 routes (strategies.create, strategy_operations.pause/resume/stop_deployment, strategy_operations.delete_backtest, signals.replay_signal_trace, billing.delete_payment_method) answering 500 instead of a handled 4xx; six of the seven 500 bodies show `"message":"[Errno -2] Name or service not known"` -- a DNS resolution failure reaching some configured hostname, not yet root-caused as either a genuine missing-error-handling defect or an artifact of this CI runner's network policy. tests/test_webhook_duplicate_delivery_real_redis.py has 4 ERRORs: 'the application cache manager REFUSED a write it was handed a real cache for (`set` returned False)' across all 4 of its tests (duplicate-delivery lock, different-event-id, in-flight-blocks-concurrent, invalid-signature).

`Execution Tests (production posture)` (job 117452877705): `5 failed, 270 passed, 1 xfailed, 15 warnings in 43.32s`. test_simulated_orders_reach_the_simulator.py has 2 failures: 'place_order reached=False, expected True' for both the <unstated>-True-LIVE-admitted and LIVE-True-LIVE-admitted parametrizations. test_single_execution_pipeline.py has 3 failures -- test_single_execution_gateway_flow, test_concurrent_idempotency_100_signals (assert 0 == 100), test_anti_bypass_validation_token_verification -- all logging the same CRITICAL line first: 'TRADE-07: could not record submission evidence for execution ... (OperationalError: (sqlite3.OperationalError) no such table: execution_records' -- this job's own SQLite database was never given the execution_records table before these tests ran, so execution_engine.py's TRADE-07 evidence-recording guard (by design) refuses every order rather than risk an unrecoverable row. This looks structurally like CI-08 (a job whose database setup is missing a table a test needs) rather than a defect in the gate itself, but has not yet been root-caused against this job's own provisioning step the way CI-08 was.

None of these 45 failures appear anywhere in this ledger's prior entries because neither job had ever actually executed on this branch before CI-06's fix (see CI-06); they were masked behind a dependency-audit false negative for this branch's entire history. This finding exists to make sure that discovery is not lost, not to assert each failure's root cause or fix -- those still need individual triage.

Follow-up triage, this ledger entry's own remaining_action items (2) and (4): (2) the six 'Name or service not known' 500s (plus a seventh route, signals.replay_signal_trace, found during the same pass) were confirmed by reading each route's source to construct its own Supabase/Stripe client independent of test_validation_sweep.py's 4 DI overrides -- a real environment gap (no network route to Supabase/Stripe from this sandbox), not a missing-error-handling defect, and not fixable by changing the routes. Fixed by adding the 6 missing route keys to the test's own named allowlist for exactly this case (`_ENVIRONMENT_GAP_ROUTE_KEYS`), which already existed and already held other routes with the identical gap -- it was just incomplete. Commit 5f1b492 (PR #37, merged). (4) the real-Redis cache manager's `set` returning False was root-caused to a cross-test event-loop leak: backend_app.backend.redis_manager.get_redis_manager() keeps its own module-level singleton holding redis.asyncio connections bound to whichever event loop was running when they opened, and its fast path keeps handing that same object back (its `._connected` never resets) even after pytest-asyncio closes that loop and hands the next test a new one. tests/conftest.py already reset the shared cache wrapper's own seams one layer up but never reached this deeper module. Reproduced locally against a real redis-server (any two of the file's tests run together fail this way; either alone passes). Fixed by adding a sibling autouse fixture that resets the deeper module's three globals after every test, forcing a fresh connection in the next test's own loop. Commit bce6009.

Full-suite closure, this session: ran the real `01-pr-check.yml` 'Unit & Integration Tests' job's exact command locally (`pytest tests/ --tb=line -k 'not chaos and not load' -m 'not frontend_bundle'`, same env vars) to completion for the first time this remediation effort has managed -- this entry's own earlier evidence already notes two prior attempts (3600s and 7200s budgets) were killed with no flushed output. All 9 remaining failures are already-known, already-triaged items, none of them new: 5 are tests/regression/test_baseline_unchanged.py's drift-guard parametrizations (surface_authentication/backtester/exchange_connection/sign_in/sign_up), 1 is test_p10d_exchange_reconciliation_fails_safely.py (ties to RECON-01's own not-yet-designed service-wiring decision), 1 is test_save_performs_no_backtest.py's importer-set pin, 1 is test_schema_table_reference_drift.py's coverage pin, and 1 was test_terraform_iam_ssm_scoping.py -- confirmed on inspection to be a FALSE POSITIVE, not a real security gap or a stale baseline: the test asserted `Resource = "*"` does not appear ANYWHERE in terraform/iam.tf, which started failing the moment CI-02's later OIDC deploy role addition to that same file legitimately used `Resource = "*"` on two unrelated, correctly-commented statements (ecr:GetAuthorizationToken, six ecs:* actions, neither of which supports resource-level scoping at all) -- the actual ssm:GetParameters resource this test is about was never un-scoped.
