findings.title: One kill-switch toggle issued TWO PUT /api/risk/settings requests: saveRiskConfig was called from inside a React state updater, which StrictMode double-invokes
findings.evidence: RECLASSIFIED from P2/Medium 'flaky frontend test' to P1/High. The flake was a SYMPTOM; the cause is a product defect in a risk-control write path, found by doing the instrumented local run this entry's own remaining_action asked for rather than leaving it labelled flaky. ORIGINAL OBSERVATION (unchanged, still accurate): algo22-terminal/tests/unit/pages/riskSettingsKillSwitch.test.jsx failed on three CI runs across two commits -- runs 39731286176 (both attempts) and 39755298417 on main, where every other job passed -- with 'expected "vi.fn()" to be called 1 times, but got 2 times', a DIFFERENT test case each time because they share one helper. THE CAUSE: RiskSettings.handleToggleSwitch called saveRiskConfig -- an async PUT /api/risk/settings -- from INSIDE the setKillSwitches updater, alongside a second setState. A React state updater must be pure, and src/main.jsx wraps the app in <React.StrictMode>, which DELIBERATELY double-invokes updaters to surface exactly this impurity. So every kill-switch toggle in the real application issued two writes. React also re-invokes updaters when rebasing during concurrent rendering, so a production build is not safe from it either, merely less reliably unsafe. MEASURED, not inferred -- reverting the handler and running the new test gives, every time: 'expected 1 times, but got 2 times' on the pointer path, the same on the keyboard path, and 'expected 2 times, but got 4 times' for two toggles. WHY THE DUPLICATE WAS NOT HARMLESS: the second PUT races the first's response handler, which writes res.data's limits back into the form via setMaxLoss/setMaxPos/setLeverage, so two in-flight writes can land out of order and leave the form AND the server holding something other than the user's last action -- on a kill switch. WHY IT PRESENTED AS FLAKE: that test file asserts the count with 'await waitFor(() => expect(risk.updateConfig).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1))'. An exact-count assertion inside a RETRYING waitFor is only safe while a second call is impossible, because waitFor polls until the callback stops throwing -- so whether it sees 1 or 2 depends on whether the first poll lands between the two calls. That file also mounts with plain render(), without StrictMode, so it never got the deterministic double invocation. THE FIX (commit 81b7823f): the payload is computed from the current committed state OUTSIDE the updater and the state is set to that value, so no updater function remains to be double-invoked. The request BODY is unchanged by construction, which is what task 7.1's strongest assertion (keyboard body deep-equals pointer body) pins -- and that assertion still passes untouched. NOTABLY this is the exact fix the page's own file header had DEFERRED, calling the shape 'an antipattern ... deliberately not fixed here' because the correction changes when the write happens relative to the state change and that commit's subject was typography and colour. That was a correct deferral; the header is now updated so it no longer tells a future reader the shape is still deliberate. NEW tests/unit/pages/riskSettingsStrictModeSingleWrite.test.jsx (5 tests) mounts under <React.StrictMode>, which is how the real app renders, making the double invocation DETERMINISTIC rather than a race; and asserts the count OUTSIDE waitFor (awaiting the write's observable settled effect first), so an extra call fails every time instead of racing a poll. It carries a positive control (two toggles must give exactly two writes, not zero and not four), a payload assertion proving the surviving write is the RIGHT one and still leaves the three unenforced guards as the server reported them (RISK-02), and a check that nothing is written on mount, since StrictMode double-invokes effects too. VERIFICATION: 5 passed alone; 24 passed with the existing kill-switch file, three runs in a row. Negative control run TWICE -- once on the first draft and again on the finalised file after adding explicit settle timeouts, specifically to prove the timeouts did not weaken detection -- failing deterministically both times with the counts above. eslint clean on both changed files (one pre-existing unused-React warning; CI's threshold is 226).
findings.verification_level: code+test; the defect was reproduced deterministically under StrictMode and the fix verified locally with a negative control run twice
findings.remaining_action: None for the defect. Two notes for whoever reads this next. (1) THE SAME SHAPE MAY EXIST ELSEWHERE: handleStrategyAllocationChange and handleSliderChange in the same file were NOT audited for impure updaters in this pass -- the slider path debounces through a ref, which changes the reasoning, and it was out of scope for a fix whose subject was the toggle. A sweep for 'side effect inside a setState updater' across the frontend would be the systemic version of this finding and is not done. (2) THE RACY ASSERTION PATTERN REMAINS in riskSettingsKillSwitch.test.jsx's soleUpdateBody helper: now that the product issues one write, it can no longer observe 2 and the flake is gone at the source, but an exact-count assertion inside a retrying waitFor is still a latent trap if a future change reintroduces a second call -- it would flake again rather than fail. Left alone deliberately rather than rewritten: that file's assertions are about request CONTENT and accessibility and are not this finding's subject, and the new file now covers cardinality deterministically. VERIFIED ONLY LOCALLY so far -- CI has not yet run this change.

findings.title: The Tauri desktop app's Rust dependency tree is scanned by nothing: there is no cargo-audit step anywhere in CI
findings.evidence: Found while reconciling GitHub's 42 open Dependabot alerts against the blocking dependency gate for DEP-01. Four of the 42 are Rust advisories in algo22-terminal/src-tauri/Cargo.lock: tauri (GHSA-7gmj-67g7-phm9, MODERATE), glib (GHSA-wrw7-89jp-8q8g, MODERATE), serde_with (GHSA-7gcf-g7xr-8hxj, MODERATE) and rand (GHSA-cq8v-f236-94qc, LOW). Read every job in 05-security.yml and 01-pr-check.yml: the gates are pip-audit (Python), npm audit (the frontend's package-lock.json), Bandit (Python SAST), and three Trivy scans (container image, terraform IaC, repository secrets). NONE of them reads Cargo.lock -- Trivy can scan Rust lockfiles but the container scan's input is the backend image, which does not contain the desktop app, and the IaC scan is scoped to terraform/. So the only thing reporting these four is Dependabot, which is advisory and blocks nothing. Severity kept at MEDIUM rather than higher: the desktop app is a separately-built Tauri artifact (07-desktop-build.yml), not part of the SaaS runtime, and the four advisories are 3 MODERATE + 1 LOW with no critical among them. But the GAP is categorical -- an entire language ecosystem in this repository has no blocking vulnerability gate, so a future CRITICAL there would also be reported by nothing that fails a build.
findings.verification_level: measured against the live Dependabot API and read from the workflow sources; not fixed
findings.remaining_action: Add a blocking cargo-audit (or `trivy fs --scanners vuln algo22-terminal/src-tauri`) step, following the same ratchet-from-a-known-baseline convention the pip-audit and IaC gates already use: an explicit, reasoned ignore list for the current four so the step starts green, and anything new fails. NOT attempted in this pass for a stated reason: adding a scanner whose behaviour cannot be exercised locally (no Rust toolchain and no cargo-audit binary in this environment) risks landing a step that either fails spuriously or passes vacuously, and the honest move is to record the gap precisely rather than ship an unverified gate. Whoever adds it should confirm the step actually reports the four known advisories before adding the ignore list, so the list is proven to be doing something.

findings.title: Browser roles held INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/TRUNCATE on ten platform-owned tables in production, including orders and execution_records
findings.evidence: Found by generalising SEC-07's check past `profiles` once that turned out to be live. SEC-07 was ONE INSTANCE of a systemic misconfiguration. scripts/check_production_privileges.py, run against production, reported 64 violations across all ten platform-owned tables checked: `anon` and `authenticated` each held INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE and TRUNCATE on profiles, fee_records, execution_records, orders, referral_wallets, referral_commissions, referral_payouts, billing_invoices, payment_methods and subscriptions. `orders` and `execution_records` are the order and execution ledgers; `anon` is the UNAUTHENTICATED role whose key ships in the public JS bundle by design. RLS limited which ROWS were visible for UPDATE/DELETE, but TRUNCATE is not subject to RLS at all, and INSERT was unconstrained for tables whose policies did not cover it. REMEDIATED in one transaction, verified before commit: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES and TRIGGER revoked from anon and authenticated on all ten; SELECT retained (RLS scopes it per caller); service_role and postgres untouched, with the transaction asserting service_role retains SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE on every table before committing. SAFE because the frontend writes exactly TWO tables through Supabase REST -- grepped every .js/.jsx under algo22-terminal/src for `.from('<table>')` and found only `waitlist` and `download_analytics`, neither a platform table. Every platform write goes through the FastAPI backend as service_role. A FIRST ATTEMPT ROLLED BACK ON ITS OWN SAFETY ASSERTION, which is worth recording: it asserted `anon` holds INSERT on `waitlist` and that is false, so the guard fired and production was left untouched. The assertion was rewritten as a measured before/after comparison rather than an assumed grant set. AFTER: the standing check reports 'no browser role holds a write privilege on any checked table', 0 violations across 10 tables, and the ECS service stayed healthy throughout (1/1 running, 0 pending).
findings.verification_level: applied and independently re-verified against production; service health confirmed
findings.remaining_action: None for the ten tables checked. NOT EXHAUSTIVE, and deliberately stated as such: the table list in scripts/check_production_privileges.py is the set judged platform-owned, not every table in the database. A full sweep of all ~94 tables for browser-role writes is the obvious follow-up and was not done -- it needs a per-table judgement about which are user-owned, which is a design decision rather than a mechanical one. Also unaddressed: RLS is enabled but NOT FORCED on profiles (relforcerowsecurity = false), so a table owner bypasses it; worth a separate decision. And the root cause is organisational, not technical -- nothing was checking production, which is what let SEC-07 sit misrecorded. Wire scripts/check_production_privileges.py into a schedule.

findings.title: Production schema diverges from repository source and has no migration ledger, so DEPLOY-04's close-out claim cannot be true as written
findings.evidence: Observed while remediating SEC-07 against the real production database. (1) `public.recorded_migrations` DOES NOT EXIST in production, so there is no in-database record of which migrations have been applied -- which makes DEPLOY-04's recorded claim that 'migrations 019 through 046 were closed out against production' unverifiable from the database itself, and inconsistent with migration 033 demonstrably not being applied (its privilege guard was absent; see SEC-07). (2) public.profiles in production has 25 columns and LACKS five that repository migrations reference: plan_limit_overrides, referred_by_user_id, role, is_admin, api_calls_limit. The first is named directly in the frontend's own pricing copy (components/landing/Pricing.jsx: 'recorded per agreement in profiles.plan_limit_overrides') and in backend entitlement logic, so an Enterprise override has nowhere to be stored in production. (3) public.download_analytics does not exist, yet src/lib/downloadAnalyticsApi.js inserts into it on every download -- that write has always failed. (4) public.waitlist exists but `anon` holds NO privileges on it and `authenticated` lacks INSERT, while src/lib/waitlistApi.js inserts as the public (anon) client -- so the public waitlist signup cannot work either. These are four independent symptoms of the same thing: the deployed database was never reconciled against repository source, and the provisioning tests that pass in CI run against a freshly provisioned schema rather than this one. *** RE-MEASURED AND RE-CHARACTERISED (Kiro, 2026-10-22). Two of the four symptoms above are WRONG and are retracted; the other two are worse than stated. *** RETRACTED -- symptom (4), the waitlist. The missing anon INSERT grant and policy are DELIBERATE, not drift. backend_app/migrations/018_copilot_and_waitlist_tables.sql -- which IS applied (production has public.waitlist with the corrected app_metadata-based admin policies and the trader_type/monthly_volume columns) -- omits the public INSERT policy under a header titled 'WHY THERE IS NO PUBLIC INSERT POLICY -- read this before adding one'. Its reason: the archived original granted `FOR INSERT TO anon, authenticated WITH CHECK (true)`, i.e. a world-writable production table, and the public signup form is UNMOUNTED, so that would be pure spam surface with no consumer. VERIFIED rather than taken on trust: algo22-terminal/src/components/waitlist/WaitlistForm.jsx is imported by NOTHING outside tests, and LandingPage.jsx's own header records its removal ('WaitlistForm.jsx and the /admin/waitlist route are untouched and remain available for a future campaign'). tests/test_schema_table_reference_drift.py fails the moment the form is re-mounted without the policy, so the two cannot drift apart. There is nothing to fix. RETRACTED -- symptom (3), download_analytics. The claim that src/lib/downloadAnalyticsApi.js 'inserts into it on every download' so 'that write has always failed' is wrong in its premise: `track()`, the only INSERT, is called from NOWHERE. components/download/DownloadPage.jsx carries an explicit comment that it deliberately does not import the module ('an artifact nobody can fetch has no download to count'), and the sole importer -- components/admin/AdminDashboard.jsx -- calls only `getStats()`, which is a SELECT. So the live break is the opposite of the one recorded: the ADMIN download-stats panel reads a relation that does not exist, and nothing has ever written to it. The table also has NO DECLARATION anywhere in the repository (no CREATE TABLE in any .sql), so it is not schema drift at all -- it is a vestigial feature referencing a table that was never designed. That needs a build-or-remove decision, not a reconciliation. I had repeated symptom (3) myself in SEC-21's work, pre-authorising `download_analytics: {INSERT}` for the anon role in scripts/check_production_privileges.py on the strength of this finding's description without checking it. Corrected in the same change as this note -- the allowlist is now empty, which is the right state, because an entry there would have pre-approved a grant nothing needs. WORSE THAN STATED -- symptom (2). It is not five missing columns on profiles. TWO WHOLE MIGRATIONS NEVER RAN, and only two of the five named columns are actually wanted. Measured against production: backend_app/migrations/017_plan_entitlements.sql is entirely absent -- profiles.billing_interval ABSENT, profiles.plan_limit_overrides ABSENT, table public.plan_usage_ledger ABSENT, constraint chk_profiles_plan_limit_overrides_object ABSENT. migrations/referral_system_redesign.sql is entirely absent too -- profiles.referral_code ABSENT, profiles.referred_by_user_id ABSENT, constraint fk_profiles_referred_by ABSENT. Seven declared objects, none of them present. AND THE ORDERING IS PROVABLY BROKEN, which is the real point: production DOES have profiles.payment_provider and profiles.next_billing_date, which core/subscription_dependencies.py records as arriving with migration 037. So 037 was applied and 017 was not. Migrations have been applied out of order and out of band, which is precisely what a ledger would have caught. OF THE FIVE COLUMNS NAMED, ONLY TWO ARE WANTED, and the finding should not have asked for the other three. `plan_limit_overrides` is real and needed: it is the contracted capacity of the custom Enterprise tier, read by SubscriptionEngine.get_effective_quotas, and its absence is silent because subscription_dependencies.py carries a column-set fallback ladder (_PROFILE_COLUMN_SETS) that retries with fewer columns when PostgREST rejects an unknown one -- so an Enterprise override simply never applies and nothing errors. `referred_by_user_id` is real and needed: routers/auth.py:233 writes it with a service-role client on referral signup, so that write currently fails (the relationship is still recorded in referral_relationships, so the column is a denormalised copy). `is_admin` and `api_calls_limit` have ZERO references anywhere in backend_app -- adding them would be adding columns nothing reads. `role` is not needed either: admin authority comes from the JWT (`app_metadata.role`, which is what routers/admin.py, the waitlist policies and the frontend's AdminGuard all read), and routers/user.py's get_profile already treats a profiles-side role as optional with the token as the source of truth. For those three the DATABASE is right and the migration is aspirational. SHARPENED -- symptom (1). `public.recorded_migrations` does not exist, but neither does any declaration of it: grepping every .sql in the repository for `recorded_migrations` returns NOTHING. So this is not drift between source and production -- the ledger DEPLOY-04 claimed to have written to was never designed. What does exist: `public.alembic_version` holds exactly one row (d97ffff9c3bb, the execution schema rebuild) and `supabase_migrations.schema_migrations` holds exactly ONE row (20261017160919), against 50+ migration files in the repository. Building a migration ledger is a design decision, not a reconciliation, and improvising a schema-tracking mechanism at the end of a session is how the next DEPLOY-04-style claim gets made. *** THE TWO NEVER-APPLIED MIGRATIONS ARE NOW APPLIED AND VERIFIED IN PRODUCTION (Kiro, 2026-10-23). *** 017_plan_entitlements.sql applied in full: profiles.billing_interval (text), profiles.plan_limit_overrides (jsonb), public.plan_usage_ledger (with its 2 indexes, RLS enabled and the pul_owner_select policy), chk_profiles_billing_interval and chk_profiles_plan_limit_overrides_object. So Enterprise/custom-tier contractual overrides finally have somewhere to be stored instead of silently never applying -- the degradation was invisible because core/subscription_dependencies.py's _PROFILE_COLUMN_SETS ladder retries the read with fewer columns when PostgREST rejects an unknown one. HOW IT WAS APPLIED, because applying a migration blind is what this finding is about. A new tool, scripts/apply_migration_to_production.py, strips only the file's own bare BEGIN;/COMMIT; so IT owns the transaction boundary, which buys a --trial mode that executes the ENTIRE migration including its own postcondition blocks and then ROLLS BACK. Both migrations were trialled first and only applied after the trial reached 'postconditions passed' and rolled back cleanly. That mattered concretely for 017: plan_usage_ledger.user_id is REFERENCES auth.users(id), and auth.users is Supabase-managed, so creating that foreign key needed REFERENCES on a table this `postgres` role might not hold it on -- a failure that would have landed part-way through DDL, which is precisely why applying migration 033 blind was declined earlier. The trial proved the grant exists before anything was committed. The tool also enforces an invariant the migration files cannot enforce themselves: it diffs the ENTIRE browser-role write surface across public before and after, and refuses to commit if it grew. SEC-20/SEC-21 closed that surface; a migration can still GRANT explicitly, so every apply re-checks it. Reported unchanged at 143 grants for both. 051_deploy05_profiles_referral_columns.sql added, trialled and applied: profiles.referral_code (varchar(20)), profiles.referred_by_user_id (uuid), fk_profiles_referred_by (REFERENCES profiles(id) ON DELETE SET NULL) and uq_profiles_referral_code. routers/auth.py:233 writes referred_by_user_id with a service-role client on referral signup and that write was failing. WHY A NEW FILE RATHER THAN RUNNING THE ONE THAT DECLARES THEM: migrations/referral_system_redesign.sql declares both columns, but it is a REDESIGN -- it also drops and recreates functions that 006_reconcile_production_database.sql declares with DIFFERENT SIGNATURES (create_referral_code_for_user RETURNS VARCHAR vs RETURNS VOID; process_referral_commission with different parameters -- its own header documents the collision). Running it whole would have replaced live function definitions as a side effect of adding two columns. The two column declarations and their constraints were reproduced verbatim and nothing else from that file was applied. DELIBERATELY NOT ADDED, as recorded earlier: profiles.role, profiles.is_admin and profiles.api_calls_limit. The latter two have zero references anywhere in backend_app, and admin authority comes from the JWT's app_metadata.role. For those three the database is right and the migration is aspirational; 051's header records that so the question is not reopened. VERIFIED AFTER COMMIT, on a fresh connection: scripts/check_production_schema_drift.py reports 'OK: every declared object in the inventory is present in production' (was 7 of 7 absent across both migrations); scripts/check_production_privileges.py still reports all blocking invariants holding, now across 82 tables rather than 81; ECS vyomquant-api-service 1/1 running, rollout COMPLETED. AN INCIDENTAL CONFIRMATION OF SEC-20: public.plan_usage_ledger is a table created TODAY, and `anon`/`authenticated` received SELECT only on it automatically. Before SEC-20 revoked the default ACL, Supabase's stock default would have granted both roles every privilege on it the moment it was created -- so the root-cause fix demonstrably held on the first new table to test it.
findings.verification_level: production: both migrations trialled with a full execute-then-rollback against the real schema and role, then applied; every object re-queried from information_schema/pg_constraint on a fresh connection afterwards; the entire browser-role write surface diffed before and after and confirmed unchanged; ECS health confirmed.
findings.remaining_action: TWO OF THE FOUR ORIGINAL SYMPTOMS WERE RETRACTED AS MISCHARACTERISED (the waitlist's missing anon INSERT is deliberate and drift-test-guarded; download_analytics has no writer and no declaration anywhere). The schema-divergence symptom is now CLOSED: both never-applied migrations are applied and independently verified. WHAT REMAINS, and it is only the first item that is really this finding: (1) THE MIGRATION LEDGER ITSELF -- still a DESIGN TASK, not a reconciliation. Nothing declares recorded_migrations anywhere in the repository; public.alembic_version holds a single revision pointer (d97ffff9c3bb) and supabase_migrations.schema_migrations holds ONE row against 50+ migration files. Decide whether to adopt the Supabase table, adopt Alembic properly, or build something -- and then backfill from EVIDENCE by probing for each migration's declared objects, which is what scripts/check_production_schema_drift.py now does. Its inventory is hand-maintained by design: a half-working SQL parser that silently missed a declaration would restore exactly the false confidence this replaces. Extend that inventory as migrations are confirmed, and it becomes the ledger. (2) download_analytics: a build-or-remove decision. The admin dashboard's download-stats panel reads a table that has never existed and that nothing writes. (3) The general lesson stands and is not fixed by applying two files: 037 was applied while 017 was not, so the deployed schema is not any prefix of the migration sequence. Until (1) exists, any future 'migrations N through M were closed out' claim is unverifiable for the same reason DEPLOY-04's was.

findings.title: Supabase default privileges granted ALL on every newly created public table to anon and authenticated -- the generator of SEC-07 and SEC-19
findings.fix_commit: applied directly to production 2026-10-22; recorded in ce3df4b
findings.evidence: Found by asking why SEC-07 and SEC-19 looked like the same defect 11 times. pg_default_acl carried, for schema public, from TWO grantors: grantor=postgres TABLES anon=arwdDxtm authenticated=arwdDxtm, and grantor=supabase_admin TABLES anon=arwdDxtm authenticated=arwdDxtm. `arwdDxtm` is every privilege (a=INSERT w=UPDATE d=DELETE D=TRUNCATE r=SELECT x=REFERENCES t=TRIGGER m=MAINTAIN). That is Supabase's stock default for the public schema, and it means every table created in public is automatically granted full write to both browser roles. So SEC-07 (profiles) and SEC-19 (ten platform tables) were not 11 separate mistakes -- they were 11 instances of one rule, and the next migration that created a table would have silently reopened the hole, undoing both fixes. This is the root cause; the earlier per-table REVOKEs treated symptoms. REMEDIATED: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE postgres IN SCHEMA public REVOKE INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, TRUNCATE, REFERENCES, TRIGGER ON TABLES FROM anon, authenticated -- applied inside the same verified transaction as SEC-21. Confirmed afterwards: the default ACL now reads anon=rm, authenticated=rm (SELECT + MAINTAIN only), service_role and postgres unchanged at arwdDxtm. Migrations run as postgres, so application tables are covered.
findings.verification_level: production (pg_default_acl re-queried on a fresh connection after commit, not inferred from absence of error)
findings.remaining_action: PARTIAL BY NECESSITY, and deliberately left visible rather than closed: the grantor=supabase_admin default ACL is NOT fixed and cannot be fixed from this role. Verified by dry-run inside a rolled-back transaction: ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES FOR ROLE supabase_admin is refused with 'permission denied to change default privileges' because current_user postgres is not a member of supabase_admin (which is a superuser; postgres here is rolcreaterole + rolbypassrls but NOT rolsuper). Its scope is objects created BY supabase_admin in public -- extensions and Supabase-managed objects, not application tables from migrations -- so the practical exposure is small, but it is real. Needs the Supabase dashboard or Supabase support. scripts/check_production_privileges.py reports it under 'NOT FIXABLE FROM THIS ROLE' on every run so it cannot be forgotten, and deliberately does not fail on it: a permanently red check is a check nobody reads, which is how SEC-07 came to sit at VERIFIED_FIXED while live.

findings.title: The unauthenticated `anon` role held writes on 60 public tables, and could TRUNCATE user exchange credentials despite RLS being enabled
findings.fix_commit: applied directly to production 2026-10-22; recorded in ce3df4b
findings.evidence: Found by sweeping all 82 tables in public instead of SEC-19's curated list of ten. 60 of 82 carried browser-role write grants. RLS was enabled on all 60, which is why this was not a second SEC-19: for INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE the policies did constrain the caller, and that was verified rather than assumed -- acting as a real user with 27 own strategies, UPDATE and DELETE against OTHER users' rows in public.strategies both affected 0 rows, SELECT returned 27 of 187, and anon SELECT returned 0 of 187 and 0 of 2 exchange_keys. Tenant isolation holds. (An earlier probe of mine reported those cross-tenant writes as 'PERMITTED' and was WRONG: it treated 'no exception raised' as success, but RLS filters rows rather than raising, so an UPDATE matching nothing succeeds affecting zero rows. Re-run with rowcount, the finding retracted itself.) THE REAL DEFECT IS TRUNCATE. PostgreSQL has no TRUNCATE row-security policy command, so RLS cannot filter it -- a role holding TRUNCATE empties the whole table regardless of policy. Measured in production inside rolled-back transactions, counting as `postgres` (rolbypassrls) on both sides of an `anon` TRUNCATE so the counts were not themselves RLS-filtered: anon emptied public.exchange_keys (2 rows of USER EXCHANGE API CREDENTIALS), public.alembic_version (1), public.risk_settings (1), public.referral_profiles (2), public.notification_settings (1) and public.ticket_comments (2). public.strategies (187 rows) was spared only by an incidental foreign-key constraint, not by any security control. `anon` is the UNAUTHENTICATED role whose key ships in the public JS bundle by design. EXPLOITABILITY, STATED HONESTLY: not reachable through the public API today. PostgREST exposes no TRUNCATE verb, and 0 of the 33 anon-executable functions in public contain a TRUNCATE (checked via pg_get_functiondef). So this was a latent hole, not an exploited one -- recorded P1 rather than P0 for that reason. It was fixed anyway because 'no route happens to exist' is not a control. REMEDIATED in one transaction that committed only after 14 postflight assertions passed: INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE revoked from `anon` on all 82 tables; TRUNCATE, REFERENCES and TRIGGER revoked from BOTH browser roles on all 82. SELECT retained (RLS scopes it per caller; removing it breaks the UI). service_role untouched -- asserted by diffing its full 82-entry grant matrix before and after. Zero functional risk established first: no application code issues TRUNCATE (grep of backend_app finds only the word in a comment about float indexes), and REFERENCES/TRIGGER are schema-modification rights no API client needs. Also dropped public.__probe_xyz, a 1-column/0-row/0-byte probe artefact with no inbound foreign keys left in production, DDL captured first.
findings.verification_level: production (exploit reproduced against the real database in a rolled-back transaction, then re-attempted after the fix and refused; all grants re-queried on a fresh connection; ECS health confirmed after)
findings.remaining_action: None for anon or for TRUNCATE/REFERENCES/TRIGGER -- those invariants are now enforced by scripts/check_production_privileges.py, which exits non-zero on drift. The remaining `authenticated` write surface is tracked separately as SEC-22.

findings.title: `authenticated` retains write grants on ~51 backend-owned tables beyond any known application need (least-privilege backlog)
findings.evidence: After SEC-21, `authenticated` still holds 106 write grants across 51 tables that no identified code path writes -- transaction_records/checkpoints/rollbacks, the paper_* family, library_*/marketplace_*, referral_profiles, strategy_limits, positions, fills, security_logs, risk_settings_audit, idempotency_keys, alembic_version, dag_tasks and others. NOT A BLOCKING FINDING, and not an open door: every one of these tables has RLS enabled with per-user policies, and after SEC-21 `anon` holds no write at all, so reaching any of them requires a valid signed-in JWT and confines the caller to their own rows. It is a defence-in-depth gap. DELIBERATELY NOT SWEPT, and this is the substance of the finding: the backend reaches PostgREST through two clients that map to two different database roles -- the anon key plus the end user's JWT (role `authenticated`) and the service-role key (role `service_role`) -- and revoking `authenticated` writes on a table the first kind writes takes a production feature OFFLINE. Deriving that inventory from source proved unreliable three times running, because the routers wrap the two client factories in local helpers (_sb, _get_supabase, _client) so the call sites do not grep as factory names. Two full passes over the backend produced a list missing `strategies` DELETE (backend/strategy_service.py:2502 -- strategy deletion, reached from the UI), `strategy_backtests` (backend/backtest_service.py:776), `training_jobs` and `training_governance_decisions` (backend/training_status.py:573) and `model_versions` (backend/model_versioning.py:1963). Each omission, had it driven a REVOKE, would have broken a working feature. A blanket sweep would additionally have taken out strategy create/rename/edit/clone/archive/pause/resume/stop, all strategy version persistence, risk-settings saves, notifications, support tickets, profile editing and exchange-key deletion.
findings.verification_level: observed directly against production (read-only) and cross-checked against backend source; not fixed, by decision
findings.remaining_action: Drain it one table at a time, each revoke paired with that feature's integration test, then enable the ratchet: `python scripts/check_production_privileges.py --strict` already fails on this backlog and is the gate to turn on once it is empty. The 16-table path-(A) allowlist in that script, with the writing call site recorded against each entry, is the working document. Do not sweep.

findings.title: User-supplied max_daily_loss and max_positions are enforced with no server-side ceiling, so a user can disable their own circuit breakers
findings.evidence: Found while assessing whether `authenticated` UPDATE on public.risk_settings was a privilege-escalation path. It is NOT a privilege finding -- the same values are settable through the legitimate UI (PUT /api/risk/settings -> routers/risk.py:227 upsert), so writing them directly via PostgREST gains a user nothing they cannot already do. The actual defect is the missing clamp. core/risk_manager.py:111 _load_user_risk_settings reads the row with the SERVICE-ROLE key, explicitly bypassing RLS (its own docstring says so), and validate_trade_request at :556 assigns the values straight into the order-time circuit breakers: effective_max_daily_loss and effective_max_positions are used as-is, with no min(), no tier cross-check and no ceiling, overriding the hardcoded RiskThresholds defaults (max_daily_loss_pct=0.05, max_open_trades=5) that then gate the order via REJECT_DAILY_LOSS and REJECT_MAX_OPEN_TRADES. A user who sets max_daily_loss to 1e12 and max_positions to 99999 makes both breakers unreachable. The asymmetry is what makes this a defect rather than a design choice: max_leverage in the same struct IS clamped, at risk_manager.py:~646, via min(self.thresholds.drawdown_tier_1_max_leverage, effective_max_leverage), so writing max_leverage=1000 yields at most 10.0. The clamping is incomplete, not absent. The same values also feed the paper engine (backend/paper_trading_service.py:1344-1390) through the in-memory store that routers/risk.py:165 populates from this table. Separately noted: risk_settings.max_position_size_usd and daily_loss_limit_pct are read by NO backend code at all -- a grep across backend_app returns zero hits for either -- so two of the limits the UI presents are not enforced anywhere.
findings.verification_level: code (enforcement path read end to end) + production (the write confirmed to change 1 row as a signed-in user, in a rolled-back transaction); not fixed
findings.remaining_action: Clamp max_daily_loss and max_positions against the account's plan tier the way max_leverage already is, in validate_trade_request, and reject or clamp out-of-range values at the API boundary in routers/risk.py rather than only at order time. Then decide whether max_position_size_usd and daily_loss_limit_pct should be enforced or removed from the UI -- presenting a limit that nothing reads is worse than not offering it. Gated behind live trading being OFF, so not launch-blocking on its own.

findings.title: CVE-2026-114603 in opentelemetry-api failed the blocking pip-audit gate; the eleven opentelemetry packages were unused and are removed
findings.evidence: Surfaced on a real CI run (39845453588, job 120057408416): pip-audit reported 'Found 1 known vulnerability' -- opentelemetry-api 1.25.0, CVE-2026-114603, fix 1.45.1. NOT caused by the change under test; main's own 05 Security run on 0bb637e2 passed this job about two hours earlier. pip-audit queries live advisory data, so an unchanged manifest flips from pass to fail when an advisory is published -- main was latently red too. Advisory detail from OSV: GHSA-xcq7-p3pf-p88h, 'OpenTelemetry Python: Unbounded tracestate parsing in opentelemetry-api', CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:L -- availability only, no confidentiality or integrity impact. All versions below 1.45.1 affected. NOT REACHABLE IN THIS APPLICATION, established before deciding what to do. Only two files under backend_app import opentelemetry at all (backend/observability/opentelemetry_tracing.py and optimized_tracing.py), and an AST walk of every .py in backend_app found ZERO unguarded imports -- both sit inside try/except ImportError setting OPENTELEMETRY_AVAILABLE=False. Neither module's TracingManager is ever constructed: grepping main.py, core/, routers/ and api_ws/ for TracingManager / initialize_tracing / optimized_tracing / get_tracing_manager returns nothing, so FastAPIInstrumentor().instrument() is never called and no global text-map propagator is installed. With no instrumentation and no propagator, nothing parses an inbound tracestate header, which is the vulnerable path. REMOVED RATHER THAN UPGRADED, because upgrading is not possible here: opentelemetry-proto 1.45.1 requires protobuf>=5.0,<8.0 while tensorflow==2.16.1 requires protobuf!=4.21.0-4.21.5,<5.0.0dev,>=3.20.3 -- a direct conflict, and escaping it by upgrading tensorflow was already attempted and reverted under DEP-02. The old pin had the mirror-image problem: opentelemetry-proto 1.25.0's protobuf<5.0 ceiling is DEP-02's recorded blocker, so removing it clears that constraint instead of entrenching it. SAFETY VERIFIED BY EXECUTION, not by reading the guard: a sys.meta_path finder was installed to make every `opentelemetry*` import raise ModuleNotFoundError, reproducing the uninstalled state. Both modules then imported successfully with OPENTELEMETRY_AVAILABLE=False, TracingManager constructed without raising, get_tracer() returned a NoOpTracer, and NoOpTracer.start_as_current_span worked as a context manager whose span accepts set_attribute/is_recording. TRANSITIVE CHECK: every name==version pin across requirements-base.txt, requirements.txt and requirements-cpu.txt was resolved against PyPI metadata; no remaining package ACTIVELY requires opentelemetry, so removing the explicit pins removes the packages outright rather than leaving them to be resolved transitively at an unpinned version. sentry-sdk==2.11.0 does declare 48 opentelemetry requirements, but every one is gated behind extra == 'opentelemetry' or 'opentelemetry-experimental', and the manifest pins sentry-sdk[fastapi] -- so they are inert. (A first version of that check ignored extras markers and reported sentry-sdk as a blocker; it was wrong and was corrected to evaluate the markers.) VERIFIED ON A REAL CI RUN: PR #64 went green on all 14 checks, including the job that raised this -- 'Blocking Dependency Vulnerability Audit (pip-audit + npm audit)' SUCCESS -- plus Database Tests (PostgreSQL), Unit & Integration Tests, Execution Tests (production posture), Docker Build Validation and Provisioning, Privilege Hardening & Tenant Isolation, so the removal broke no test lane. Merged to main as 97dae06. One follow-up surfaced during that run and is part of this fix: the repository's OWN guard, scripts/dependency_audit.py, then failed with 'imported but not declared: opentelemetry' -- correctly, since the pins were gone while the two guarded import sites remained. Resolved using the mechanism that script already carries for this case, OPTIONAL_DEPENDENCIES (filtered at line 227, already holding torch for the same class of reason), with a comment requiring the entry be removed at the same time as any future re-add so the audit goes back to demanding the pins.
findings.verification_level: root-caused against a real GitHub Actions job log; non-reachability established by AST analysis plus a grep of every wiring site; removability proven by executing the degraded path with the package blocked at import; transitive impact checked against PyPI metadata for all 54 pins; cleared on a real CI run (PR #64, 14/14 green) and merged
findings.remaining_action: None for the CVE. Two notes for later: (1) if tracing is ever wanted, re-add opentelemetry-api/sdk at >=1.45.1 AND the instrumentation packages at >=0.66b1 (the two version tracks move in lockstep) TOGETHER with a tensorflow release whose protobuf floor is >=5.0 -- they cannot move independently -- remove the OPTIONAL_DEPENDENCIES entry from scripts/dependency_audit.py, and actually wire TracingManager into main.py's lifespan, which has never been done. (2) DEP-02 should be revisited: opentelemetry-proto's protobuf<5.0 ceiling was its recorded blocker and that package is now gone, so the protobuf/tensorflow upgrade it reverted may now be reachable.

findings.title: The observability readiness check resolved PyPI distribution names through __import__, so three of its four dependency checks could never pass
findings.evidence: Found while removing the opentelemetry pins for DEP-04. backend/observability/validation_checklist.py::_check_dependencies_installed held dependencies = ['prometheus-client', 'opentelemetry-api', 'opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-grpc', 'psutil'] and resolved each with __import__(dep). Those are DISTRIBUTION names, and a hyphen is not legal in a Python module name, so the call raises ModuleNotFoundError even when the package is installed and working. Measured in an environment where all four were installed: prometheus-client, opentelemetry-api and opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-grpc each reported ImportError; only psutil succeeded, and only because its distribution name and module name are identical. So the check reported success=False with three missing dependencies on every run, in every environment, since it was written -- it could not distinguish a broken deployment from a healthy one, which is the whole purpose of a readiness check. FIXED by querying importlib.metadata.version(), which is keyed by distribution name, instead of the import system, which is keyed by module name; the result now also reports the resolved versions. The two opentelemetry entries were dropped from the required list because DEP-04 removes those packages deliberately -- requiring them here would assert the opposite of the manifest.
findings.verification_level: code+test (the failure reproduced directly against an environment where all four packages were installed, and the fix confirmed to resolve prometheus-client 0.20.0 and psutil 6.0.0)

findings.title: The whole-window outlier rejection makes Requirement 19.11's >=10,000-bar correctness floor unreachable at any threshold, so no market-data source can ever be admitted
findings.evidence: MEASURED AGAINST LIVE BINANCE DATA (12,000 real BTC/USDT 1m bars, 11,999 log-returns, fetched 2026-10-23). This is the recalibration `market_data_validation.Z_SCORE_THRESHOLD_DEFAULT`'s own comment says is still owed: it concedes the 5.0 default is 'a principled default, not a result of fitting real market data, which this sandbox has none of'. HOW IT WAS FOUND: not by reading the code. RT-04's operator tool was run with a 60-second window as a smoke test before starting a multi-day one, and Candidate B came back NOT_MEASURED with 'DATA_QUALITY: ... Found 1 outliers in close log-returns using z_score for UNKNOWN. Dataset rejected - no synthetic data allowed.' The exchange was reachable and healthy (4,697 markets loaded; a direct klines fetch returns bars normally) -- the platform's own validator refused real exchange data. (1) THE NORMAL MODEL THE DEFAULT RESTS ON IS WRONG BY ORDERS OF MAGNITUDE. The comment computes per-point P(|Z|>5) ~ 5.7e-7. Measured on real data the rate is 3.667e-3 -- understated 6,396x. Crypto log-returns are fat-tailed; the observed max |z| was 12.13, and 44 of 11,999 returns exceeded 5 sigma. Measured understatement at other thresholds: 4.0 by 99x, 6.0 by ~1.0e6x, 8.0 by ~6.0e11x. (2) BUT RECALIBRATING THE THRESHOLD CANNOT FIX IT, AND THAT IS THE ACTUAL FINDING. `OutlierDetector._z_score_filter` raises on `outliers.any()` -- the ENTIRE window is rejected if ANY single bar exceeds. So the quantity that matters is per-WINDOW, not per-point: P(reject) = 1 - (1-p)^n, which tends to 1 as n grows for any p > 0. Measured by sliding over the real series, the share of windows rejected at the 10,000-bar size Requirement 19.11 demands is 100% at every threshold tested from 3.0 through 10.0, and still 50% at 12.0 -- a threshold above the largest z-score present in the sample. Smaller windows degrade gracefully (500 bars: 46.5% rejected at 5.0; 900 bars: 69.4%), which is why this never surfaced in shorter-horizon use. THE WHOLE-WINDOW REJECTION RULE AND THE >=10,000-BAR FLOOR ARE THEREFORE INCOMPATIBLE BY CONSTRUCTION. No value of MARKET_DATA_Z_SCORE_THRESHOLD makes RT-04 measurable. The codebase already half-knew this and recorded it as a tolerated strictness rather than an impossibility: `backend/training_worker.py:118` states '`_z_score_filter` REJECTS a window containing any close beyond 3 sigma, and a real multi-thousand-bar market series is near-certain to contain one. That component is REUSED AS-IS and its threshold is not relaxed', and `routers/strategy_operations.py:5882` records mapping it to a classified DATA_QUALITY block 'rather than loosening the threshold'. Both describe the symptom accurately. Neither connects it to Requirement 19.11's floor, which it makes unsatisfiable -- so RT-04 was recorded as needing a week of wall-clock measurement when in fact the measurement cannot succeed at all. Measurement script: kiro-session-artifacts/measure_zscore_reality.py (read-only; fetches live klines, computes the platform's own log-return z-scores, and reports per-point exceedance against the normal model plus per-window rejection rates by sliding over the real series). ||| RESOLVED AS A+C ON THE OWNER'S DECISION (Kiro). A+C is the only coherent pair, and this entry already said so: (C) alone leaves P(reject) -> 1, so it helps only combined with (A). Option (B) -- keep whole-window rejection and restate Requirement 19.11's floor -- was NOT taken: the floor is a correctness requirement, and weakening it to accommodate a detector defect would have made the requirement describe the bug. (A) OutlierPolicy.FLAG_AND_ADMIT, now the default. Detection and response were fused -- every detector raised on the first exceedance -- so 'this window contains an extreme bar' and 'this window is unusable' were one statement, and the quantity deciding admission was per-WINDOW rather than per-point. Now: flag the extreme bars, report how many, admit the window AS OBSERVED, refuse only when the flagged FRACTION exceeds max_outlier_fraction. The guarantee becomes BOUNDED contamination instead of ZERO contamination, which is a promise real market data can keep. (C) OutlierMethod.ROBUST_Z_SCORE, now the default: median/MAD, not mean/std. This is a CORRECTNESS fix rather than a threshold tweak, and the measurement is the argument. std / (1.4826*MAD) = 1.49 (BTC), 1.38 (ETH), 1.46 (DOGE) over 12,000 live 1m bars each -- so a few extreme returns inflate the scale and thereby DEFLATE every ordinary point's z-score, the textbook masking effect. max|robust z| (15.60/15.57/14.99) EXCEEDS max|classic z| (10.47/11.31/10.27): the classic rule was hiding its own most extreme points, because stats.zscore divides by a quantity computed from the very points it is judging. NO BAR IS MODIFIED, EXCLUDED OR WINSORISED, and the measurement is why: what this rule calls an 'outlier' in real crypto data is overwhelmingly an ORDINARY LARGE MOVE, so the bar is the venue's own true observation and replacing it would be the fabrication. Winsorising a close manufactures a price that never traded, which this module forbids everywhere else (_synthetic_fill, GapHandler's refusal). Excluding the bar would punch a hole GapHandler then refuses on the next step -- trading one unsatisfiable gate for another. TWO GUARDS, NOT ONE, which is what reconciles this with DATA-02. A fraction budget cannot catch a single bad tick: one corrupt bar in 10,000 is 0.01% contamination, far inside any usable budget, and DATA-02 requires that a genuine single-bar spike still rejects the window. So the budget answers 'are there too many extreme points?' (fat tails, ordinary) and a new MAGNITUDE CEILING answers 'is any single point impossible?' (bad ticks, never ordinary). The pre-DATA-03 rule had ONE threshold for both, which is exactly why it could not catch the second without rejecting all real data for the first; DATA-02's own spike fixtures pass unchanged against the new default as a result. The ceiling is an ABSOLUTE single-bar log-return bound, not a robust-z multiple, because a robust-z ceiling moves with the window's own dispersion -- a quiet market shrinks MAD and an ordinary move would breach it, the same self-referential defect that made the classic z-score wrong. Price columns only; volume routinely doubles. CONSTANTS FITTED, NOT ASSERTED -- the recalibration Z_SCORE_THRESHOLD_DEFAULT's own comment conceded was owed -- reproducible via `scripts/measure_market_data_outlier_reality.py --robust`, which this change added: robust-z 5.0 -> per-point 8.5e-3..1.1e-2, worst 10,000-bar contamination 1.07%; 8.0 -> 2.3e-3..3.0e-3, 0.35%; 10.0 -> 1.2e-3..1.4e-3, 0.16% (CHOSEN); 12.0 -> 5.0e-4..6.7e-4, 0.07%; 20.0 -> 0, 0.00%. 10.0 is where the rule still DETECTS something real (~1 bar in 850) while the worst case sits ~6x inside the 1% budget; a higher threshold trends towards the classic rule's own failure mode at 12.0, where it passed every window only because 12.0 exceeded the largest z-score present -- a detector that detects nothing is not a safety control. The ceiling, log(2) = 0.6931 (2.00x), sits 82x above the largest real single-bar move measured (0.0048..0.0084) and 5.6x below DATA-02's smallest spike fixture (3.9116; the sine-pool fixture is 7.0457). ACCEPTANCE, against the LIVE venue through the REAL validator (MarketDataValidator.validate, not a reimplementation): all three instruments ADMITTED at 12,000 bars, quality score 95.0 EXCELLENT, 12000 bars in and 12000 out (unmodified), contamination 0.117%/0.142%/0.125%. The SAME bars under the legacy policy: REFUSED, all three. With a 0% budget: REFUSED, so the budget is enforced rather than decorative. REQUIREMENT 19.11's >=10,000-BAR FLOOR IS NOW SATISFIABLE ON REAL DATA. Also fixed in passing: DataQualityReport.outliers_detected counted ISSUE RECORDS, not outliers (`sum(1 for i in issues ...)`), so a field named for a count of outliers could only ever report 0 or 1 per column. NEGATIVE CONTROL, behavioural, against HEAD's own detector: a 10,000-bar fat-tailed window is REFUSED at HEAD ('Found 38 outliers') and ADMITTED with the fix, while the 50x spike is refused BOTH ways -- so the fix flips the defect and preserves DATA-02's requirement. At HEAD the two cases were indistinguishable in the logs (both 'Found N outliers'); they now carry different messages. Regression: 19 new tests (tests/test_data03_outlier_policy_and_robust_scale.py); 302 passed across the five affected suites; 4375 passed / 135 skipped across the whole market-data/validation/paper/training/feed/contract/indicator/backtest selection. The 5 pre-existing errors in test_route_contract.py's Wave-4 class are identical at HEAD. ||| OPEN ON PR #85, NOT MERGED, AND NOT CLAIMED AS PASSING CI. The 'Unit & Integration Tests' job fails on that branch with exactly one failure, tests/property/test_protected_logic_containment.py::test_trace_and_export_surfaces_contain_no_protected_logic, while the same job SUCCEEDS on main (run 39987240090, commit ac11d030) -- so it is this branch, not flake: reproduced on a re-run of the identical commit. Everything else on the PR is green except 'Provisioning, Privilege Hardening & Tenant Isolation', which fails identically on main and is pre-existing. WHAT IS KNOWN. The reported error is NOT an assertion from the test: it is `ValueError: 48 is not in list` raised inside Hypothesis itself, at `internal/intervalsets.py:107` via `index_from_char_in_shrink_order` (48 is ord('0')), reached from `engine.shrink_interesting_test_cases` -> `greedy_shrink` -> `minimize_individual_choices`. Two consequences: (1) Hypothesis DID find a failing example -- shrinking only runs on an interesting case -- and (2) the shrinker's own crash MASKS whatever that example asserted, so the actual defect is still unseen. The crash signature is a library bug class: the collection shrinker's `short_circuit` tries `[zero] * min_size` for a text draw whose alphabet does not contain the zero character. WHAT WAS RULED OUT. Not reproducible locally: 5 consecutive whole-file runs, 3 explicit --hypothesis-seed values, then a 24-seed sweep with the shrink phase disabled -- all passed. Local Python is 3.12.10; CI is 3.11.17, with hypothesis pinned to the SAME 6.165.10 in both, so a version skew is excluded and the difference is the interpreter or the environment. A first hypothesis -- that the new autouse `_no_on_demand_venue_quotes` guard in tests/conftest.py was function-scoped and therefore wrapped every Hypothesis `@given` test -- was WRONG: it was changed to session scope (commit 49f29660, which is better engineering regardless: one substitution instead of fifteen thousand) and CI failed again identically. A temporary no-shrink profile was pushed to make CI print the real assertion; GitHub Actions never scheduled a run for that commit, so it yielded nothing and was reverted rather than left in. WHY A CAUSAL LINK TO THIS SESSION'S CHANGES IS NOT ESTABLISHED. The failing test exercises `strategy_operations.preview_node` and `compare_versions` for a NON-OWNER, NON-ENTITLED caller, whose authorisation refusal is reached before any market-data work; `_preview_data_quality` is called at strategy_operations.py:5030, downstream of that refusal. Neither the outlier policy nor the paper price path is reachable there. The likelier mechanism is indirect: two new test modules change collection, which changes Hypothesis's example stream, which surfaces a LATENT counterexample main's stream happened to miss. That is a hypothesis, NOT a measurement, and it is recorded as such. NEXT STEP, cheapest first: get the real assertion rather than the shrinker's crash -- either run that one test under Python 3.11 locally, or land a no-shrink profile that CI actually schedules, then read the falsifying example. Do not merge #85 until the underlying failure is identified; a protected-logic containment property (Requirements 1.19, 2.19) is not something to merge past on the assumption that it is noise.
findings.verification_level: Measured against the live venue through the real validator, test-pinned, with a behavioural negative control against HEAD. NOT production_verified: the running image predates these constants, so production still evaluates windows with whole-window rejection until it is rebuilt. Note this does NOT hold paper sessions shut -- the per-candle feed path (paper_market_feed._validate_candle) deliberately runs only the structural and candle-integrity validators, never OutlierDetector, so the outlier rule governs WINDOW validation (validated_window, training, backtest) rather than a live session's bar-by-bar ingest.
findings.remaining_action: Deploy, so production's window validation matches the measured policy. Until the image is rebuilt, re-running the RT-04 measurement harness against the DEPLOYED image would refuse again for the original reason, even though the measurement already recorded is valid evidence about the venue data and the current validator.

findings.title: Every stored exchange credential is encrypted under a master key that no longer exists, so all of them are permanently unreadable
findings.evidence: Found 2026-10-23 by the safety guard in scripts/rotate_master_encryption_keys.py --plan, which refuses to rotate when ciphertext decrypts under no available key. MEASURED AGAINST PRODUCTION: exchange_keys holds 2 rows (users d97d59c5.../85f4b896..., both exchange_id='binance', created 2026-06-21T09:00:44Z and 2026-06-21T09:18:01Z) carrying 4 non-NULL ciphertext values across encrypted_api_key/encrypted_secret_key (encrypted_password is NULL on both). ALL 4 ARE GENUINE FERNET TOKENS -- they are valid urlsafe-base64, 100 and 120 characters, and begin 'gAAAAAB' with version byte 128, which is Fernet's own format. So this is not placeholder or garbage data; a real key really did encrypt them. NONE OF THEM DECRYPT. Tested against: (1) the current MASTER_ENCRYPTION_KEYS as the MultiFernet api_key_vault.py:96-99 builds -- 0/4; (2) the PBKDF2(master key, CREDENTIAL_VAULT_SALT) derivation core/credential_vault.py:285 uses, in case the rows were written by that vault instead -- 0/4; (3) EVERY Fernet-shaped key recoverable from the entire git history -- 265 structurally valid candidates harvested by regex from `git log --all -p`, each tried against all 4 values -- 0 hits. The key that encrypted these rows exists in neither Secrets Manager nor git history, so the credentials are unrecoverable rather than merely misplaced. WHAT THIS MEANS OPERATIONALLY: api_key_vault._decrypt raises ValueError('Decryption failed. Key rotation issue or corrupted data.') on InvalidToken, so any attempt to use these credentials already fails -- these two users cannot trade live and could not have at any point since the key was lost. It is masked today only because live trading is hard-gated off by RT-15, so nothing exercises the path. THE ONE PIECE OF GOOD NEWS, and it materially narrows SEC-01: because no key in public git history opens these values, the leaked master_encryption_keys exposes NO customer exchange credential. That part of SEC-01 is a much smaller exposure than its CRITICAL classification implied, and the correction is recorded in SEC-01 as well.
findings.remaining_action: TWO SEPARATE THINGS, AND THE SECOND IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS FOR LAUNCH. (1) THE TWO AFFECTED USERS must re-enter their exchange API keys; nothing else can recover them. Their existing rows should be deleted or flagged rather than left to raise, because the current failure mode is an exception from _decrypt at use time rather than a clear 'reconnect your exchange' state the UI can act on. Decide whether to delete the rows (simplest, and they carry no recoverable value) or add an explicit unreadable/needs-reconnect state. Note both rows predate much of this effort (2026-06-21) and may well be the owner's own test accounts -- worth confirming before contacting anyone. (2) THE CAUSE IS UNDIAGNOSED AND THAT IS THE REAL RISK. A master key was replaced without re-encrypting what it protected, and nothing detected it -- not a health check, not a test, not an alarm. With live trading off and 2 rows affected the cost was nil; the identical event after launch, with real customers holding funded exchange connections, silently breaks every one of them. REQUIRED: a startup or health check that samples exchange_keys and asserts the configured key set can decrypt it, so a key swap fails loudly and immediately instead of at first use; and a documented rotation procedure, which scripts/rotate_master_encryption_keys.py now implements and enforces the ordering of (prepend -> redeploy -> reencrypt -> verify -> retire, refusing to retire while any value still needs the old key). WORTH CHECKING SEPARATELY: whether the lost key is recoverable from anywhere outside this repository and this AWS account -- an old .env on a developer machine, a terminated task definition revision, a CI log, or a previous Secrets Manager version beyond the two currently retained. AWSPREVIOUS on master_encryption_keys was not examined for this and should be.
